Alfonso X of Castile patronised scholars of many backgrounds, including Jews, but the legal code compiled in his reign, the Siete Partidas, imposed restrictions on Jews, among them distinguishing clothing and residential segregation. In the summer of 1391 anti-Jewish riots began in Seville and spread across Castile and Aragon. Jewish quarters were looted, synagogues destroyed, thousands killed and thousands more forcibly baptised, and the Jewish communities of Valencia and Barcelona were wiped out.

On 31 March 1492 the Catholic Monarchs issued the Alhambra Decree, ordering practising Jews out of Castile and Aragon by 31 July, and King Manuel I of Portugal issued a similar edict. Over 200,000 Jews converted to Catholicism, and between 40,000 and 100,000 were expelled. Many found refuge in the Ottoman Empire, where Istanbul's Jewish population grew to around 40,000 between 1477 and 1535 and Thessaloniki's, nonexistent in 1478, to over 16,500 by 1519. Others settled in North Africa, in Italian ports such as Venice and Livorno, and in Amsterdam. Many conversos stayed in Iberia, some secretly keeping Jewish practices; they were investigated by the Spanish Inquisition and by the Portuguese Inquisition, established in 1536.

Sephardic Jews spoke variants of Spanish, Catalan or Portuguese. Ladino or Judaeo-Spanish, also called Judezmo, derives from Old Spanish and Old Portuguese, with additions from Hebrew and local languages, and was often written in Rashi script. In North Africa the variety known as Haketia took on Arabic influences. Wherever Sephardim settled they founded schools that used Spanish. They are commonly divided into Eastern Sephardim in the Ottoman lands, North African Sephardim, and Western Sephardim, descendants of conversos, who in the 17th century were prominent in Amsterdam. They reached England in the mid-17th century.
septimius-severus: Lucius Septimius Severus was born on 11 April 145 at Leptis Magna, the son of Publius Septimius Geta and Fulvia Pia, in a wealthy family of equestrian rank. His father's family was of Libyan-Punic origin and his mother's descended from the Italian Fulvii, so he is considered the first emperor born into a provincial family of non-Italian origin.

He grew up speaking Punic, and was educated in Latin and Greek, which he spoke with a slight accent. Around 162 he sought a career in Rome, where Marcus Aurelius admitted him to the senatorial order. He married Paccia Marciana about 175 and, after her death, Julia Domna in 187. They had two sons, Caracalla and Geta.

In 191 the emperor Commodus appointed Severus governor of Pannonia Superior. After the murder of Pertinax in early 193 his legion XIV Gemina acclaimed him emperor at Carnuntum on 9 April. He marched on Italy, where Didius Julianus, who had bought the throne at an auction, was condemned by the Senate and killed. Severus dismissed the Praetorian Guard that had murdered Pertinax and replaced it with veterans of his Danubian legions. He defeated the rival claimant Pescennius Niger at the Battle of Issus in 194, and Clodius Albinus, the governor of Britannia, at the Battle of Lugdunum on 19 February 197. He then had 29 senators executed for supporting Albinus.

Severus sacked the Parthian capital Ctesiphon and annexed the northern half of Mesopotamia, though he failed twice to take the fortress of Hatra. He also expanded the Limes Arabicus. In 202 he campaigned in Africa and Mauretania against the Garamantes, capturing their capital Garama and extending the Limes Tripolitanus along the southern desert frontier. He raised the number of legions from 30 to 33 and raised the soldiers' pay from 300 to 400 denarii a year. He was the first emperor to station part of the imperial army in Italy. His relations with the Senate were poor, and Cassius Dio records that executions of senators continued.

Severus travelled to Britain in 208 and strengthened Hadrian's Wall. In 209 he invaded Caledonia with an army of 50,000 men, but he died of an infectious disease in early 211 at Eboracum, now York. His sons Caracalla and Geta, advised by Julia Domna, succeeded him. They founded the Severan dynasty, the last dynasty of the Roman Empire before the Crisis of the Third Century. The Arch of Septimius Severus in Rome commemorates his victory over the Parthians.
septuagint: Biblical scholars agree that the first five books of the Hebrew Bible were translated into Koine Greek by Jews living in the Ptolemaic Kingdom, probably in or around Alexandria, and can be dated with confidence to the mid- or late 3rd century BCE. The remaining books were presumably translated in the 2nd century BCE. Few people could read Hebrew in the Second Temple period, and Koine Greek and Aramaic were the lingua francas of the Jewish community, so the translation met a need.

According to tradition, Ptolemy II Philadelphus sent seventy-two translators, six from each of the Twelve Tribes, from Jerusalem to Alexandria to translate the Torah for the Library of Alexandria. The story is told in the Letter of Aristeas to his brother Philocrates, which some scholars regard as pseudepigraphical, and was repeated by Philo, Josephus and the Babylonian Talmud.

The name derives from the Latin phrase for the version of the seventy translators, and it was not until Augustine of Hippo that the Greek translation was called Septuaginta. The Greek text was produced within Hellenistic Judaism and completed by 132 BCE, though it continued to be revised in Jewish and Christian communities through the fourth century CE.

The Septuagint is not a single unified corpus but a collection of ancient translations of the Tanakh along with other Jewish texts now called apocrypha. The canon of the Hebrew Bible was still evolving while it was written, and the books were translated by different people, in different places and for different purposes, in styles that range from literal to paraphrase. Samuel and Kings form one four-part book, Of Reigns, and Chronicles is titled Of Things Left Out. Books found in it but not in the Hebrew Bible include Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, the additions to Daniel and Esther, and 1 to 4 Maccabees.

Most Jews abandoned it around the 2nd century. The earliest gentile Christians had used it out of necessity, since it was the only Greek Bible and most could not read Hebrew, and its association with a rival religion may have made it suspect. Differences between it and the contemporary Hebrew scriptures were also discovered, and Greek-speaking Jews tended to prefer other versions, such as that of Aquila. The New Testament writers freely used the Greek translation when citing the scriptures. It formed the basis of the Old Latin versions and of the Old Church Slavonic, Armenian, Georgian and Coptic versions of the Old Testament. Origen's Hexapla produced the first major Christian recension.
serapis: Serapis, or Sarapis, derives from the worship of the Egyptian god Osiris and the bull Apis as a single deity, called in Demotic wsjr-ḥp, Osiris-Apis. Ptolemy I Soter promoted the cult in the third century BCE as a means to unify the Greek and Egyptian subjects of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, and later Ptolemaic kings continued it as a matter of deliberate policy. There is evidence that the cult existed before the Ptolemies came to power in Alexandria: Plutarch and Arrian mention a temple of Serapis in Egypt in 323 BCE.

According to Plutarch, Ptolemy took the cult statue from Sinope in Asia Minor after a dream in which an unknown god told him to bring it to Alexandria, where two religious experts declared it to be Serapis. One was of the Eumolpidae, the family that supplied the hierophant of the Eleusinian Mysteries, and the other was the Egyptian priest Manetho.

The Greeks had little respect for animal-headed figures, so a Greek-style human statue was chosen and proclaimed the equivalent of the popular Apis. Serapis was shown as a Greek god with Egyptian trappings. The statue Ptolemy erected in Alexandria resembled Hades or Pluto, enthroned with the modius, a grain-measure basket, on his head, a sceptre in his hand and Cerberus at his feet, with what appeared to be a serpent at its base, matching the Egyptian uraeus.

He was identified with many gods, including Hades, Osiris, Dionysus, Zeus and Asclepius, and his symbols, the cornucopia and the basket, signified abundance and resurrection. He was generally regarded as god of the underworld, healer and protector of the distressed, who gave asylum in his temple.

Serapis became popular during the Roman Empire, often replacing Osiris as the consort of Isis in temples outside Egypt. With Isis and their son Horus, in the form of Harpocrates, he won an important place in the Greek world: Pausanias, in his 2nd-century Description of Greece, notes two Serapeia above Corinth and one at Copae in Boeotia. At Rome he was worshipped in the Iseum Campense. The cults of Isis and Serapis gained in popularity late in the 1st century, when Vespasian attributed events he experienced in Alexandria to their miraculous agency. From the Flavian dynasty on, Serapis might appear on imperial coinage.

The cult declined under Theodosius I, whose laws restricted paganism. The main cult at Alexandria survived until the late 4th century, when a mob directed by Pope Theophilus of Alexandria destroyed the Serapeum around 391 CE.
serbia: Serbia lies in the Balkans and the Pannonian Basin. It covers 88,499 square kilometres including the disputed territory of Kosovo, or 77,589 square kilometres excluding it. It has eight neighbouring countries, more than any other European country except Germany. The Pannonian Plain covers the northern third of the country, central Serbia is chiefly hills traversed by rivers, and mountains dominate the southern third.

Elevation ranges from 2,169 metres at the Midžor peak in the Balkan Mountains to just 17 metres near Prahovo in the Timok Valley. Karst topography is prominent in the Dinaric Alps and the Carpathian Mountains, and the country hosts about 1,500 deep caves.

A hominid jaw fragment from Mala Balanica Cave is believed to be up to 525,000 years old. Around 6500 BCE the Starčevo and Vinča cultures were present near modern Belgrade, and Lepenski Vir and Vinča-Belo Brdo lie along the Danube. The Celtic Scordisci settled the area in the 3rd century BCE and built fortified settlements, including Singidunum (present-day Belgrade) and Naissos (present-day Niš). The Romans conquered much of the territory from the 2nd century BCE, and some historians believe 18 Roman emperors were born there, among them Constantine the Great.

Slavs migrated into Byzantine territory in large numbers by the 6th century. The first Serbian proto-state was established in the 7th century and had become a more stable principality by the beginning of the 9th century, remaining a Byzantine vassal state throughout. It was conquered and annexed by the Byzantine Empire in the late 10th century. The Serbian Kingdom lasted from 1217 to 1346, followed by the Serbian Empire from 1346 to 1371 and the Serbian Despotate from 1402 to 1459.

Serbia is a parliamentary republic under a constitution adopted in 2006, after the dissolution of the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro. The National Assembly has 250 deputies elected for four years. The 2022 census counted a population of 6,647,003, excluding Kosovo, of whom 80.6% were Serbs; Hungarians (2.8%) and Bosniaks (2.3%) are the largest minorities.

The country has five World Heritage sites, among them Stari Ras, the Studenica Monastery and the Roman palace complex of Felix Romuliana, and six traditions on the intangible heritage list, including the slava and kolo dance. Its cultural identity was shaped by its position as a frontier between the Byzantine Empire and Western Christianity, and later between the Ottoman and Habsburg empires.
serbs: The origin of the name Serb is unclear. The most prominent theory holds that it is of Proto-Slavic origin, meaning family kinship or alliance, and ultimately rooted in a word for sipping or breast-feeding, so that it carries the idea of milk kinship and brotherhood. Early Slavs, especially the Sclaveni and Antae, including the White Serbs, invaded and settled Southeastern Europe in the 6th and 7th centuries. Until the late 560s they mainly raided across the Danube, but large-scale settlement overwhelmed the Danube and Sava frontier in the late 6th and early 7th centuries. The region of Raška was the centre of Serb settlement, and Serb tribes also occupied most of modern Herzegovina and Montenegro.

The first Serb states, Serbia (c. 780–960) and Duklja (10th century to 1186/9), were formed chiefly under the Vlastimirović and Vojislavljević dynasties. As Duklja declined in the late 11th century, Raška gained independence and became the most powerful Serbian state. Grand Prince Stefan Nemanja, (r. 1166–96), founded the Nemanjić dynasty, which ruled Serbia until the 14th century. His son Stefan Nemanjić became the first recognised king, and his younger son Rastko founded the Serbian Orthodox Church in 1219 and became known as Saint Sava.

Under the Ottomans, the devshirme took Christian boys from the Balkans, many of them Serbs, from their families, converted them by force to Islam and trained them for the Janissary corps. Some Serbs who converted rose to the highest ranks, among them the grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha. The Serbian Revolution (1804–1817) began with the First Serbian Uprising under Karađorđe Petrović, which created an independent state for almost a decade until the Ottomans crushed it in 1813. The Second Uprising under Miloš Obrenović won substantial autonomy in 1815–1816, the last Ottoman troops withdrew in 1867, and full international recognition of independence came at the Congress of Berlin in 1878.

Serbs are predominantly Eastern Orthodox Christians, traditionally affiliated with the Serbian Orthodox Church. During the centuries of Ottoman rule it remained the only permitted Serb institution, and through its monasteries and clergy it preserved the Serbian language, literacy and national consciousness. When the Principality of Serbia became independent, Orthodoxy became crucial in defining national identity, since language was shared with other South Slavs.

Serbs are noted for icon painting, frescoes, literature, music and medieval architecture, shaped by Byzantine tradition. The gusle, a bowed single-stringed instrument, accompanies a centuries-old oral tradition of epic songs, most of which centre on the Ottoman occupation and the struggle for liberation. The Kosovo Myth is a central national myth that symbolises martyrdom and the defence of the homeland against the Ottomans.
seretse-khama: Seretse Khama was born in 1921 in Serowe, in the Bechuanaland Protectorate, the son of Queen Tebogo and Sekgoma Khama II, paramount chief of the Bamangwato, and the grandson of Khama III. His name means the clay that binds, chosen to celebrate the reconciliation of his father and grandfather. At the age of four he became kgosi, with his uncle Tshekedi Khama as regent. He studied at Fort Hare University College, graduating in 1944, then at Balliol College, Oxford, and the Inner Temple in London.

In June 1947 he met Ruth Williams, an English clerk at Lloyd's of London, and they married in September 1948. The marriage alarmed South Africa, which had banned interracial marriage in 1949 under apartheid, and it angered the Bamangwato elders. After a series of kgotla meetings in 1949 the elders reaffirmed him as kgosi. Britain, fearing the loss of South African gold and uranium supplies, announced on 8 March 1950 that he could not return to Bechuanaland for at least five years, and exiled him and his wife in 1951. A judicial enquiry found him fit to rule but its report was suppressed for thirty years.

In 1956 Khama and his wife were allowed to return as private citizens, after he renounced the chieftainship. He was elected secretary of the tribal council in 1957 and founded the Botswana Democratic Party, which swept the 1965 elections. As prime minister he pressed for independence, and Botswana became independent on 30 September 1966, with Khama as its first president.

At independence the country had only 12 kilometres of paved roads and few graduates. Khama set out to build an export economy on beef, copper and diamonds, helped by the discovery of diamonds at Orapa in 1967. His government renegotiated the diamond mining agreement in 1975 to secure 50 per cent of the revenues, and spent them on infrastructure, health and education. The Botswana pula replaced the South African rand in 1976. His party won the elections of 1969, 1974 and 1979.

Khama had heart and kidney ailments and was diagnosed with diabetes in 1960. In June 1980 he was found to have terminal pancreatic cancer, and he died in his sleep on 13 July 1980. Vice President Quett Masire succeeded him. Forty thousand people paid their respects as he lay in state, and he was buried in the Royal Cemetery on a hill in Serowe. Sir Seretse Khama International Airport, opened in 1984, bears his name, and the film A United Kingdom, released in 2016, told the story of his marriage.
serfdom: Institutions similar to serfdom existed in antiquity; the status of the helots of Sparta resembled that of medieval serfs. By the 3rd century CE the Roman Empire faced a labour shortage, and large landowners relied increasingly on free tenant farmers, later called coloni, instead of slaves. Diocletian's tax system assessed both land and its inhabitants, so it became administratively inconvenient for peasants to leave the land where they were counted. Medieval serfdom really began with the breakup of the Carolingian Empire around the 10th century, when powerful lords encouraged it as a source of agricultural labour. The word serf comes from Middle French, from Latin servus, and serfdom was coined only in 1850.

A serf lived on and worked a parcel of land within the manor of a lord, who owed protection and justice in return. Unlike a slave, a serf could not be sold individually, although serfs passed with the land when it was sold. A serf could not leave without permission and had no saleable title to the land. A freeman usually became a serf through force or necessity, sometimes in a ceremony of bondage, and children inherited the status.

Serfs paid dues mainly in seasonally appropriate labour on the lord's demesne and in produce, and Easter eggs or a Christmas goose might be owed on top. They had rights in land and could take their disputes to the manorial court. A well-off serf might buy his freedom, and in England one who reached a chartered borough and lived there a year and a day became free.

Serfdom varied greatly in time and place. In Poland the labour owed was commonly a few days a year per household in the 13th century, one day a week in the 14th, four in the 17th and six in the 18th. Serfdom began to disappear west of the Rhine in the later Middle Ages while it spread through eastern Europe, becoming dominant there around the 15th century. The decline in the west has sometimes been attributed to the Black Death. In Russia it became the dominant relation between peasants and nobility in the 17th century.

Abolition came by stages. France abolished serfdom in Crown lands in 1779 and formally on 4 August 1789. Joseph II issued the Serfdom Patent for the Habsburg monarchy in 1781, though dues and unpaid labour continued until the revolutions of 1848. Prussia abolished it in 1807, and Alexander II freed Russia's privately held serfs in 1861, with owners compensated through taxes on the freed serfs. The United Nations 1956 Supplementary Convention on the Abolition of Slavery prohibits serfdom.
sergei-eisenstein: Sergei Mikhailovich Eisenstein was born on 22 January 1898 in Riga, then in the Russian Empire, to a middle-class family. His father, the architect Mikhail Osipovich Eisenstein, came from a Jewish family but had converted to the Russian Orthodox Church before his marriage in 1897. His mother took Sergei to Saint Petersburg in 1905. He was raised an Orthodox Christian and later became an atheist. At the Petrograd Institute of Civil Engineering he studied architecture and engineering, but in 1918 he left to join the Red Army in the Russian Civil War. In Minsk in 1920 he saw Kabuki theatre and studied Japanese, learning about 300 kanji characters, which he cited as an influence on his pictorial development.

In 1920 Eisenstein moved to Moscow and worked in the theatre for Proletkult, an experimental institution that aimed at a revolutionary working-class aesthetic. In 1923 he began as a theorist with the essay The Montage of Attractions. His first full-length film was Strike in 1925, followed in the same year by Battleship Potemkin, which was acclaimed around the world, and by October: Ten Days That Shook the World, made for the tenth anniversary of the Revolution. His attention to camera angles, crowd movements and montage drew criticism in the Soviet film community and led to self-criticism and promises to conform to socialist realism.

In 1930 Paramount Pictures gave him a short contract in Hollywood, but his projects failed to impress the studio and it ended by mutual consent. He then made a film in Mexico, Que viva Mexico, financed by the author Upton Sinclair and other investors. It ran far beyond the three or four months agreed, and Sinclair shut down production, leaving the footage in the United States, where others edited it into films that Eisenstein never saw. Alexander Nevsky, made in 1938 with music by Sergei Prokofiev, was received well in the Soviet Union and the West and won him the Order of Lenin and the Stalin Prize.

During the war he worked on the film about Tsar Ivan IV, with Prokofiev scoring it. Ivan the Terrible, Part I won a Stalin Prize. Part II was criticized by various authorities and went unreleased until 1958, and the footage of the unfinished Part III was confiscated and mostly destroyed.

Eisenstein suffered a heart attack on 2 February 1946 and died of a second on 11 February 1948, aged 50. His ashes were buried in the Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow. He was a pioneer in the theory and practice of montage.
sergei-prokofiev: Sergei Sergeyevich Prokofiev was born on 27 April 1891 (15 April in the old style) on the rural estate of Sontsovka, in what is now Ukraine. His father was an agronomist and his mother came from a family of former serfs. In 1902 she met Sergei Taneyev, the director of the Moscow Conservatory, who arranged for Reinhold Glière to teach the boy at Sontsovka that summer. At eleven Prokofiev tried to write a symphony. Later he complained that Glière had given him conventional phrase structure that he had to unlearn, and he began experimenting with dissonant harmony in short piano pieces.

Prokofiev studied at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory and in 1914 won its competition for the best piano students by playing his own Piano Concerto No. 1. In London he met the impresario Sergei Diaghilev, who rejected his first ballet as non-Russian and commissioned Chout instead. In the summer of 1917 he wrote the Classical Symphony, in the style he said Joseph Haydn would have used had he lived then. After the Revolution he left with the approval of the commissar Anatoly Lunacharsky and reached San Francisco in August 1918. His opera The Love for Three Oranges was delayed by the illness and death of the Chicago Opera's director, and in 1920 he left for Paris.

He toured the Soviet Union in 1927 and settled in Moscow with his family in 1936, after four years of moving between Moscow and Paris. That year he wrote Peter and the Wolf for Natalya Sats's Central Children's Theatre. His Cantata for the 20th Anniversary of the October Revolution was effectively blocked and was not performed until 1966. The German invasion of 22 June 1941 led him to begin War and Peace, for which Mira Mendelson, who became his second wife, co-wrote the libretto. He was evacuated to Tbilisi, where he wrote the first version.

On 10 February 1948, the day before the decree of the Zhdanov Doctrine was published, Prokofiev was honoured at the Kremlin as a People's Artist of the RSFSR. He was then attacked for anti-democratic formalism, but he kept the support of younger performers, among them Sviatoslav Richter, for whom he wrote his Ninth Piano Sonata. He died on 5 March 1953 at the age of 61, the same day as Joseph Stalin. Crowds mourning Stalin made it impossible to hold the funeral service at the Composers' Union headquarters, and his coffin was carried by hand through back streets. About thirty people attended, Dmitri Shostakovich among them. He is buried in the Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow.
sergei-witte: Sergei Yulyevich Witte was born on 29 June 1849. His father, from a Lutheran Baltic German family, converted to Russian Orthodoxy on marrying Yekaterina Fadeyeva, and Sergei was raised on the estate of his mother's parents. He studied at Novorossiysk University in Odessa, graduating at the top of his class in 1870. He had planned an academic career in mathematics, but his relatives thought it unsuitable for a noble, and he was persuaded to enter the railways.

After six months of training on the Odessa Railways he became chief of the traffic office. A wreck in late 1875 cost many lives and led to a four-month prison sentence, but in the Russo-Turkish War he directed the Odessa Railways and attracted the notice of Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich, who commuted the sentence to two weeks.

From 1889 to 1891 Witte was Director of Railway Affairs in the Finance Ministry, expanding the railways under state control and assigning staff by merit rather than patronage. Appointed Minister of Finance in August 1892, he held the post for eleven years and nearly doubled the empire's revenues. He accelerated the construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway, established a state alcohol monopoly in 1895 and, in 1896, placed the ruble on the gold standard, which increased investment and the inflow of foreign capital. In 1896 he concluded the Li-Lobanov Treaty with Li Hongzhang, which gave Russia the right to build the Chinese Eastern Railway.

Under pressure from the landed gentry and his enemies at court, he was moved in August 1903 to the chairmanship of the Committee of Ministers, a post with no real power. In 1905 the tsar sent him to the United States to negotiate the end of the Russo-Japanese War at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, where he is credited with negotiating well for Russia, and he was made a count.

On 9 October 1905 Witte told Nicholas II that the country faced a catastrophic revolution and offered two choices: a military dictator or broad reforms. He framed the October Manifesto, and on 20 October 1905 he was appointed the first chairman of the Council of Ministers, effectively prime minister. With his Council he designed Russia's first constitution, but within months court opposition discredited him as a reformer, and he resigned before the First Duma met on 10 May 1906. He remained a member of the State Council but never again held an administrative post. Witte died in St Petersburg in 1915. His memoirs, completed in 1912, were published in translation in 1921.
sergipe: Sergipe covers 21,910 square kilometres and borders Bahia to the south and west and Alagoas to the north. The São Francisco River forms its northern boundary. Inland the state is almost entirely savanna, called caatinga, while the coastline has mangroves, swamps and sandy beaches. The rivers that drain the southern half into the Atlantic are obstructed by sandbars at their mouths, so there are no good ports on the coast. The name comes from an Old Tupi word meaning in the river of the siri, a species of crab.

The region was home to numerous Indigenous peoples, including the Kanindé, the Aratus and the Tupi. Gaspar de Lemos briefly landed there in 1501, and the Portuguese Crown declared it part of the Captaincy of Bahia. It was one of the last coastal regions of Brazil whose Indigenous population resisted Portuguese rule, and it was fully brought under it after about two decades of warfare, during which thousands of Indigenous people were killed and thousands more enslaved to work on sugar plantations. The first Portuguese settlement was at São Cristóvão, then called Sergipe D'El-Rey.

Sergipe was invaded several times by the Dutch and often raided by French buccaneers, who were drawn by its king-wood, a prized commodity. The territory belonged to Dutch-controlled Brazil until the Portuguese regained control in 1645. By 1723 Sergipe, still part of Bahia, produced a third of Bahia's sugar. Land unsuitable for sugarcane was used for livestock, and Sergipe supplied draft animals to farms in Bahia and Pernambuco.

John VI of Portugal signed a decree separating Sergipe from Bahia on 8 July 1820. It kept its separation after the independence of Brazil in 1822, first as a captaincy and then as a province. On 17 March 1855 the provincial president moved the capital from São Cristóvão, inland, to Aracaju on the coast. Sergipe became a state when the Republic of Brazil was proclaimed in 1892.

Sergipe is the smallest Brazilian state by area, larger only than the Federal District, with Aracaju as its capital and largest city. São Cristóvão, the fourth oldest town in the country and the state capital until 1855, has a main square, São Francisco Square, that became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
sergo-ordzhonikidze: Sergo Ordzhonikidze was born Grigol Ordzhonikidze on 24 October 1886 in Ghoresha, a village in the Kutais Governorate of the Russian Empire, now in the Imereti region of Georgia. His father Konstantine belonged to an impoverished noble family and his mother Eupraxia was a peasant; she died six weeks after his birth. He was raised by an uncle and aunt, and his father died when he was ten. He trained as a medical orderly and briefly worked as a medical assistant.

He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1903, at 17, and worked in an underground printshop for the Bolshevik faction. He was first arrested in December 1905 for transporting arms, worked in Baku, and was imprisoned several times by the Russian police. He was in Siberian exile when the February Revolution began in 1917, then returned and took part in the October Revolution.

During the Civil War he was the leading Bolshevik in the Caucasus. In 1918 he persuaded Chechen and Ingush leaders that the soviet system resembled the Islamic order they favoured, and with Ingush help the Bolsheviks retook Vladikavkaz. After Lenin ordered him on 17 March 1920 to prepare an invasion of Azerbaijan, he oversaw the invasions of Azerbaijan, Armenia and Georgia. As head of the Kavbiuro he clashed with the Georgian Bolsheviks, especially Budu Mdivani, whose advice he ignored. He backed their union in the Transcaucasian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic and was its First Secretary until 1926. Colleagues called him authoritarian; Lenin explained that he shouted because he was deaf in one ear.

In 1926 Stalin made him head of the Workers' and Peasants' Inspectorate and the Central Control Commission. In 1930 he took over Vesenkha, reorganised in 1932 as the People's Commissariat of Heavy Industry, and became a full member of the Politburo. He argued Stalin down to a yearly industrial growth target of 13 to 14 per cent for the second five-year plan and helped launch the Stakhanovite movement in 1935. He tried to protect his officials from the hunt for wreckers and saboteurs and had prosecutors barred from factories, which strained his friendship with Stalin.

Ordzhonikidze died on 18 February 1937, a few days before a Central Committee plenum at which he was expected to speak on wrecking in his commissariat. Rumours spread at once that Stalin had ordered his death or driven him to suicide. The historian Oleg Khlevniuk thinks suicide likely, and the cause remains contested. His brother Papulia was shot in November 1937, and other relatives and colleagues were arrested. Vladikavkaz was renamed Ordzhonikidze in 1931 and bore the name again from 1954 to 1990.
sericulture: Sericulture, or silk farming, is the cultivation of silkworms to produce silk. The caterpillar of the domestic silkmoth is the species most widely used and intensively studied. It is no longer found in the wild, because selective breeding has left most of these moths flightless and without defence against predators. Silk is believed to have first been produced in China as early as the Neolithic period.

According to a Confucian text the discovery of silk production dates to about 2700 BCE, while archaeological records point to silk cultivation as early as the Yangshao period, 5000 to 3000 BCE. A ceramic piece made to look like a silkworm, found in 1977 at Nancun in Hebei and 5,400 to 5,500 years old, is the earliest known evidence. Silk fibre found on Indus Civilization sites dating to 2450 to 2000 BCE suggests that silk was used over a wide region of South Asia.

By about the first half of the 1st century CE the practice had reached ancient Khotan through a series of interactions along the Silk Road, and by 140 CE it was established in India. In the 6th century CE the smuggling of silkworm eggs into the Byzantine Empire led to its establishment in the Mediterranean, where it remained a monopoly of the Byzantine Empire for centuries.

In 1147, during the Second Crusade, Roger II of Sicily attacked Corinth and Thebes, two important centres of Byzantine silk production. He captured the weavers and their equipment and set up his own silkworks in Palermo and Calabria, which eventually spread the industry to Western Europe.

The silkworms are fed with mulberry leaves, and after the fourth moult they climb a twig and spin their cocoons. The silk is a continuous filament of fibroin protein, secreted from two salivary glands in the head of each worm, held together by a gum called sericin. Placing the cocoons in hot water removes the sericin, a step known as degumming, and frees the filaments for reeling. The hot water also kills the pupa inside.

One cocoon holds approximately 1,000 yards of filament, and about 2,500 silkworms are needed to produce a pound of raw silk. Mahatma Gandhi criticised silk production on the philosophy of ahimsa, not to hurt any living thing, and promoted silk made without boiling the pupa and wild silk from the cocoons of wild and semiwild moths.
serres: Serres stands on a fertile plain at an elevation of about 70 metres, some 24 kilometres north-east of the Strymon river and 69 kilometres north-east of Thessaloniki. The ancient city was built on a high, steep hill known as Koulas, just north of the modern one, and controlled the land road that followed the Strymon valley from the Strymonian Gulf to the Danubian countries. Herodotus mentions it as Siris in the 5th century BCE; Livy later calls it Sirae, and the name has stayed plural since.

The earliest known inhabitants were the Bryges and Strymonians, followed by the Paeonian tribes of the Siropaiones and Odomantes. In the Roman period the city, called Sirra, was an important city of the province of Macedonia and the seat of a federation of five cities, the Pentapolis. It flourished under the Pax Romana, declined in the crisis of 235 to 284 CE and recovered under Diocletian. Its first attested bishop took part in the Second Council of Ephesus in 449.

In about 803 Emperor Nikephoros I rebuilt the town and installed a garrison against the Slavic tribes. It was pillaged by Bulgarians in the 10th century and taken by Ivan Asen I's forces after the Byzantine defeat at the Battle of Serres in the late 12th century. After the Fourth Crusade it passed to Boniface of Montferrat and then to Kaloyan of Bulgaria, who according to George Akropolites reduced it to a small settlement around the citadel.

The Nicaean Empire took it in 1246, and by the 14th century Nikephoros Gregoras called it large and marvellous. The Serbs took it on 25 September 1345, and after Stefan Dušan's death in 1355 it became the Principality of Serres, ruled first by the Empress-dowager Helena and from 1365 by the Despot Jovan Uglješa, whose administration worked in Greek.

The Ottoman Empire took Serres definitively on 19 September 1383, and it became a fief of Evrenos Beg. In the 17th century Evliya Çelebi recorded a prosperous town with 2,000 shops in its market. A fire in 1849 destroyed most of its churches. A Bulgarian army took the city on 6 November 1912, and Greek forces entered it on 11 July 1913; the retreating Bulgarians set fire to it. In 1943 its Jewish population was deported to the Treblinka death camp.

Serres is the capital of the Serres regional unit and the second largest city of Central Macedonia after Thessaloniki. Its municipal population was 70,703 in 2021. It is a trade centre for tobacco, grain and livestock, and it hosts a campus of the International Hellenic University and a department of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki. The Archaeological Museum is housed in an Ottoman bezesten.
servius-tullius: Most Roman sources name the mother of Servius Tullius as Ocrisia, a young noblewoman taken at the Roman siege of Corniculum and given to Tanaquil, wife of King Tarquinius Priscus. Several traditions describe his father as divine, either the household Lar or Vulcan. Livy tells how members of the royal household saw a ring of fire about the head of the sleeping boy, a sign of divine favour, after which he became a protégé of the royal family and married their daughter. Livy argues that no slave could have been granted so great an honour. The Emperor Claudius offered a different account, based on Etruscan tradition, in which Servius was an Etruscan mercenary named Mastarna who fought for Caelius Vibenna.

According to Livy, the sons of Ancus Marcius had Tarquinius Priscus wounded by assassins, and Tanaquil announced from a palace window that he had named Servius regent. When the king's death became known, the senate elected Servius, the first time the people were not involved in choosing a king. He fought Veii and the Etruscans.

The so-called Servian reforms extended voting rights to commoners and defined the fiscal and military obligations of all citizens. Tradition holds that Servius held the first Roman census and formed the comitia centuriata, which displaced the comitia curiata as the central legislative body. The census grouped male citizens in classes by wealth, each divided into centuries, and the wealthiest centuries voted first. Modern scholars think the reforms were a long, piecemeal process that extended beyond his reign. He is also said to have extended the city, protected it with a rampart, moat and wall, built a temple of Diana on the Aventine and founded or reformed the Compitalia.

In Livy's account Servius gave his two daughters to the sons of Tarquinius Priscus. The younger Tullia and her husband Lucius Tarquinius Superbus had their siblings murdered and conspired against the king. Tarquinius went to the senate house with armed men and threw Servius down the steps, and Servius was killed in the street. Livy calls this a tragic crime and makes it the just cause for the end of the monarchy.

Servius is described as Rome's second founder and as a kind of proto-Republican magistrate. Claudius's identification with Mastarna draws some support from the François Tomb at Vulci, whose paintings show a Macstrna among the allies of the Vibenna brothers.
sesame: Sesame, Sesamum indicum, is a plant also called benne. Most of the other species of its genus are wild and native to sub-Saharan Africa, while the cultivated type originated in India. It was described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, and its epithet means of India. The seeds, which are white or black and grow in pods, have one of the highest oil contents of any seed. The plant tolerates drought and heat and will grow where other crops fail, so subsistence farmers at the edge of deserts have grown it. The word sesame comes through Latin and Greek from ancient Semitic languages such as the Akkadian šamaššamu.

Sesame is considered the oldest oilseed crop known to humanity. Charred remains dated to about 3500 to 3050 BCE show that it was domesticated in the Indian subcontinent at least 5,500 years ago. The archaeobotanist Dorian Q. Fuller states that sesame was traded between Mesopotamia and the Indian subcontinent by 2000 BCE, and the Indus Valley civilization may have exported sesame oil to Mesopotamia, where it was called ilu in Sumerian and ellu in Akkadian. Some believe it may instead have originated in Ethiopia.

Egyptians called it sesemt, and it appears in the list of medicinal drugs of the Ebers Papyrus of about 1550 BCE. Baskets of sesame were found among the grave goods of King Tutankhamen, which suggests it was present in Egypt by 1350 BCE. It was grown and pressed for oil at least by 750 BCE in the empire of Urartu.

The seeds are a common ingredient in many cuisines, made into tahini paste and halva in the Middle East and a part of the spice mixture za'atar. Enslaved West Africans brought sesame to colonial America in the 17th century and grew it as a subsistence crop. In Southern Italian cuisine sesame sweets such as giurgiulena remain from the Arabic period. In the early twentieth century sesame oil was a compulsory ingredient of margarine in Europe, because its presence made it simple to detect margarine used to adulterate butter. Around 1920 Burma exported about 197,400 tons of the oil a year.
seth: Set was the son of Geb, the Earth, and Nut, the Sky, and his siblings were Osiris, Isis and Nephthys; he married Nephthys. In art he is usually shown as an animal that Egyptologists call the Set animal, which has not been identified with any known species. It has a downward curving snout, long ears with squared-off ends and a thin, forked tail. Proposed identities include the Saluki, aardvark, hyena, donkey and giraffe. The earliest certain Set animal appears on a ceremonial macehead of Scorpion II, a ruler of the Naqada III phase. The meaning of his name is unknown.

Set was lord of the Red Land, the desert, balancing Horus as lord of the Black Land, the fertile land. In the Osiris myth he murders and mutilates his brother Osiris. Isis reassembles the body, and Osiris lives long enough to father Horus, who seeks revenge. The conflict appears as early as the Pyramid Texts, where the two gods are sometimes uncle and nephew and sometimes brothers. In the account called Contendings, the gods race in boats and fight as hippopotami before an assembly of deities, and the dispute lasts eighty years, largely because the judge favours Set. Horus loses an eye to Set, and the restored eye represents the return of the moon to full brightness and of kingship to Horus.

Set also stood on the prow of Ra's barge and helped overcome the serpent Apep. In the Second Intermediate Period (1650 to 1550 BCE) the Hyksos, who ruled the Nile Delta from Avaris, took him as patron, identifying him with their own god Hadad. After Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos, the cult at Avaris continued. Ramesses I came from a military family from Avaris with ties to Set's priesthood, and several Ramesside kings took names from the god, among them Seti I and Setnakht. Ramesses II set up the Year 400 Stela at Pi-Ramesses for the cult's 400th anniversary.

Egyptologist Herman te Velde holds that Set was demonised after foreign conquests in the Third Intermediate and Late Periods, when the god of foreigners became linked with the Kushite and Persian rulers. His murder of Osiris was emphasised and his defeat by Horus welcomed. The Greeks later associated him with Typhon. Even so, in outlying places such as Kharga and Dakhla he remained a chief deity, called Lord of the Oasis, and he was worshipped at Ombos, Oxyrhynchus and parts of the Faiyum. Today he is honoured in Kemetism, a revival of ancient Egyptian religion, and in the Temple of Set, founded in 1975.
setif: Sétif lies in north-eastern Algeria, about 270 kilometres east of Algiers and about 132 kilometres west of Constantine, in the Hautes Plaines region. It stands at an altitude of roughly 1,100 metres, which makes it the second-highest provincial capital in Algeria. The city sits between the Tellian Atlas to the north and the Aurès mountains to the south, on sedimentary rock of sandstones, marls and limestones.

Its streams, the Boussalem and El Kébir wadis, flow irregularly. The climate is continental with a strong Mediterranean influence, with warm dry summers and cold, very rainy winters. The name comes from the Latin Sitifis, which is drawn from a Berber word Zdif, meaning black lands, a reference to the fertility of the soil.

The city is of Numidian origin and was part of the kingdom of the Massaesyli in 225 BCE; it was small under the Numidian kings. Near Sétif the Numidian king Jugurtha campaigned and lost against Marius in 105 BCE. Under Rome it became the capital of Mauretania Sitifensis. The first Muslim expedition to Africa took place in 647, and by 700 the area had been conquered and converted to Islam. Little is known of the early Islamic town, but by the 10th century the area outside the fortress was again filled with houses, and over a dozen with large courtyards were excavated on the site of the Roman baths.

A column of the French colonial army took the city in 1838, as part of the operations against Constantine. At first the occupation was military, but civilians soon arrived. A first urban plan was set up by decree in 1843, a European city was laid out in 1846, and on 11 February 1847 a royal decree created it with an endowment of 2,509 hectares of land.

From 1850 it was a centre of colonial settlement, drawn by the farming potential of the region. The protests and massacre of 8 May 1945 began in the city and were a crucial factor in the start of the Algerian War. The municipality was created at the start of independence, on 5 July 1962.

Sétif is the capital of Sétif Province and is regarded as one of the most important trading and industrial cities of Algeria. Agriculture in the region rests on grain and livestock, and local wheat is turned into semolina, couscous and noodles. One of its main historical monuments is the Ain El Fouara fountain, a sculpture by the French sculptor Francis de Saint-Vidal that was brought to the city at the end of the 19th century and was classified as national heritage on 3 November 1999. The local cuisine includes the couscous dish Berboucha, and a music genre called Staifi, based on the zendali rhythm, is popular across the Maghreb.
setubal: Setúbal stands on the northern bank of the Sado estuary, about 50 km by road from central Lisbon, and belongs to the Lisbon metropolitan area. The Arrábida hills begin at its western beaches, and the Tróia peninsula lies across the river. In the time of Al-Andalus it was called Shaṭūbar in Andalusian Arabic, after the older pre-Roman name Caetobriga. English traders of the 17th century called the port Saint Ubes.

Remains of human occupation in the municipality date from the Neolithic onwards. Phoenicians, Greeks and Carthaginians came to Iberia in search of salt and tin, and in Roman times the settlement developed fish-salting factories and pottery kilns. No records survive for the period between the 6th and 12th centuries. After the Christians took Alcácer do Sal in 1217, Setúbal came under the Order of Santiago, which granted it a municipal charter in March 1249. In 1343 an agreement settled its territory against its neighbours Palmela and Alcácer do Sal, and a wall was built.

In the 15th century shipbuilding and maritime trade brought wealth, and in 1458 Afonso V sailed from its port to conquer Ksar es-Seghir. The Convent of Jesus, designed by Master Diogo Boitaca, was built in the late 15th and early 16th centuries. John III granted the title of notable town in 1525. In 1580 the town supported Dom António, Prior of Crato, against Philip II of Spain and was besieged by Spanish troops under the Duke of Alba; Philip later ordered the Fort of São Filipe, the work of Filippo Terzi. Salt made the 17th century the town's most prosperous age, and new walls were built after 1640. The earthquake of 1755 interrupted this prosperity.

The railway arrived in 1860, the year Pedro V made Setúbal a city, and sardine canning, oranges and muscatel wine made it known in the 19th century. It became the seat of a district in 1926 and of a diocese in 1975.

The municipality had 123,496 inhabitants at the census of 2021. Its main historical monument is the Monastery of Jesus, a church of the 15th and 16th centuries that is one of the first buildings in the Manueline style. The cathedral of Our Lady of Grace has a Mannerist façade, and the Fort of São Filipe overlooking the city is now a hotel. The port and its industries, among them paper, cement, fertilisers and shipbuilding, still tie the city to the sea.
sevastopol: Sevastopol lies at the south-western tip of the Crimean Peninsula, on the Heracles Peninsula, on the coast of the Black Sea. Much of the city is gathered around the long Bay of Sevastopol, and its navigable harbours made it an important port and naval base throughout its history. Its name joins the Greek sebastós, venerable, and pólis, city, and probably honours Empress Catherine II, who founded it. In the west of the city stand the well-preserved ruins of the ancient Greek port of Chersonesos, founded in the 5th century BCE by settlers from Heraclea Pontica.

Sevastopol was founded in June 1783, in the area of the ruined Greek city of Chersonesus, as a base for a naval squadron under the name Akhtiar, White Cliff, by Rear Admiral Thomas MacKenzie, a Scot in Russian service. In February 1784 Catherine the Great ordered Grigory Potyomkin to build a fortress and call it Sevastopol, and Captain Fyodor Ushakov, commander of the port from 1788, carried out the plans. The name Sevastopol was restored on 29 April (10 May) 1826.

In the Crimean War the allies chose Sevastopol as Russia's main Black Sea naval base. They landed in September 1854 and settled into a siege marked by brutal conditions on both sides. The city fell after eleven months, and the Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856 forbade Russia to base warships in the Black Sea. In the Second World War it withstood intensive German bombardment in 1941-42, in which the Germans used the 80-cm railway gun Schwerer Gustav, and after 250 days of fierce fighting fell to Axis forces in July 1942. The Red Army liberated it on 9 May 1944.

In the Soviet era it was a closed city. In 1954 Sevastopol and the rest of Crimea were transferred from the Russian SFSR to the Ukrainian SSR. Russia annexed Crimea, with Sevastopol, in March 2014; the annexation is not recognised internationally.

Sevastopol is the largest city of Crimea and a major Black Sea port, with a population mostly of ethnic Russians and a substantial minority of Ukrainians. Because of its military history most of its streets are named after Russian and Soviet military heroes, and hundreds of monuments and plaques recall its military past.
seven-sages-of-greece: The Seven Sages, or Seven Wise Men, were an honorary title given to seven philosophers, statesmen and lawgivers of the 7th and 6th centuries BCE who were especially noted for their wisdom. The oldest explicit mention of a standard list of seven is in Plato's Protagoras. There Socrates names Thales of Miletus, Pittacus of Mytilene, Bias of Priene, Solon of Athens, Cleobulus of Lindos, Myson of Chenae and Chilon of Sparta. He says they emulated Spartan education and made the brief remarks Know thyself and Nothing too much their joint first fruits of wisdom to Apollo at Delphi. The passage is elaborately ironical, so it is unclear which parts are meant seriously.

Diogenes Laertius reports that seven men were held in high esteem for wisdom well before Plato. According to Demetrius Phalereus, they first became known as the wise men in the archonship of Damasias, 582/81 BCE, with Thales the first so acknowledged.

The members were various. Thales is the first well-known Greek philosopher, mathematician and astronomer. Pittacus governed Mytilene on Lesbos with the support of the common people. Solon framed laws that shaped Athenian democracy. Cleobulus was tyrant of Lindos, and Chilon was a Spartan politician credited with the militarisation of Spartan society.

Diogenes Laertius points out that his sources disagreed greatly about who belonged. Periander of Corinth or Anacharsis the Scythian was often put in the place of Myson. Plutarch says some counted Epimenides the seventh if they would not admit Periander. Dicaearchus gave ten names, Hippobotus twelve and Hermippus seventeen, from which people chose seven. Aesop was also a popular contender.

Later tradition ascribed a pithy saying to each sage, though ancient and modern scholars have doubted this. A collection of 147 maxims inscribed at Delphi was preserved by Stobaeus as Sayings of the Seven Sages, but they were most likely popular proverbs later attributed to individuals. Stories told of a golden tripod, or a bowl or cup, to be given to the wisest, which passed from sage to sage until Thales or Solon, depending on the version, dedicated it to Apollo. Diogenes Laertius also records that the maxims were thought sceptical and the sages precursors of Pyrrho's scepticism, and that Dicaearchus held the seven to be merely shrewd men who had studied legislation.
seven-wonders-of-the-ancient-world: After the conquests of Alexander the Great in the 4th century BCE, Hellenistic travellers gained access to the civilizations of the Egyptians, Persians and Babylonians, and began to list the landmarks that impressed them. The ancient Greeks spoke not of wonders but of theamata, meaning sights or things to be seen, so the list was the ancient counterpart of a travel guidebook. Later the word for wonder, thaumata, was used instead.

The first known list of seven dates to the 2nd to 1st century BCE, and at least eight full lists and ten partial lists are known. Diodorus Siculus mentioned only the Walls of Babylon and the Pyramids. The epigrammist Antipater of Sidon, who lived around or before 100 BCE, listed six of the present wonders and put the walls of Babylon where the Lighthouse of Alexandria now stands. Lists by Herodotus and by the poet Callimachus of Cyrene survive only as references.

The seven names now generally given are the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Colossus of Rhodes and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. This canonical list was first established in the 1572 publication Octo Mundi Miracula from a combination of historical sources. Two wonders stood in Greece, two in Turkey, two in Egypt and one in Iraq. Five of the seven celebrate Greek construction; the exceptions are the pyramids and the Hanging Gardens.

Only the Great Pyramid survives, and it lost its white stone facing around 1300 when local communities removed it for building. The Colossus, finished after 280 BCE, fell to an earthquake in 226 or 225 BCE, so all seven stood together for less than sixty years. The Temple of Artemis and the statue of Zeus were destroyed by fire, and the Lighthouse and the tomb of Mausolus by earthquakes.

Sculptures from the tomb and the temple are in the British Museum. Scholars debate the nature of the Hanging Gardens and whether they existed. Later lists added Roman and Christian sites, and Gregory of Tours named the Temple of Solomon and Noah's Ark. Wilhelm Heinrich Roscher found 22 distinct places across 18 classical lists in 1906.
seven-years-war: In North America the boundary between British and French possessions was largely unsettled in the 1750s. France claimed the entire Mississippi River basin, which Britain disputed, and in the early 1750s the French began building a chain of forts in the Ohio River Valley. British settlers resented French troops near their western borders and wanted the fertile Ohio land for newcomers. In Europe, Frederick II of Prussia had seized the province of Silesia from Austria in the War of the Austrian Succession. Empress Maria Theresa signed the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748 to gain time to rebuild her forces and find new allies.

The result was a strategic realignment known as the Diplomatic Revolution, which ended the long rivalry between Austria and France. The two powers signed the Treaty of Versailles in 1756, and a second agreement in 1757 brought Prussia into the war on the side of Britain. Britain's allies included Hanover and several small German states, which together supplied nearly 50,000 troops.

In 1756 the French attacked Menorca, and a British relief attempt failed at the Battle of Menorca; Admiral Byng was court-martialled and executed. In 1757 Frederick marched into Bohemia and won the Battle of Prague on 6 May, but then suffered his first defeat at Kolín and withdrew from Bohemia. In 1759 he lost half his army at Kunersdorf, the worst defeat of his career, which drove him to the brink of abdication. William Pitt the Elder, head of the British government from 1756 to 1761, committed Britain to seizing the French Empire, especially in North America and India, using the Royal Navy and subsidies to European allies that tied down the French army.

Outside Europe, Robert Clive recaptured Calcutta in India and ousted the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, a French ally, at the Battle of Plassey in 1757. In 1758 the British took the French settlement at Saint-Louis in Senegal. Spain became a French ally in 1762, invaded Portugal unsuccessfully and lost Havana and Manila to Britain. In 1762 Russia withdrew after the death of Peter III, and when Catherine II took power she ended the alliance with Prussia. By 1763 the war in central Europe was essentially a stalemate between Prussia and Austria.

The Treaty of Hubertusburg, signed in 1763, confirmed Prussian occupation of Silesia and Prussia's status as a great power, challenging Austria for dominance within Germany. The Treaty of Paris, also of 1763, ended the hostilities between Britain and France. France ceded Louisiana to Spain and the rest of New France to Britain, and Britain returned the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon to assist French fishing rights. Havana and Manila were returned to Spain. France lost its possessions in North America, and Britain established its commercial dominance in India.
seventh-crusade: The Kingdom of Jerusalem and the Ayyubid dynasty were both weakened by internal strife in the years after the Barons' Crusade. On 17 and 18 October 1244 a Crusader army and a Damascene army met the Egyptian and Khwarezmian armies at Hirbiya, the Battle of La Forbie or Gaza. About 5,000 Crusaders died and 800 were taken prisoner, and Jerusalem had already been lost. At the end of 1244 Louis IX of France fell gravely ill with malaria and vowed to go on crusade if he recovered. He took the cross from William of Auvergne, bishop of Paris, without papal authorisation. Pope Innocent IV, in exile at Lyons, directed a new crusade under Louis at the First Council of Lyon in 1245.

The preparations took three years. The costs came to over 1.5 million livres tournois, six times his annual revenues, partly raised by taxing towns and by expelling Jewish moneylenders from the kingdom and confiscating their property. The crusade formally began on 12 August 1248, when Louis left Paris. He reached Cyprus on 17 September 1248, where disease killed many men during the long wait, and the army landed at Damietta the following year.

The Frankish army set out for Mansurah on 20 November 1249. After weeks facing the Egyptians across a canal, the Crusaders crossed a ford on 8 February 1250. Robert I of Artois attacked the Egyptian camp against orders, and the attack on Mansurah ended in an Ayyubid victory on 11 February 1250. During the retreat Louis and most of his army were captured. The sultan estimated his prisoners at 30,000, certainly an exaggeration, and the infirm were executed. Louis ransomed himself by surrendering Damietta and his army by a payment of a million bezants, later reduced to 800,000.

Louis sailed to Acre and decided on 3 July 1250 to stay, remaining four years as de facto ruler of the kingdom. He resolved the succession crisis at Antioch, negotiated with the Assassins and sent William of Rubruck to the Mongol prince Sartaq, but no alliance followed. A popular Shepherds' Crusade in 1251 set out to rescue him and ended in disaster. After his mother's death on 27 November 1252 and unrest in France, he sailed from Acre on 24 April 1254 and landed at Hyères in July.

The crusade cost the Kingdom of Jerusalem a manpower it never recovered. Jean de Joinville's Life of Saint Louis is the most detailed personal account of any crusade. Troubadours such as Austorc d'Aorlhac wrote poems on the defeat.
seventh-day-adventist-church: The church is the largest of several Adventist groups that arose from the Millerite movement of the 1840s in upstate New York, a phase of the Second Great Awakening. William Miller predicted from Daniel 8:14 to 16 and the day-year principle that Jesus Christ would return between the spring of 1843 and the spring of 1844. His followers came to expect the return on 22 October 1844, and the failure of the prediction became known as the Great Disappointment.

As the early Adventists consolidated their beliefs, the question of the day of rest arose. Its foremost advocate was Joseph Bates, who had learned of the Sabbath doctrine from a tract by the Millerite preacher Thomas M. Preble. The periodical The Present Truth took up the subject in July 1849. For about twenty years the movement was a small, loosely knit group, whose leading figures were Joseph Bates, James White and Ellen G. White. Ellen White's visions and leadership convinced her fellow Adventists that she had the gift of prophecy.

The church first published its beliefs at Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1872 in a brief statement, "A Synopsis of Our Faith". Conservative evangelicals at first regarded it as a cult. Adventist scholars credit the writings of Ellen White with moving it towards Trinitarian theology, which the church adopted early in the 20th century. It then began dialogue with other Protestants and gained wide recognition as a Protestant church.

Members keep Saturday as the Sabbath, preparing on Friday and attending worship the next day, which begins with Sabbath School, a structured period of small-group Bible study. The church advocates a vegetarian diet and the avoidance of pork, shellfish and other foods held unclean in Leviticus 11, and it discourages alcohol and tobacco. It is governed by a General Conference through unions, local conferences and local churches, a representative system resembling Presbyterian church government.

Adventist mission work began in the late 19th century. Until J. N. Andrews was sent to Switzerland in 1874, global efforts had consisted entirely of posting tracts. The church has a presence in over 200 countries and territories, and much of its membership lives outside the United States, in Africa, Asia and Latin America. It runs more than 7,500 schools, colleges and universities and a network of hospitals, clinics and sanitariums. The Adventist Development and Relief Agency provides non-sectarian relief.
severus-alexander: Severus Alexander was born on 1 October 208 at Arca Caesarea in Phoenicia. He and his cousin Elagabalus were grandsons of Julia Maesa, the sister of the empress Julia Domna. When Elagabalus became unpopular, Maesa had him adopt the young Alexander and arranged his murder. The army hailed Alexander as emperor on 13 March 222 and the Senate ratified the acclamation the next day. At about 13 he was the youngest sole emperor of the united empire, and he relied on the guidance of Maesa, until her death in 224, and of his mother Julia Mamaea.

Under Mamaea's influence the court's extravagance was reduced and jurists such as Ulpian were employed to oversee justice. Alexander restored the Baths of Nero and built the Nymphaeum of Alexander at the end of the Aqua Claudia. He lightened taxes, set up loan offices that lent at moderate interest, and confirmed the rights of soldiers to make wills and to keep property gained in service. Military discipline nevertheless broke down: in 228 the Praetorian Guard murdered its prefect Ulpian in the emperor's presence, and soldiers fought the people of Rome for three days.

In 231 Ardashir I of the Sassanid Empire invaded the eastern provinces. In 233 Alexander launched a threefold invasion from Antioch. The northern army had some success, but the southern army was destroyed by Ardashir's horse-archers, and Alexander retreated after an indecisive campaign, though Mesopotamia was retaken. He held a triumph at Rome in 233. In 234 Germanic tribes crossed the Rhine and Danube, and he went north, hoping to win time by buying them off on the advice of his mother.

Many soldiers saw the bribery as dishonourable, and the legions turned to Maximinus Thrax, a Thracian soldier with a high reputation. In early March 235 the Legio XXII Primigenia mutinied at Moguntiacum, the modern Mainz, and killed Alexander and his mother during a meeting. Ancient accounts differ about the details. Maximinus succeeded him. Alexander was deified after the death of Maximinus in 238.

His death ended the Severan dynasty and was the first overthrow of an emperor by military discontent on a wide scale. His economic policies were discarded and the currency was devalued. Historians treat it as the opening of the Crisis of the Third Century, which brought nearly fifty years of civil war, foreign invasion and the collapse of the monetary economy.
seville: Seville lies on the lower reaches of the River Guadalquivir in the southwest of the Iberian Peninsula, in a fertile valley, at an average height of 7 metres above sea level. Its port, about 80 kilometres from the Atlantic, is the only river harbour in Spain. The summers are very hot and dry.

The city is about 2,200 years old. The original core dates to the 8th century BCE, when the site was on an island in the Guadalquivir, and the Phoenicians and the Tartessians called it Hisbaal. It was founded as the Roman city of Hispalis, and after the Islamic conquest of 711 was called Ishbiliyah. It was the seat of the Wali of Al-Andalus until 716, when the capital moved to Córdoba. After the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in the early 11th century it became the centre of the independent Taifa of Seville, and it was later ruled by the Almoravids and the Almohads, who built its main mosque in the 12th century. It was incorporated into the Crown of Castile in 1248.

Following the voyages of Columbus, Seville was chosen in 1503 as the headquarters of the Casa de Contratación, which made it the gateway to the Indies, though ships had to sail about 80 kilometres up the Guadalquivir to reach it. In the 16th century it was one of the largest cities in Western Europe. Worsening drought in the river gradually moved the trade away to the Bay of Cádiz, which received the fleets of the Indies in 1680 and the Casa de Contratación in 1717.

Seville is the capital of Andalusia and of the province of Seville. Its old town contains a UNESCO World Heritage Site made up of three buildings: the Alcázar, the Cathedral and the General Archive of the Indies. Its motto, NO8DO, is popularly read as a rebus for the Spanish No me ha dejado, She has not abandoned me.
sewing-needle: A sewing needle for hand-sewing is a long slender tool with a point at one end and an eye to hold the thread. The earliest were made of bone or wood, and modern ones are made of high-carbon steel wire, plated with nickel or gold against corrosion. Needles have come in many kinds for their uses: sharps for general sewing, embroidery needles with longer eyes, quilting needles, tapestry needles with blunt tips for loose weaves, leather needles with a triangular point, and long upholstery needles that may be straight or curved. Sizes are not standardised, and within a class a higher number means a shorter, thinner needle.

The first sewing was probably the tying together of animal skins, with shards of bone as needles and sinew or plant material as thread. The early limit was making an eye small enough not to damage the material. Bone awls from Blombos Cave in southern Africa date to 73,000 to 70,000 years ago, and a point that may come from a bone needle, found in Sibudu Cave, to 61,000 years ago.

Later needles are better dated. A bone needle from Potok Cave in Slovenia belongs to the Aurignacian, 47,000 to 41,000 years ago. Ivory needles about 30,000 years old come from Kostenki in Russia, and 8,600-year-old needles from Ekşi Höyük in western Anatolia. Flinders Petrie found copper needles at Naqada in Egypt from 4400 to 3000 BCE, and iron needles from the third century BCE were found at the oppidum of Manching. Needles apply the wire-making technology that appeared in the second millennium BCE.

Native Americans used needles from natural sources. The agave leaf, soaked until only long fibres and a sharp tip remained, gave both needle and thread. Steel-making from China reached Spain in the tenth century in the form of the Catalan furnace and later Germany and France. England began making needles in 1639 at Redditch, with the drawn-wire technique still in common use, and about 1655 a Guild of Needlemakers was established in London. In Japan the Festival of Broken Needles, Hari-Kuyo, dates back to the 1600s.
sexagesimal: According to Otto Neugebauer, the origins of sexagesimal are not as simple, consistent or singular in time as they are often portrayed. Throughout its centuries of use, sexagesimal notation has always contained a strong undercurrent of decimal notation, and it has always been applied inconsistently, even within a single text. The strongest driver of a fully consistent use was its advantage for writing and calculating fractions, which is why it appears most uniformly in mathematical tables.

The number 60 has twelve divisors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30 and 60. With so many factors, many fractions simplify. An hour divides evenly into sections of 30, 20, 15, 12, 10, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 minutes, and 60 is the smallest number divisible by every number from 1 to 6. Any fraction whose denominator has only 2, 3 and 5 as prime factors can be written exactly, so that one third is 0;20 and one eighth is 0;7,30.

In Mesopotamia the system was not a pure base-60 system with sixty distinct digit symbols. Cuneiform digits used ten as a sub-base: narrow wedges for units up to nine and wide wedges for up to five tens. Numbers above 59 were written in blocks in place value notation. With no symbol for zero, the signs for 1 and 60 were identical and a value sometimes had to be judged from context. Later Babylonian texts used a placeholder for zero, but only in the middle of a number, not at its right-hand end.

The Old Babylonian Period (1900–1650 BCE) approximated the square root of 2 in sexagesimal. Ptolemy's Almagest, written in the 2nd century CE, expressed fractions in base 60, and its table of chords was the only extensive trigonometric table for more than a millennium. Al-Biruni first divided the hour into minutes, seconds, thirds and fourths in 1000, and the Parisian version of the Alfonsine tables of about 1320 recorded fractions of a day in base 60. European astronomers still used it for calculation as late as 1671; Jost Bürgi, in a work presented to Emperor Rudolf II in 1592, used sexagesimal multiplication tables to calculate sines.

The system survives in a modified form in the 60 minutes of an hour, the 60 seconds of a minute, the 360 degrees of a circle and in geographic coordinates. The modern signs for degrees, minutes and seconds descend from the notation John Wallis generalized in the 17th century.
sextus-pompey: Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius was the son of Pompey by his third wife, Mucia Tertia, with an elder brother, Gnaeus Pompeius, and a sister, Pompeia. When Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, Gnaeus followed their father to the East while Sextus stayed in Rome in the care of his stepmother, Cornelia Metella. After the defeat at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE the two met Pompey on Lesbos and fled with him to Egypt, where Sextus watched his father killed by treachery on 29 September of that year.

He then joined the resistance to Caesar in the African provinces alongside Metellus Scipio, Cato the Younger and his brother. Caesar defeated the Pompeius brothers at the Battle of Munda in Hispania in 45 BCE. Gnaeus died soon afterwards in a last stand at Lauro; Sextus escaped and raised another army in Spain.

After Caesar's death Mark Antony moved that Sextus be recalled, paid 50 million Attic drachmas for his father's confiscated property and given command of the whole Roman navy. He accepted, but went no further than Massilia before returning to Sicily. When the Second Triumvirate began its proscriptions, many of the proscribed fled to him, and after the battles of Philippi in 42 BCE survivors of the party of Brutus and Cassius did the same. With the whole island as his base he built an army and a strong navy.

In 40 BCE his admiral, the freedman Menas, seized Sardinia from Octavian's governor Marcus Lurius. By the Pact of Misenum in 39 BCE the triumvirs recognised his control of Sicily and Sardinia in exchange for keeping the grain supply to Rome open and his pirates in check. The peace was short. Each side accused the other of breaking it, and Menas betrayed Sardinia to Octavian. Sextus defeated Octavian at sea off Messina in 37 BCE.

Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa spent a winter building and training a fleet near Lake Avernus. He fought Sextus at Mylae in August 36 BCE, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Titus Statilius Taurus invaded Sicily, and after Naulochus Sextus fled to Asia Minor. Captured in 35 BCE, he was put to death without trial at Miletus by Marcus Titius, whom he had once spared, either on Titius's own initiative or possibly on the orders of Antony or Plancus. Plutarch gives him a minor role in the fall of the Republic; Appian treats him as a central figure who might even have emerged as the final victor.
seychelles: Seychelles is an archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean, with its capital and largest city, Victoria, about 1,500 kilometres east of mainland Africa. The islands lie northeast of Madagascar. The inner islands, 42 granitic and 2 coralline, occupy the shallow Seychelles Bank and hold 54% of the land area. The granitic islands rest on a submerged granite block, the Seychelles microcontinent, which lay between Madagascar and India before the breakup of Gondwanaland. Alfred Wegener cited this granite as evidence of continental drift.

The islands were uninhabited before sustained outside contact. Arab sailors knew of them through Indian Ocean trade routes, and scholars identify them with the Zarin islands described by al-Mahri. Europeans learnt of them in the early 16th century. The first sighting was made on 15 March 1503 by Thomé Lopes, during Vasco da Gama's fourth Portuguese India Armada. The earliest recorded landing was in January 1609, by the crew of the Ascension under Captain Alexander Sharpeigh, on a voyage of the British East India Company.

France began to take control in 1756, when Captain Corneille Nicholas Morphey laid a Stone of Possession on Mahé. The islands were named after the French politician Jean Moreau de Séchelles and formed part of the colony of Isle de France. In August 1770 the ship Thélémaque landed 15 white settlers and 13 African and Indian slaves on Ste. Anne Island. Enslaved Africans were then brought to work the plantations.

In 1794 the senior administrator, Jean-Baptiste Quéau de Quinssy, negotiated with the British frigate HMS Orpheus and kept the islands under French control as neutral territory. Britain took control after invading Isle de France in December 1810, formalised by the Treaty of Paris of 1814. Slavery was prohibited in 1835, and indentured labourers from India were later employed. Seychelles became a separate crown colony from Mauritius in 1903. It gained independence as a republic in 1976, and a coup in 1977 ousted its first president, James Mancham.

Seychelles is a republic whose president is both head of state and head of government. French, English and Seychellois Creole are official languages, and the Creole, a French-based language, is the most widely spoken. The population was estimated at 100,600 in 2022, making it the smallest African country by area and the least populated sovereign African state. Most people descend from African, French, Indian and Chinese immigrants. It belongs to the United Nations, the African Union and the Commonwealth of Nations.
sfax: Sfax lies about 270 km south-east of Tunis on a low coastal strip about 15 km wide, with an average altitude of 20 m. The rivers of the region are shallow and rarely reach the sea. The climate is hot and semi-arid, and because the city is sheltered from the winter storms of the Mediterranean it receives about half the rainfall of Tunis.

The present city was founded by the Aghlabids in 849 on the site of the town of Taparura. By the end of the 10th century it was an independent city-state. In the 12th century the geographer al-Idrisi described a thriving city with a stone wall, lively markets and a harbour, whose olive oil was of a quality found nowhere else. Roger II of Sicily conquered it in 1148; it was liberated by a revolt in 1156 and taken by the Almohads. Venice mounted an unsuccessful invasion in 1185, as Sfax had become a base of Barbary piracy.

The city returned to Hafsid rule around 1370. In 1534 the privateer Barberousse entered Tunis and reunited the towns of the coast, Sfax among them. Under the Husseinid dynasty the ramparts were restored, the Great Mosque was enlarged and in 1776 the Frankish quarter was built to the south for Jews and Christians. Venetian ships bombarded the city four times in 1785–86.

After the Bardo Treaty of 1881 made Tunisia a French protectorate, an insurrection broke out in Sfax; French ironclads bombarded it and troops took it on 16 July after hard fighting. The Axis powers used it as a major base in the Second World War until British forces took it on 10 April 1943.

Sfax is the second most populous city in Tunisia, with 341,999 inhabitants at the census of 2022. It is the country's largest fishing port and a centre of olive and nut processing, phosphate shipping and trade. Its medina, home to about 113,000 residents, is dominated by the Great Mosque and enclosed by walls 2,750 m long and seven to eleven metres high. The kasbah in its south-western corner, once an Aghlabid control tower and later army barracks, is now a museum of traditional architecture.
shaanxi: Shaanxi covers more than 205,000 square kilometres and borders Inner Mongolia to the north, Shanxi and Henan to the east, Hubei, Chongqing and Sichuan to the south, and Gansu and Ningxia to the west. It is divided into northern Shaanxi on the Loess Plateau, central Shaanxi or Guanzhong, where most of the population lives, and the mountainous south beyond the Qinling Mountains. The Wei River valley between them is a cradle of early Chinese civilisation. The name means west of Shan and is attested around 1000 BCE, when the dukes of Shao and Zhou marked their borders along the Shan plateau.

Thirteen dynasties established their capitals in Shaanxi over more than 1,100 years, from the Zhou to the Tang.
