The leadership vacuum was large, and the organization suffered defeats from rural self-defence organizations of campesinos, supposedly its social base. When Guzmán called for peace talks, it split between those for and those against them.

The party was designed on a concentric model, with Communist Party organs at the centre, the paramilitary wing around them and the political wing on the outside, so that the party controlled both. Its ideology moved from Marxism–Leninism–Mao Zedong thought to Marxism–Leninism–Maoism–Gonzalo thought, and some authors see a cult of personality around Guzmán.

It has been widely condemned for brutality against peasants, as in the Lucanamarca massacre, and against trade unionists, rival Marxist groups and elected officials. The Asháninka minority suffered disproportionately, with about 6,000 killed, over 10% of their 1993 population.
shinto: Shinto has no single founder, no canonical text and no central authority, so beliefs and practices vary widely. One proposed broad definition is that Shinto is a belief in kami, the supernatural beings that practitioners hold to inhabit all things, including forces of nature and prominent places. They are not regarded as omnipotent, omniscient or necessarily immortal, and the dead may become kami. Kami are worshipped at household shrines called kamidana and at public shrines called jinja, where priests known as kannushi offer food and drink. Shinto stresses ritual over doctrine, and above all purity: humans are seen as fundamentally pure, and pollution, or kegare, is a temporary condition removed by rites of purification.

Kami veneration has been traced back to the Yayoi period, from 300 BCE to 250 CE, when bronze bells, weapons and mirrors seem to have played a role in ritual. Historians debate when it is suitable to speak of Shinto as a distinct religion. Buddhism reached Japan at the end of the Kofun period and spread quickly, and the two merged so closely, in a process called shinbutsu-shūgō, that kami came to be seen as part of Buddhist cosmology.

The earliest written tradition of kami worship is in the 8th-century Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, which were commissioned by ruling elites to legitimise and consolidate their rule. They describe a universe in three parts: the Plane of High Heaven, where the kami live, the world of humans, and the Nether World. Although never of great importance to Japanese religious life, their accounts were proclaimed factual by the government in the early 20th century.

Japan has around 100,000 public shrines, about 80,000 of them affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines, which shrines formed in 1946. Festivals, called matsuri, mark the seasons of the agricultural year and give thanks to the kami, while rites of passage include a child's first visit to a shrine and weddings. Shinto was formally separated from the state during the U.S. occupation after World War II. A new constitution separated religion from the state, and the emperor declared that he was not a kami.

Numerically Shinto is the largest religion in Japan, with Buddhism second, but most people take part in both. Many Japanese say they have no religion, partly because they dislike the connotations of the Japanese word shūkyō, which suggests sect doctrine. Aspects of Shinto have been taken into new religious movements such as Tenrikyo and Oomoto.
shiraz: Shiraz is the capital of Fars province, historically known by the exonym Persia proper. It lies in a green plain at the foot of the Zagros Mountains, 1,500 metres above sea level, and has been a regional trade centre for over a thousand years. The earliest reference to the city, as Tiraziš, is on Elamite clay tablets dated to 2000 BCE, and tablets from the Persepolis treasury archives mention major workshops there. The name became Old Persian Širājiš and then the modern Persian Shirāz.

The Arab Muslim army conquered Fars in expeditions between 640 and 653 and captured the area around Shiraz in 641. Because the Sasanian capital Istakhr was deeply associated with the Sasanian Empire and the Zoroastrian religion, the Arabs sought to establish a rival cultural and administrative centre in nearby Shiraz. It was founded or restored in 693 by Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi, brother of the Umayyad viceroy al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, or by the latter's kinsman Muhammad ibn Qasim. In the 13th century it became a leading centre of the arts and letters, through its ruler's encouragement and the presence of Persian scholars and artists.

Ismail I, founder of the Safavid dynasty, captured Shiraz in 1504. After the fall of the Safavids the city declined, and a revolt of its governor against Nader Shah ended with a siege of many months and a sack. By Nader Shah's murder in 1747 most of its historical buildings were damaged or ruined, and its population had fallen to 50,000, a quarter of that in the 16th century. Karim Khan, de facto ruler of Iran from 1760 until 1779, made Shiraz his capital.

Shiraz is the fifth-most-populous city of Iran, with 1,995,500 inhabitants at the 2021 census. It is known as the city of poets, gardens, wine, nightingales and flowers. Hafez and Saadi were born there, and their tombs lie on the north side of the present city. The Eram garden is among its old gardens, and the Arg of Karim Khan, the citadel, stands beside the Vakil Bazaar and Vakil Bath. Shiraz has historically had major Jewish and Christian communities.
shiva: The name Shiva means auspicious, propitious or gracious. In the Rig Veda (c. 1700 to 1100 BCE) the word is an adjective applied to several deities, among them Rudra, a fearsome god of the roaring storm. Shiva is associated with Rudra, and the Hindu scriptures treat the two as the same figure. The Shiva of later Hinduism is, however, regarded as an amalgamation of various older Vedic and non-Vedic deities into a single god, a process linked to the Hindu synthesis of post-Vedic times. How this composite figure formed is not well documented and has attracted much speculation.

Some authors have read Mesolithic rock paintings at Bhimbetka as depictions of Shiva, but Howard Morphy holds that in context they more probably show hunting parties with animals. The Yajurveda gives both terrifying (rudra) and benign (shiva) attributes, and later texts such as the Atharvashiras Upanishad declare that all gods are Rudra.

For Shaivas, the followers of Shaivism, Shiva is the Supreme Lord who creates, protects and transforms the universe. In the Shakta tradition the Goddess is the equal and complementary partner of Shiva. Within the Trimurti he is the destroyer or transformer beside Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver, though ancient and medieval texts also contain many triads that do not include him.

Shiva is a god of ambiguity: fierce and benevolent, an ascetic yogi on Kailasa and a householder with his wife Parvati and their children Ganesha and Kartikeya. His attributes include the third eye, with which he burned Kama, desire, to ashes, the crescent moon in his hair, the river Ganga flowing from his matted locks and the trident. He is shown as Nataraja, Lord of Dance, and is usually worshipped in the aniconic form of the linga, which the Linga Purana presents as the manifested sign of the signless.

Shiva is revered across India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Indonesia, especially Java and Bali, where he is known as Batara Guru, a spiritual teacher blended with local spirits and heroes. His worship spread in Central Asia under the Kushan and Hephthalite empires, and wall paintings from Penjikent in Sogdia show him with a halo, a sacred thread and a tiger skin.

The Siva Sutta shows him conversing with the Buddha, and he appears as Mahakala in Vajrayana, as Maheshvara in Mahayana and as Ishana in Theravada Buddhism, in most forms ranked below Mahabrahma or Sakra. The Japuji Sahib of the Guru Granth Sahib names Shiva beside Vishnu and Brahma.
shivaji: Shivaji was born in the hill fort of Shivneri near Junnar, now in Pune district, and was named after a local deity, the goddess Shivai Devi. Scholars disagree on his date of birth. He belonged to the Bhonsle family. His father Shahaji served as a chieftain in the Maratha uplands under the Sultanate of Bijapur, hoping for rewards of jagir land, and Shahaji's campaigns against the Mughals were generally unsuccessful.

In 1647 the 16-year-old Shivaji captured Torna Fort, by stratagem or bribery, while the Bijapur court was in confusion, and used the treasure found there to build Rajgad, which served as his seat for over a decade. In 1657 Bijapur sent the veteran general Afzal Khan to arrest him. After Shivaji defeated forces sent against him, Siddi Jauhar besieged him at Panhala in 1660. Shivaji escaped by night, and at the pass of Ghod Khind the sardar Baji Prabhu Deshpande and 300 soldiers volunteered to fight to the death to hold back the pursuers.

Until 1657 Shivaji kept peaceful relations with the Mughal Empire, then raided its Deccan territory. After his defeat by Jai Singh I at Purandar he entered Mughal vassalage. In 1666 Aurangzeb summoned him to Agra, where he took offence at being made to stand among low-ranking nobles and was placed under house arrest, and he later escaped. Peace followed until 1670, when Shivaji recovered much of the territory he had surrendered.
In 1674 he was formally crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad Fort despite opposition from local Brahmins, a title that gave him a legal basis to rule and set him above other Maratha leaders.

Shivaji set up the Ashta Pradhan Mandal, a council of eight ministers who advised him on political and administrative matters. At his court Marathi replaced Persian, his royal seal was engraved in Sanskrit, and in 1677 his official Raghunath Pandit produced the Rājavyavahārakośa, a thesaurus of state usage. He employed people of all castes and religions, including Muslims and Europeans, and many commentators regard his religious policies as tolerant.

His army was small but effective, built on Maratha and Kunbi peasants. He avoided pitched battles against the heavy Mughal cavalry and used guerrilla tactics, known in Marathi as Ganimi Kawa, cutting supply lines and luring enemies into hills and jungle. Hill forts were central to his strategy: the historian Jadunath Sarkar counted some 240–280 at his death, each held by three officers of equal status so that no single traitor could hand it over.
shkoder: Shkodër extends over the Mbishkodra Plain between Lake Shkodër and the foothills of the Albanian Alps, on a hill where the lake drains into the Buna. It is bounded by the Kir to the east, the Drin to the south and the Buna to the west. Lake Shkodër, the largest lake in southern Europe, forms the frontier between Albania and Montenegro. The city has been continuously inhabited since the Early Bronze Age and has roughly 2,200 years of recorded history. Its ancient name Skodra, in Latin Scodra, is certainly pre-Roman, and the forms Scutari and Skadar later spread in Italian, English and Serbo-Croatian.

An urban settlement called Skodra was founded in the 4th century BCE by the Illyrian tribe of the Labeatae. It became the capital of the Illyrian kingdom under the Ardiaei and Labeatae. The Romans annexed and sacked it after the third Illyrian War in 168 BCE, when King Gentius was defeated. In the 3rd century CE it became the capital of Praevalitana under Diocletian's reform, and in the 4th century the Archdiocese of Scodra was founded.

In the Middle Ages the city passed among Byzantines, Serbian rulers of Zeta and the Balšić family, who surrendered it to the Republic of Venice in 1396 as a protection against the Ottomans. Mehmed II laid siege to it in 1478 and 1479; an agreement between Venice and the Ottomans ended the siege, letting the citizens leave unharmed. It then became the seat of the Ottoman Sanjak of Scutari. From 1757 to 1831 it was the centre of the pashalik of the Bushati family, and in the later 19th century the centre of a vilayet and a trading hub with over 3,500 shops.

The city was important in the Albanian national movement. After the Balkan Wars Montenegro left it to the new Albania in May 1913. Under the communist regime the Shkodër Bazaar and the port on the Buna were demolished.

Shkodër is regarded as the traditional capital of northern Albania and the centre of Roman Catholicism in Albania, with the Metropolitan Archdiocese of Shkodër-Pult. Its mosques and churches reflect its religious diversity. Rozafa Castle, linked to a legend of a woman who sacrificed herself so it could be built, and the Marubi National Museum of Photography are among its landmarks.
shogun: Shōgun is short for sei-i taishōgun, a title meaning commander-in-chief of the expeditionary force against the barbarians. The barbarians in question were the Emishi, tribes of northern Japan who resisted the governance of the imperial court at Kyoto. In the early Heian period the title was given to commanders for the length of a campaign. Sakanoue no Tamuramaro (758–811), who brought the Emishi lands of Mutsu and Dewa under the Yamato state, is generally recognised as the first shogun, although sources also name Ōtomo no Otomaro and Tajihi no Agatamori. In this early period shoguns held no real political power, and the Fujiwara clan controlled the court.

When Minamoto no Yoritomo gained ascendancy over Japan in 1185, the title was revived to regularise his position. He established a system based at Kamakura in which the samurai gained some political powers, while the emperor and aristocracy remained the rulers in law. Emperor Go-Toba awarded him the title in 1192. The Hōjō clan, the family of Yoritomo's wife, then took power from the Kamakura shoguns. Ashikaga Takauji was awarded the title in 1338 and established the Ashikaga shogunate, which nominally lasted until 1573.

Tokugawa Ieyasu was given the title in 1603 and set up the Tokugawa shogunate at Edo, now Tokyo. Fifteen Tokugawa shoguns ruled the Edo period, which ended in 1867 when Tokugawa Yoshinobu relinquished the office to Emperor Meiji in the Meiji Restoration.

The shogun's officials were known as the bakufu, tent government, a term that recalled the shogun's role as field commander and suggested an office meant to be temporary. The shogun held civil, military, diplomatic and judicial authority and in theory served the emperor, who acted as chief priest of Shinto. No shogun tried to usurp the throne, partly because the shogun's authority was held to come from the emperor and partly because of a tradition that traced the imperial line from the age of the gods. During parts of the Kamakura and Sengoku periods the shoguns were figureheads. The shogunate lasted nearly 700 years.
shota-rustaveli: Almost nothing is known about Rustaveli from contemporary sources. In the prologue of his poem the poet calls himself a certain Rustveli. This is not a surname but a territorial epithet, meaning of or holder of Rustavi, though a 10th-century manuscript fragment found in 1975 at Saint Catherine's Monastery in Sinai attests its use as a cognomen by a noble house of Ru(i)staveli. Georgian authors of the 15th to 18th centuries are more informative and almost unanimously name him Shota Rustaveli.

Both folk tradition and the 17th-century royal poet Archil II make him a native of Meskheti in southern Georgia, where his home village of Rustavi lay. A legend says he was educated at the academies of Gelati and Ikalto and then in Greece, meaning the Byzantine Empire. He knew Persian well enough to read its poetry without translations and may have composed Persian verse.

Rustaveli wrote The Knight in the Panther's Skin, regarded as the national epic of Georgia. He must have composed it no earlier than the 1180s and no later than the first decade of the 13th century, most probably in 1205 to 1207. The poem is set in a fictional India and Arabia, and events in those distant lands are read as an allegory of the rule of Queen Tamar and the size and glory of the Kingdom of Georgia in its Golden Age.

The poem was first printed in 1712 in Tbilisi. Two folios from the 16th century and some lines from the 14th century are kept at the Georgian National Center of Manuscripts in Tbilisi. All other known copies date from the 17th century.

A name preserved on a fresco and in a document from the former Georgian Monastery of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem identifies Shota as a sponsor of the monastery and a high treasurer, which echoes a popular legend that he served at Tamar's court and retired to the monastery in old age. The fresco, the only known contemporary portrait, was described by the Georgian pilgrim Timote Gabashvili in 1757 and rediscovered by Georgian scholars in 1960. It was defaced in 2004 and has since been restored.

The highest Georgian state prize for art and literature bears his name, as do Rustaveli Avenue in Tbilisi and many other landmarks. The Hungarian painter Mihály Zichy made the illustrations most often used in editions of the poem.
shrewsbury: Shrewsbury is a market town on the River Severn, about 9 miles (14 km) east of the border between England and Wales. It is the county town of Shropshire and serves as the commercial centre for the county and parts of mid-Wales. The town lies to the west of Haughmond Hill, where some of the oldest rocks in the county are found, and stands on largely Carboniferous rock.

Traces of earlier settlement include a Neolithic place of worship found at Sutton Farm, an Iron Age double ring ditch at Meole Brace and a roadside settlement on the Roman military road linking Viroconium Cornoviorum and Caersws. A hoard of more than 9,000 Roman coins was found near the town in 2009.

Shrewsbury has Anglo-Saxon roots, and its institutions may represent a cultural continuity reaching back as far as the 8th century. William the Conqueror gave the town to Roger de Montgomery, who was created Earl of Shrewsbury. He built Shrewsbury Castle around 1074, a work that destroyed 51 properties and probably relied on forced local labour, and he founded Shrewsbury Abbey as a Benedictine monastery in 1083.

The town is described as a borough in the Domesday Book of 1086, and its earliest known charter was issued by Henry II. The Black Death reached it in the spring of 1349, and church records show twice as many vacant benefices in that year as in the previous ten years together.

In the 1470s Edward IV established the Council of Wales and the Marches with its headquarters in the town. The Abbey closed in 1540 in the Dissolution of the Monasteries. Henry VIII meant to make Shrewsbury a cathedral city, but the citizens declined, which is the origin of the term Proud Salopians. In the 16th and 17th centuries the town was at the height of its commercial importance, controlling the Welsh wool trade, which the Shrewsbury Drapers Company dominated; Draper's Hall of 1560 and Ireland's Mansion of 1575 date from this time.

During the English Civil War it was a Royalist stronghold. Charles I had a temporary base there in the autumn of 1642, and Prince Rupert made his headquarters there on 18 February 1644. By the 18th century it was a stopping point for stagecoaches between London and Holyhead.

Shrewsbury's centre has a largely undisturbed medieval street plan and over 660 listed buildings, including several timber-framed examples from the 15th and 16th centuries. The castle and the abbey both survive. The town suffered very little from air raids in the Second World War, which is why many ancient buildings remain intact. It is the birthplace of the naturalist Charles Darwin.
shropshire: Shropshire is a ceremonial county on the border with Wales, bordered by Cheshire, Staffordshire, Worcestershire and Herefordshire in England and by Powys and Wrexham in Wales. It covers 3,487 square kilometres, with Shrewsbury as its county town and Telford as its largest settlement. The south-west is upland, taking in the Stiperstones, the Clee Hills, the Long Mynd and Wenlock Edge, and the Wrekin stands isolated west of Telford. The north is a plain, an extension of the Cheshire Plain, where most of the larger towns lie. The River Severn enters from the west, flows through Shrewsbury and leaves the county south of Bridgnorth.

There is evidence of Neolithic and Bronze Age occupation, and the hillfort at Old Oswestry dates from the Iron Age. The remains of the Roman city of Viroconium Cornoviorum survive. After the Roman occupation ended in the 5th century the area lay in the eastern part of the Welsh kingdom of Powys, and in the Anglo-Saxon period it was part of Mercia. The county is first recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in the annal for 1006, under the Old English name Scrobbesbyrigscīr, meaning the shire of the fortified place in the scrublands. Much Wenlock grew up around the priory founded by the abbess St Milburga, daughter of King Merewalh of the Magonsæte.

In the High Middle Ages Shropshire was part of the Welsh Marches. From 1472 to 1689 Ludlow was the seat of the Council of Wales and the Marches, which administered justice in Wales and in Herefordshire, Shropshire, Worcestershire and Gloucestershire. The border with Wales was fixed in the 16th century. In the English Civil War the county was Royalist, and Charles II fled through it after his defeat at the Battle of Worcester, hiding in an oak tree. In the 19th century Much Wenlock was the birthplace of the modern Olympic movement.

The area around Coalbrookdale in the Ironbridge Gorge is regarded as one of the birthplaces of the Industrial Revolution and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The first iron-framed building in the world was built at the Flaxmill Maltings in Shrewsbury. The Shropshire Hills form a national landscape. The county has no cities but 22 towns, among them Oswestry, Bridgnorth, Ludlow and Market Drayton. It was called Salop in the official record from 1972 until 1980, when the name Shropshire was restored. For local government it consists of two unitary authority areas, Shropshire and Telford and Wrekin.
shroud-of-turin: The shroud is a rectangular linen cloth measuring approximately 4.4 by 1.1 metres, woven in a three-to-one herringbone twill. It bears a faint, brownish image of the front and back of a naked man with his hands folded across his groin. Reddish-brown stains on the cloth correlate with the wounds in the Gospel descriptions of the crucifixion. In 1898 Secondo Pia produced the first photographs and found that the image can be discerned more clearly in a black-and-white negative.

There are no definite historical records of this particular cloth before the 14th century. It began to be exhibited in the new collegiate church of Lirey in 1354. In 1389 the bishop of Troyes, Pierre d'Arcis, denounced it as a forgery, and in 1390 Antipope Clement VII allowed its display but ordered that it be declared a painting or panel made to represent the Shroud. In 1506 Pope Julius II reversed this position and authorised its public veneration, with its own mass and office.

The House of Savoy acquired the cloth in 1453. A fire damaged it at Chambéry in 1532, and in 1578 the Savoys moved it to their new capital, Turin. In 1694 it was placed in the Chapel of the Holy Shroud, designed by Guarino Guarini, and in 1993 it was moved to the cathedral. After the death of Umberto II of Italy in 1983, ownership passed from the House of Savoy to the Catholic Church.

The first direct examination by a scientific team took place in 1969 to 1973. In 1978 the microscopist Walter McCrone concluded from tape samples that the image had been painted with dilute red ochre in a gelatin medium and the stains with vermilion, findings other researchers disputed. In 1988 laboratories at the University of Oxford, the University of Arizona and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology dated the cloth with 95 per cent confidence to between 1260 and 1390. Experts accept the result, though defenders of authenticity have argued that the samples may have been contaminated or repaired, hypotheses that have been refuted. The Catholic Church neither endorses nor rejects the shroud as a relic of Jesus.
shudra: Shudra is one of the four varnas of the Hindu class system in ancient India. The word appears once in the Rigveda, in the Purusha Sukta, a creation story in which the four varnas form from the body of a primeval man: the brahmin from his mouth, the kshatriya from his arms, the vaishya from his thighs and the shudra from his feet. This verse is now generally considered a later insertion, possibly a charter myth. The historian Ram Sharan Sharma suggests that it may have been meant to show a common lineage for all the varnas.

Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel Brereton find no evidence in the Rigveda for an elaborate, much-subdivided caste system and describe the varna system there as embryonic, a social ideal rather than a social reality. According to Sharma, the Shudra class arose from Indo-Aryans and non-Indo-Aryans relegated to that position through external and internal conflicts.

The legal texts list disabilities for shudras. They were barred from studying and hearing the Vedas and from performing Vedic sacrifices, although they could hear the Itihasa and Purana texts and build wells, temples and parks. The Manusmriti, according to Patrick Olivelle, allows brahmins to seize property from shudras, who own nothing, and says shudras should not accumulate wealth. The texts vary widely: the Apastamba Grhyasutra excludes shudra students from hearing the Vedas, while the Mahabharata states that all four varnas may hear them.

Traditionally shudras were peasants and artisans, and their duty was service of the other three varnas. Scholars note that this is a theoretical account found in select texts. G. C. Ghurye argues that in reality the hereditary occupations of the varnas were missing from large parts of India, and that members of all four were farmers, traders or warriors as opportunity required. Some early texts describe shudras as ministers and kings.

Evidence from medieval India is mixed. Cynthia Talbot notes that varna is rarely mentioned in the medieval records of Andhra Pradesh, and Richard Eaton finds that in the Kakatiya population of the Deccan between the 11th and 14th centuries shudras were part of the nobility and that fathers and sons often had different professions. Several poet-saints of the Bhakti movement, among them Tukaram and Namdev, were born in shudra families, and Sikh Gurus included sixty of Namdev's compositions in the Guru Granth Sahib.

Bhim Rao Ambedkar argued that the shudras were originally kshatriyas denied the initiation ritual of upanayana by the brahmins, a claim Sharma contested. In Bali, among Hindu communities, the Soedra have typically been temple priests.
shunzhi-emperor: The Shunzhi Emperor, personal name Fulin, was the ninth son of Hong Taiji and the grandson of Nurhaci, the founder of the Eight Banners system. When Hong Taiji died on 21 September 1643 without naming a successor, a committee of Manchu princes chose the five-year-old Fulin and appointed two co-regents, Dorgon and Jirgalang. His mother was the Khorchin Mongol Bumbutai, honoured as Empress Dowager Zhaosheng. Dorgon took control of the government and, by early June 1644, firm control of the military.

In June 1644 Dorgon entered Beijing, ordered his Banner troops not to loot and had all claimants to the Ming throne executed. The Shunzhi Emperor was enthroned in Beijing in November 1644. Under Dorgon the Qing subdued almost all of China and pushed the Southern Ming loyalists into the far south-west, despite unpopular measures such as the hair-cutting edict of 1645. Li Zicheng, who had taken Beijing, was killed in September 1645.

Dorgon died on 31 December 1650, and the emperor then ruled personally. He announced a purge of corruption in April 1651, issued the Six Edicts in 1652, encouraged Han Chinese to take part in government and in 1658 re-established the Hanlin Academy and the Grand Secretariat. Court factions frustrated his efforts. Ming resistance revived in the 1650s, but by 1661 his armies had defeated the last enemies, Koxinga and the Prince of Gui, both of whom died the following year. In the late 1650s he became a fervent follower of Chan Buddhism.

His favourite consort, Donggo, died in September 1660. The emperor contracted smallpox on 2 February 1661, chose his seven-year-old third son Xuanye as heir and died on 5 February at the age of twenty-two. His will named four regents, Oboi, Soni, Suksaha and Ebilun, but they and the empress dowager clearly tampered with it before it was published. It expressed regret for his Chinese-style rule and neglect of Manchu traditions. Rumours that he had retired to a monastery circulated, but the evidence suggests that his death was not staged.

Citing the will, the regents abolished the Thirteen Eunuch Bureaus, eliminated the Hanlin Academy and limited the Deliberative Council to Manchus and Mongols. Because fewer documents survive from his reign than from later ones, it is a relatively little-known period of Qing history. He was succeeded by the Kangxi Emperor.
shusha: Shusha, or Shushi in Armenian, stands at an altitude of 1.4 to 1.8 kilometres in the Karabakh mountains, and was a mountain resort in the Soviet era. Several historians derive its name from the New Persian shīsha, meaning glass or flask, and Armenian sources from the dialectal Armenian shosh or shush, meaning tree sprout or, figuratively, a high place. Its earlier name Panahabad honoured Panah Ali Khan. The town matters religiously, culturally and strategically to both Armenians and Azerbaijanis, and is often considered a cradle of Azerbaijani music and poetry. It also contains Armenian Apostolic churches, among them Ghazanchetsots Cathedral.

The origin of the city is disputed. In the 1750s Panah Ali Khan founded the Karabakh Khanate, and the city developed with the building of the fortress of Shusha, in alliance with Melik Shahnazar, the Armenian prince of Varanda. Some Armenian sources identify an earlier fortress called Shosh on the site. From the mid-18th century to 1822 Shusha was the capital of the khanate, which withstood a six-month siege by Fath-Ali Khan Afshar in 1756 or 1759. After the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813 Russia held the khanate, and the town became a cultural centre of the South Caucasus, home to many Armenian and Azerbaijani intellectuals, poets and musicians.

Clashes between Armenian and Azerbaijani inhabitants in August 1905 killed hundreds and burned more than 200 houses. In the Shusha massacre of 1920 the Armenian half of the city was destroyed by Azerbaijani forces, resulting in the death or expulsion of its Armenian population, up to 20,000 people. The Mountainous Karabakh Autonomous Region was set up within the Azerbaijan SSR in 1923, and Stepanakert soon became its capital.

In the First Nagorno-Karabakh War Azerbaijani forces shelled Stepanakert from Shusha. Armenian forces captured the town on 9 May 1992, its Azerbaijani population fled, and most of the city was destroyed. It was under the control of the unrecognised Republic of Artsakh until Azerbaijani forces took it on 8 November 2020.
shushtar: Shoushtar is an ancient fortress city about 92 kilometres from Ahvaz, the centre of Khuzestan province. Much of its past agricultural productivity derived from an irrigation system centred on the Band-e Kaisar, the first dam bridge in Iran. The whole water system consists of 13 sites, called the Shoushtar Historical Hydraulic System, which UNESCO registered as a World Heritage Site on 26 June 2009. It was then the tenth work of Iran on the list.

The Band-e Kaisar, or Caesar's dam, is an overflow dam about 500 m long over the Karun. Tradition holds that after the Sasanian Shah Shapur I defeated the Roman emperor Valerian, he ordered the captive Roman soldiers to build a large bridge and dam. The structure shows typical Roman building techniques, and its dual-purpose design influenced Iranian civil engineering and the development of Sasanian water management. The traditional account is disputable, but it is not implausible that Roman prisoners were involved. It was repaired many times in the Islamic period and fell out of use in the late 19th century.

In Elamite times the city was known as Adamdun, and in the Achaemenid era as Šurkutir. According to tradition it was founded by king Hushang after he built Susa. In the Sasanian era it was an island city on the Karun, chosen as a summer capital; the river was channelled to form a moat, and qanats connected the river to private reservoirs, supplying water for homes and irrigation and during wartime when the gates were closed. Sugar cane cultivation there dates back to 226.

Shoushtar was always among the most important textile-producing cities in Khuzestan. Al-Istakhri, writing about 933, listed brocade and tiraz, and al-Maqdisi, about 1000, listed brocade, carpets, cotton and Merv-style clothes. Its commercial importance was recognized when it was chosen in 933 to produce the Kiswah, the embroidered covering for the Kaaba.

In 1831 a cholera epidemic killed about half of the inhabitants. The Karun steamship service of 1887 made Shoushtar the farthest point upstream, and it became the main commercial centre of south-western Iran, with 28,000 residents by 1938. After the Trans-Persian Railway bypassed it in favour of Ahvaz, its commerce and population declined.

Shoushtar is the capital of Shoushtar County in Khuzestan province. Most of its people speak Shoushtari, a dialect of Persian. It has a hot semi-arid climate. The Mandaean community of the Subbi Kush neighbourhood lived there for centuries, though Mandaeans no longer lived there by the 21st century because of emigration.
siad-barre: Mohamed Siad Barre was born to pastoral parents at a time when no birth records were kept, and guesses at his birth year range from 1909 to 1921. His father was Marehan and his mother Ogaden, both of the Darod clan family. By concealing his unofficial birthplace, as many others did, he became eligible for the Italian colonial police force and military in Somalia. He rose to command the Somali National Army.

After the assassination of President Abdirashid Shermarke, Barre came to power in the coup of 21 October 1969. The Supreme Revolutionary Council renamed the country the Somali Democratic Republic and made it a one-party Marxist–Leninist state, and a personality cult styled him the Victorious Leader. Early policies included the nationalisation of banks, industry and land, public works, and a literacy campaign. In 1972 Somali became the language of instruction, replacing Italian in the south and English in the north, and in 1973 highways linked the two regions. Somalia joined the Arab League in 1974, the year Barre chaired the Organization of African Unity. A law of 1970 allowed the security service to detain critics indefinitely without trial.

In 1977 Barre launched the Ogaden War against Ethiopia, and between September 1977 and March 1978 his forces captured virtually the whole Somali region. The Soviet Union then turned against him; he expelled its advisers and moved towards the United States, which gave about US$100 million a year in aid until 1989. His popularity declined after the defeat. After a coup attempt in 1978 most of those accused were summarily executed, and survivors who escaped abroad formed the first of the groups that opposed his regime by force. In May 1986 he was badly injured in a car accident.

Barre fled Mogadishu on 26 January 1991 as the Somali Rebellion ended his government, and the Somali Civil War followed. He twice tried to retake the capital from his family's stronghold at Burdhubo, but was overwhelmed by the army of Mohamed Farrah Aidid in May 1991 and went into exile, first in Nairobi and then in Nigeria. He died of a heart attack in Lagos on 2 January 1995, and his body was returned to Garbaharey for burial.
siberia: Siberia is a geographic and historic concept, not a political entity, so it has no single precise border. It stretches from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific Ocean and from the lands inside the Arctic Circle to the northern borders of Kazakhstan, Mongolia and China, and it covers over 13.1 million square kilometres, about three-quarters of Russia's area. Great rivers such as the Ob, the Yenisey and the Lena cross it. The climate runs from Arctic to temperate, with long, extremely cold winters; the January average is −25 °C.

Many nomadic groups lived in parts of Siberia over the millennia, among them the Xiongnu, the Huns, the Scythians and the Nenets. Later states reaching into the region included the Turkic khaganates, the Kyrgyz Khaganate, the Mongol Empire and the Khanate of Sibir. The Russian conquest began with the fall of the Khanate of Sibir in 1582. By the mid-17th century Russia controlled areas reaching the Pacific, and some 230,000 Russians had settled in Siberia by 1709.

Siberia became a destination for internal exiles, with more than 800,000 people exiled in the 19th century. The Trans-Siberian Railway, built in 1891–1916, tied the region to industrialising Russia, and around seven million Russians moved to Siberia between 1801 and 1914. In the Soviet period the Gulag administered penal labour camps, many of them in Siberia; according to semi-official Soviet estimates, more than 14 million people passed through the camps and prisons between 1929 and 1953.

Siberia holds roughly a quarter of Russia's population. Its largest cities are Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk and Omsk. More than 85 per cent of its people are of European descent, chiefly Russian, and the predominant religious group is the Russian Orthodox Church. Indigenous peoples include the Yakuts, Tuvans, Altai, Khakas and Buryats, and Siberia is traditionally regarded as the archetypal home of shamanism. The Trans-Siberian Railway still runs from Moscow to Vladivostok.
sibiu: Sibiu lies in the historical region of Transylvania, some 275 kilometres north-west of Bucharest, near the geographical centre of Romania. It straddles the Cibin River, a tributary of the Olt, in the Cibin Depression, about 20 kilometres from the Făgăraș Mountains. Its position makes it one of the important transport hubs of the country. In German the city is Hermannstadt, in Hungarian Nagyszeben, in Latin Cibinium and in the dialect of the Transylvanian Saxons Härmeschtat. It is nicknamed the Town with Eyes, for the eyebrow dormers on many old buildings.

The town was founded by Saxon settlers from territories of the Holy Roman Empire and the Kingdom of France, brought by King Géza II of Hungary in the mid to late 12th century as part of the Ostsiedlung. In 1191 Pope Celestine III confirmed the free prepositure of the Saxons in Transylvania, with its headquarters at Cibinium. The German name Hermannstadt dates from 1366. By the 14th century Sibiu was an important trade centre, and in 1376 its craftsmen were divided into 19 guilds. It was the most important of the seven cities that gave Transylvania its German name, Siebenbürgen.

Sibiu was home to the Transylvanian Saxon University, the community of ministers, councilmen and officials that built a legal and political order for the Saxons from the 1400s. After the Ottomans withdrew in the late 17th century it became capital of the Principality of Transylvania. In the 18th and 19th centuries it also became a major centre of Transylvanian Romanians, housing the first Romanian-owned bank and the cultural association ASTRA. Between 1848 and 1867 it was the meeting place of the Transylvanian Diet. From the 1950s to 1990 most of its ethnic Germans emigrated.

Sibiu is the seat of Sibiu County. Its museums are organised around the Brukenthal National Museum and the ASTRA National Museum Complex, which includes a 96-hectare open-air museum. The Radu Stanca National Theatre, with origins in 1787, has Romanian and German sections. Several fortified villages near the city were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993, and Sibiu was a European Capital of Culture in 2007, together with Luxembourg City.
sicilian-vespers: The rising had its origin in the struggle between the papacy and the Hohenstaufen Holy Roman Emperors for control of Italy. In 1245 Pope Innocent IV excommunicated Frederick II and declared him deposed. After Frederick's death in 1250 and that of his son Conrad IV in 1254, Frederick's illegitimate son Manfred seized the Kingdom of Sicily and reigned from 1258 to 1266. The popes would not recognise him. Pope Urban IV chose Charles of Anjou, who defeated and killed Manfred at the Battle of Benevento in 1266. Conradin, who invaded in 1268, was defeated at the Battle of Tagliacozzo and executed, leaving Charles undisputed master of the kingdom.

Charles regarded Sicily as a springboard for Mediterranean ambitions, including the capture of Constantinople. Sicilian nobles had no share in government, and the heavy taxes he imposed were spent on wars outside the island. Byzantine agents and Peter III of Aragon, Manfred's son-in-law, who saw his wife Constance as the rightful heir, fomented the unrest.

The revolt began at the Vespers prayer on Easter Monday, 30 March 1282, at the Church of the Holy Spirit just outside Palermo. The accounts differ on the spark. In Steven Runciman's version, a French sergeant named Drouet pestered a married woman, her husband killed him, and the crowd killed the other Frenchmen as the church bells rang. By the next morning some two thousand French men and women lay dead. According to Runciman, foreign friars were made to pronounce the word ciciri, which French speakers could not say correctly. Local tradition made John of Procida the mastermind, but modern sources consider that an exaggeration or an error.

The rebels controlled most of the island within a fortnight and all of it within six weeks except Messina, which rose on 28 April and burned Charles's fleet in its harbour. About 13,000 French men and women were slain or expelled. The towns asked Pope Martin IV to recognise them as free communes under his suzerainty, but the French pope directed them to accept Charles. They then turned to Peter III of Aragon, who landed at Trapani on 30 August 1282 and was crowned in Palermo on 4 September, becoming Peter I of Sicily.

Peter's involvement changed the revolt from a local rising into a European war, the War of the Sicilian Vespers. With the pope's blessing Charles's fleet from Naples blockaded Messina and tried several landings on the island, but all were repulsed. Pope Martin IV excommunicated Peter III, Michael VIII Palaiologos and John of Procida in 1282. Bartholomaeus of Neocastro later wrote the Historia Sicula, an important if sometimes contradictory source.
sicily: Sicily is roughly triangular, which gave it the ancient name Trinacria, from the Greek for having three headlands. The Strait of Messina, about 3 km wide in the north and about 16 km wide in the south, separates it from Calabria. The island covers 25,711 km2, and the Autonomous Region of Sicily, which includes the smaller islands of Lipari, Egadi, Ustica and Pantelleria, covers 27,708 km2. Inland the terrain is mostly hilly and intensively cultivated, and the mountain ranges of Madonie, Nebrodi and Peloritani along the north coast extend the mainland Apennines. Mount Etna dominates the east coast, and the fertile soil is the result of past volcanic eruptions.

Humans first colonized Sicily towards the end of the Late Pleistocene, around 16,000 years ago, and dolmens date to the second half of the third millennium BCE. The original classical-era inhabitants were three peoples: the Sicani, the Elymians and the Sicels. Thucydides writes that the Sicani, the earliest, arrived from the Iberian Peninsula. The Elymians are thought to have come from the Aegean. The Sicels, whose name the island bears, are thought to have originated in Liguria and arrived from mainland Italy in 1200 BCE, forcing the Sicani to the middle of the island. By around 750 BCE there were three Phoenician and about twelve Greek colonies along the coasts, and Sicily became a centre of Magna Graecia.

The Sicilian Wars of 580-265 BCE were fought between Carthaginians and Greeks, and the Punic Wars of 264-146 BCE between Rome and Carthage. The name Sicilia was given to the Roman province in 241 BCE. Later rulers included the Vandals, the Ostrogoths, the Byzantine Empire and the Emirate of Sicily. The Norman conquest created the County of Sicily in 1071 and the Kingdom of Sicily in 1130. After the Sicilian Vespers in 1282 the island was ruled by the Crown of Aragon and then Spain. In 1816 the kingdom joined with Naples to form the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and after Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand and a plebiscite the island joined Italy in 1860.

Sicily is one of Italy's twenty regions and one of its five autonomous ones, with special status granted on 15 May 1946. Its capital is Palermo. It has seven UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Valle dei Templi at Agrigento, the Roman mosaics of the Villa Romana del Casale, the Aeolian Islands and the Late Baroque towns of the Val di Noto. Millions of people of Sicilian origin live abroad, the result of emigration that began after Italian unification, first to the United States between the 1880s and the 1920s.
sidi-bel-abbes: Sidi Bel Abbès is named after Sidi bel Abbass, a Muslim marabout who is buried there. It lies 75 km from the Mediterranean, astride the Sig River, in a semi-arid climate, with Oran 70 km to the north and Tlemcen 90 km to the west. It is the commercial centre of an area of vineyards, market gardens, orchards and grain fields, and its economy rests on cereals, wheat and barley and the grape industry.

The present city developed around a French camp built in 1843 on the Wadi Sig. In 1849 a planned agricultural town was established around the existing military post, and the town was surrounded by a wall with four gates. It was closely associated with the French Foreign Legion until 1962, as the site of its basic training camp and the headquarters of its 1st Foreign Regiment. The main buildings stood in the French military district of the Quartier Vienot. In the late 1890s the town, described as having a Spanish appearance, had a civilian population of about 30,000.
In the 1930s much of the old city walls were demolished, and wide boulevards and squares replaced the traditional quarters, so that the town lost much of its former character.

Sidi Bel Abbès is the capital of the province of the same name and has the Djillali Liabès University. French-style landmarks remain, among them Place Carnot, renamed Place 1er Novembre after independence, Perrin Castle, and the town hall, which was formerly a cathedral. Raï music is the best-known music of the city. Natives of Sidi Bel Abbès include the French politician René Viviani, the mathematician Gaston Julia, known for the Julia set, and the boxer Marcel Cerdan.
sidon: Sidon stands on a mainland promontory with two harbours. Its Phoenician name, Ṣīdūn, probably meant fishery or fishing town. As a Roman colony it was renamed Colonia Aurelia Pia Sidon, and the Crusaders called it Sagittus in Latin and Saete or Sayette in Old French. Excavations show that the site has been inhabited since early prehistory: a stone tool assemblage of the Acheulean was found at Sidon II, and a Neolithic one at Sidon III. A settlement of the late Early Bronze Age I lies near the ruined Crusader castle.

Sidon may have been the oldest of the Phoenician cities, and a great Mediterranean trading network grew from it and other ports. Homer praised the skill of its craftsmen in glass and purple dye and of its women in embroidery. Tradition says a colonising party from Sidon founded Tyre, and the two cities later each claimed to be the mother city of Phoenicia. Around 1350 BCE it was part of the Egyptian Empire and ruled by Zimredda.

It was conquered in turn by the Assyrians, Babylonians, Egyptians, Persians, Greeks and Romans. Persian rule began in the 6th century BCE, and in exchange for its help in the conquest of Egypt, Cambyses II gave Sidon the territories of Dor, Joppa and the Plain of Sharon. Alexander the Great occupied it in 333 BCE.

Under Rome the city kept minting its own silver coins, and Herod built a theatre there. On 4 December 1110 King Baldwin I of Jerusalem and King Sigurd I of Norway captured it, and it became the centre of the Lordship of Sidon, a vassal state of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Saladin took it in 1187, and German Crusaders restored Christian rule in 1197. The Ayyubids destroyed it in 1249 and the Mongols under Kitbuqa again in 1260.

After Ottoman Turkish rule began in the early 16th century it became the capital of the Sidon Eyalet and regained much of its earlier commercial importance. In the 18th century the Hammud family of notables dominated the city and monopolised cotton exports. After the First World War it was part of the French Mandate of Lebanon.

Sidon is the capital of the South Governorate of Lebanon, and Beirut and Tyre are each about 40 kilometres away. The Sidon Sea Castle, built by the Crusaders in the early 13th century, stands near the port. The Khan al-Franj is a 16th-century caravanserai named for the French merchants it housed, though it was once wrongly credited to Emir Fakhreddine II. The Sidon Soap Museum traces the history of soap making in the region. Palestinian refugees who arrived after 1948 were settled in the camps of Ein el-Hilweh and Mieh Mieh.
sidonius-apollinaris: Gaius Sollius Modestus Apollinaris Sidonius was born at Lugdunum, the modern Lyon, into the Gallo-Roman aristocracy. His father was Prefect of Gaul under Valentinian III, and his grandfather Apollinaris held the same office from 408 to 409. Around 452 he married Papianilla, the daughter of Emperor Avitus.

His father-in-law became emperor in 455, and Sidonius wrote a panegyric for him. When Majorian deprived Avitus of the empire in 457 and seized Lyons, Sidonius fell into his hands, but his reputation for learning earned him respectful treatment. He composed a panegyric for Majorian, which won him a statue at Rome and the title of comes. In 468 the emperor Anthemius appointed him Urban Prefect of Rome, probably in part to win the support of the aristocrats of Gaul, and later made him a Patrician and Senator.

Sidonius was elected bishop of Clermont in succession to Eparchius, a relative of his wife. He says little about it and seems not to have wanted the post. He declared that he would give up pagan poetry as incompatible with religious life, but he went on writing verse privately. From 473 to 475 he and his brother-in-law Ecdicus led the defence of Clermont, which the Visigoths under King Euric attacked every year.

When the city was finally conquered he was imprisoned and exiled to Liviana, but Euric allowed him to return as bishop in 476 or 477 after the intervention of his adviser Leo. Sidonius accepted a degree of collaboration with the Visigothic court as necessary to keep the Roman aristocracy of Gaul together, yet he remained hostile to the Goths. He wrote to a senator, You shun barbarians because they have a bad reputation; I avoid them, even when they have a good one.

Twenty-four Carmina survive, occasional verse including panegyrics on emperors that draw on Statius, Ausonius and Claudian. Nine books of Letters preserve 147 documents addressed to 117 people, published in part in the early 470s and gathered in their final form around 477. Eric Goldberg calls him the single most important surviving author from 5th-century Gaul.

His Latin is deliberately elaborate and dense with classical and biblical allusion, which Sigrid Mratschek sees as a bulwark against the barbarians and a refuge from the dissolution of the old order. His letters cannot be read as plain description, since he modelled them on earlier letter writers, above all Pliny the Younger.
siege-engine: Siege engines ranged from the size of a small house to that of a large building. Some were built in place to attack from a distance, while others stood on wheels so that they could be advanced to the walls. From antiquity until the development of gunpowder they were made largely of wood, bound with rope or leather and possibly strengthened with a few pieces of metal at points of stress. Those that threw projectiles built up force by tension, by torsion or, in the trebuchet, by human power or a counterweight.

The earliest siege engines appear to be simple movable roofed towers, used with scaling ladders, depicted during the Middle Kingdom of Egypt. The Assyrians used battering rams, and in Kush siege towers and rams were built from the 8th century BCE. The Carthaginians used towers and rams against the Greek colonies of Sicily, which influenced Dionysius I of Syracuse, who developed a catapult in 399 BCE. Philip II of Macedonia and Alexander the Great were the first rulers to use siege engines to a large extent. The Helepolis of Demetrius Poliorcetes, of 304 BCE, was nine stories high, plated with iron, 40 metres tall and weighed 180 tonnes.

The Romans preferred to build earthen ramps or simply to scale the walls, their soldiers working under shelters called vineae. Roman legions first used siege towers around 200 BCE, and the onager was the main Roman invention in the field. In China the earliest documented siege artillery, a levered traction catapult and a large siege crossbow, is described in the Mozi, a Mohist text of about the 4th to 3rd century BCE.

Medieval armies used catapults such as the mangonel, the ballista, the traction trebuchet, first designed in China in the 3rd century BCE, and the counterweight trebuchet, first described by Mardi bin Ali al-Tarsusi in the 12th century though of unknown origin. Besiegers could also starve a castle out, set fires against its walls, dig mines under the foundations or throw diseased animals and human corpses over the walls to spread disease.

With gunpowder came the cannon, the petard and the mortar, which proved so effective that fortifications had to be built low and thick, as in the designs of Vauban. Specialised siege artillery culminated in the two world wars, with guns such as Big Bertha and the German Schwerer Gustav, a railway gun of 80 cm calibre. Such guns took so long to move and deploy that they were vulnerable to air attack and unsuited to rapid warfare.
siege-of-baghdad-1258: Baghdad was founded in 762 by al-Mansur, the second Abbasid caliph, and became the centre of the Islamic Golden Age. From the tenth century the Abbasids lost power, and the Buyids occupied Baghdad in 945 and the Seljuks in 1055. From 1230 Mongol generals raided Mesopotamia almost every year, though Baghdad remained unconquered.

After Möngke Khan became khan in 1251, he sent his brother Hulegu west to destroy the Nizari Ismaili Assassins and secure the submission of the caliphs, with one fifth of the empire's manpower. The Assassins' Grand Master surrendered on 19 November 1256. Hulegu had expected Caliph al-Musta'sim to provide troops, and the caliph's ministers persuaded him to refuse. A correspondence followed in September 1257, in which the caliph's reply called Hulegu young and ignorant, and his envoys were mocked by mobs in Baghdad.

Hulegu's armies invaded Mesopotamia from several sides. On 16 January 1258 the Mongol vanguard under Baiju broke the dykes of the Dujayl Canal and flooded the camp of the caliph's army, which was then routed. Hulegu reached the eastern suburbs on 22 January and encircled the city with a palisade and a moat. The assault began on 29 or 30 January, with catapults, naphtha and arrows carrying guarantees of safety for those who had not fought. The Mongols held the eastern wall by 4 February.

Hulegu insisted on unconditional surrender. On 7 February a large number of unarmed soldiers and inhabitants left the city and were divided into groups and executed. The caliph surrendered on 10 February with his family and 3,000 dignitaries. The sack began on 13 February and lasted a week. Hulegu spared Christians, scholars, sayyids and merchants who traded with the Mongols. On 20 February al-Musta'sim and his family were put to death; the caliph was wrapped in a carpet and trampled by horses, as the Mongols avoided shedding royal blood.

The number of dead is unknown. Later Muslim writers gave 800,000 to two million, and Hulegu himself claimed two million, a figure described as obviously inflated. An epidemic among the survivors raised the toll, and scholars have debated whether it was plague. Hulegu left on 8 March, ordering Baghdad rebuilt.

The fall ended the 500-year-old Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad. A member of the dynasty reached Cairo and was installed by the Mamluks as al-Mustansir II, but he and his descendants were puppets of the Mamluk state. Power moved towards cities such as Tabriz, capital of the Ilkhanate that Hulegu founded. Under the Ilkhanate Baghdad prospered, unlike the exaggerations of later Muslim historians, though it declined relative to Tabriz. The fall has traditionally been seen as the end of the Islamic Golden Age, though its real consequences are uncertain.
siege-of-jerusalem-1099: In 1095 Pope Urban II called for a crusade at the Council of Clermont, aiming to aid Byzantium against the Seljuks and to liberate Jerusalem. The main forces left Constantinople in April 1097 and besieged Antioch from October 1097, and after it fell in June 1098 the advance stood still for months amid power struggles between Bohemond of Taranto and Raymond IV of Toulouse, epidemics and shortages. Raymond resumed the march south in January 1099, following the coast and making agreements with local Muslim rulers or paying tribute rather than besieging fortified cities. The army reached Jerusalem on 7 June 1099.

Jerusalem had been under Fatimid rule since the 10th century. The governor, Iftikhar ad-Dawla, denied the crusaders water, food and wood near the city, expelled Syrian Christians who might sympathise with them and let Jews stay. Of the crusaders, between 12,000 and 14,000 reached the city, against a garrison of roughly a thousand Arab and Sudanese troops and some 400 Egyptian elite cavalry.

An attack on 13 June, prompted by a hermit's prophecy, failed for lack of siege engines. Under Guglielmo Embriaco and Gaston of Béarn the crusaders built two wheeled siege towers, an iron-headed battering ram and many ladders in almost three weeks.

The assault began in the night of 13 to 14 July, with the main attacks from Mount Zion and on the eastern part of the northern wall. On 14 July the ram pierced the wall but stuck, and the attack stopped with heavy losses, perhaps a fifth or a quarter of the Western armies. It resumed at midday on Friday 15 July, and when the tower was pushed against the wall the crusaders entered the city. Governor Iftikhar escaped, with others, to Ascalon after negotiating.

Thousands of Muslims and Jews were massacred, and the Muslim holy sites on the Temple Mount became Christian shrines. Jews who had defended the city were burned in their synagogue. There are no reliable figures: contemporary Arab claims of 70,000 or more dead are unrealistic against a population of about 30,000, and modern estimates range from 3,000 to 10,000. Atrocities after storming a city were normal in medieval warfare on both sides.

On 22 July Godfrey of Bouillon became Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri, refusing the title of king, and defeated a Fatimid army at Ascalon on 12 August. After his death on 18 July 1100, his brother Baldwin was crowned on Christmas Day in the Church of the Nativity as the first King of Jerusalem.
siege-warfare: A siege, from the Latin sedere, to sit, is a military blockade of a city or fortress, meant to conquer it by attrition or by a well-prepared assault. A siege arises when an attacker meets a place that cannot be taken by a quick assault and refuses to surrender. The attacker surrounds it to block supplies, reinforcements and escape, a step known as investment, and tries to reduce the fortifications with siege engines, artillery, mining or sapping, or through deception and treachery. Sieges were often decided by starvation, thirst or disease, which could strike either side.

City walls were essential to the first cities. The walls of Uruk in the ancient Near East were 9.5 km long and up to 12 m high, and some Indus Valley settlements were also fortified. The earliest known depictions of siege warfare, from the Protodynastic Period of Egypt about 3000 BCE, show the symbolic destruction of walls. Egyptian tomb reliefs of the 24th century BCE show the first siege equipment, wheeled ladders against Canaanite walls. Assyrian palace reliefs of the 9th to 7th centuries BCE show huge tower-shaped battering rams topped by archers.

Few siege works have been found archaeologically. The earliest known circumvallation, a trench 2.5 km long around Tell es-Safi/Gath, is thought to have been built by Hazael of Aram Damascus in the late 9th century BCE, and Sennacherib of Assyria built a siege system around Lachish in 701 BCE. During the Peloponnesian War a hundred sieges were attempted and fifty-eight ended in surrender.

Cannons were first used in Song dynasty China in the early 13th century but became significant only about 150 years later; by the 16th century they were essential to any army. In Spain the army of Ferdinand and Isabella took Moorish strongholds in Granada in 1482 to 1492 that had held out for centuries. The answer was the star-shaped fortress with low, thick walls and triangular bastions, the trace italienne. At the end of the 17th century Marshal Vauban and Menno van Coehoorn brought fortification to its height and turned the besieger's work into a methodical process.

Sieges dominated war in Western Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries, and a single siege could occupy a campaign, as at Ostend in 1601 to 1604. In the 20th century mobile warfare reduced the importance of the single fortress, though trench warfare of the First World War used siege techniques, and the Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 was met with an airlift.
siegen: Siegen lies in the basin of the upper reaches of the river Sieg, from which side valleys branch off in many directions. To the north lies the Sauerland, to the north-west the Rothaargebirge and to the south-west the Westerwald. The city covers roughly 115 square kilometres at a median elevation of 290 metres, and about 60 per cent of it is wooded. It is the seat of the district of Siegen-Wittgenstein. Municipal reforms and amalgamations in 1975 lifted its population above 100,000.

The name Siegen comes from the possibly Celtic name of the river Sieg. The place, called Sigena, is first mentioned in a document of 1079. The history of the city is shaped by mining, which began locally as far back as La Tène times, and many old mines lie within its limits. Siegen belonged at first to the Archbishopric of Mainz. The Nassau overlords introduced the Reformation in 1530, and a Franciscan monastery was dissolved in 1533.

The town was first Lutheran, but in 1550 the Principality of Nassau converted to the Reformed Church. Catholic worship regained ground in 1623, when one fifth of the townsfolk and people in the surrounding area became Catholic again, and a Jesuit monastery was founded in 1626. After the town passed to Prussia in 1815 the Lutheran and Reformed churches were united, though the parishes kept a Reformed emphasis.

Siegen had 20,000 inhabitants in 1897 and 40,000 by 1939. In World War II it lost roughly 30 per cent of its people, about 12,000, and was about 80 per cent destroyed. Its population fell to 28,000 by 1945 and regained its prewar level only in 1952.

The Oberes Schloss on the Siegberg, first mentioned in 1259, was the family seat of the House of Nassau and has housed the Siegerland Museum since 1905. Its collection centres on works by Peter Paul Rubens, arguably the best-known native of Siegen, and includes portraits of members of the Houses of Nassau and Orange. The Unteres Schloss took its present form late in the 17th century and was the home of the Protestant line of Nassau-Siegen, whose crypt lies inside. The Nikolaikirche has an unusual eight-sided shape and a golden coronet on its tower, so Siegen is sometimes called the Krönchenstadt. The Martinikirche dates from the 11th century.
siem-reap: Siem Reap is the capital and largest city of Siem Reap province in north-western Cambodia, and the second-largest city of the country. It lies close to the ancient temples of Angkor, built during the Khmer Empire, and about 30 minutes north of the Tonlé Sap, the great lake and river system that is central to Cambodia. It has a tropical wet and dry climate, with a wet season from May to October.

In the Angkor period the site was probably occupied by a town called Dvijendrapura, whose position may be marked by the old temple of Prah Einkosei. A stele there, inscribed in Sanskrit and Old Khmer and dated to 968 and 970 CE, records endowments made by the princess Indralakṣmī and her husband Divākara-bhaṭṭa.

The name Siem Reap is commonly translated as defeat of Siam. According to oral tradition King Ang Chan I (1516–1566) gave it after repulsing a Siamese army sent by King Maha Chakkraphat in 1549. Scholars such as Michael Vickery regard this as a modern folk etymology and hold that the origin of the name is unknown. Sources date the decline of Angkor to more than a century earlier, when a military expedition from Ayutthaya captured and sacked Angkor Wat in 1431, beginning a long period of vassal rule over Cambodia. Siem Reap, with Battambang and Sisophon, was under Siamese administration from 1795 until 1907, and the provinces were known collectively as Inner Cambodia.

Siem Reap was little more than a village when French explorers such as Henri Mouhot reached Angkor in the 19th century, although European visitors had seen the ruins earlier, among them António da Madalena in 1586. In 1901 the École française d'Extrême-Orient began its long work of clearing and restoring the site, and the first Western tourists arrived that year. Following a Franco-Siamese treaty in 1907 the area passed to Cambodia under French protection and Siem Reap began to grow. The Grand Hotel d'Angkor opened in 1929. In 1975 the Khmer Rouge drove the population of Siem Reap into the countryside, as in every Cambodian town.

Siem Reap has French-colonial and Chinese-style architecture in the Old French Quarter and around the Old Market. It is the gateway to Angkor, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that includes Angkor Wat, with its five towers symbolising Mount Meru and its bas-reliefs of Hindu narratives, and Angkor Thom, the royal city built by Jayavarman VII at the end of the 12th century and known for the Bayon. Tourism is the centre of the local economy. The Angkor National Museum opened on 12 November 2007.
siemens: Siemens & Halske was founded by Werner von Siemens and Johann Georg Halske on 1 October 1847. Its first product was a telegraph that used a needle to point to the letters of a message instead of Morse code, and its first workshop opened on 12 October. In 1848 the company built the first long-distance telegraph line in Europe, 500 km from Berlin to Frankfurt am Main. Werner's brother Carl Wilhelm Siemens began to represent it in London in 1850. In 1867 it completed the Indo-European telegraph line of over 11,000 km from London to Calcutta.

The firm was incorporated in 1897 and in 1903 merged part of its activities with Schuckert & Co. of Nuremberg to form Siemens-Schuckert. In 1919 it helped found the Osram lightbulb company, and in the 1920s and 1930s it began to make radios, television sets and electron microscopes. It built the Ardnacrusha hydroelectric station on the River Shannon in the Irish Free State in the 1920s. In 1932 a third parent company, Siemens-Reiniger-Werke, was formed.

From 1933 to 1945 Siemens-Schuckert exploited the forced labour of deported people. It owned a plant at Auschwitz, and a Siemens factory stood in front of the Ravensbrück concentration camp, where women were forced to work. By the end of 1944 the company ran almost 400 relocated plants because Allied air raids had destroyed factories in Berlin and other cities.

In 1962 Siemens & Halske agreed to make up to 7 million Deutsche Marks available to Jewish former forced labourers. From new bases in Bavaria the firm made computers, semiconductors and pacemakers in the 1950s, and in 1966 the three parent companies merged to form Siemens AG. Beginning in 2005 a multinational bribery scandal led to a settlement in December 2008, in which the company paid about $1.6 billion to the US and Germany.

Siemens is incorporated in Germany with its headquarters in Munich. Its principal divisions are Digital Industries, Smart Infrastructure and Mobility, with a financial services arm, and it has repeatedly sold off parts of its business, among them Infineon Technologies in 1999, Osram in 2013, Siemens Healthineers in 2017 and Siemens Energy in 2020.
sierra-leone: Sierra Leone lies on the south-west coast of West Africa, bordered by Guinea to the north and east, Liberia to the south-east and the Atlantic Ocean to the west. It has about 400 km of coastline. The east is a plateau with high mountains, where Mount Bintumani reaches 1,948 m, and lowland plains of forest, bush and farmland cover about 43% of the land. Freetown stands on a mountainous coastal peninsula. The name comes from the Lion Mountains near Freetown, which the Portuguese explorer Pedro de Sintra named Serra Leoa, meaning lioness mountains, in 1462.

The area has been inhabited for at least 2,500 years. Iron technology was adopted by the 9th century and agriculture established on the coast by about 1000 CE. Dense rainforest and swamps, and the tsetse fly, whose disease killed the horses and zebu cattle of the Mandé people, protected the region against invasion by the Mandinka Empire and limited the influence of the Mali Empire. Susu traders brought Islam in the 18th century.

European contact began in the 15th century. Traders from the Dutch Republic, England and France set up stations that came to deal mainly in slaves, brought to the coast by traders from the interior. In 1808 the coastal Sierra Leone Colony was founded as part of the British Empire, to resettle Africans returning after the abolition of the slave trade, and in 1896 an inland Protectorate was created. Independence came in 1961 under Prime Minister Sir Milton Margai. A constitution of 1971 made the country a presidential republic under Siaka Stevens. In 1991 a civil war began between the government and the Revolutionary United Front. It lasted 11 years and ended in 2002 after intervention by ECOMOG forces and then the United Kingdom.

Freetown is the capital and largest city. The country is a presidential republic, and English is the official language, while Krio, derived from English and several African languages, is spoken across the country. About 18 ethnic groups live there, the Temne and Mende being the largest, and the Creole people descend from freed African-American and Afro-Caribbean slaves and liberated Africans. Bunce Island, near Freetown, holds the ruins of a slave fortress of the Atlantic slave trade.
sierra-nevada-spain: The name Sierra Nevada means snow-covered mountain range. The range was formed during the Alpine Orogeny, the mountain-building event that also raised the European Alps and the Atlas Mountains of northern Africa, and its present form dates from the Paleogene and Neogene Periods, from 66 to 1.8 million years ago, when the African and Eurasian continental plates collided. At its foothills lies the city of Granada, with Almería and Motril a little further south.

A ridge running west-south-west to east-north-east is central to the range, and for a substantial distance the watershed stays above 3,000 metres. The southern side has several long, narrow river valleys leading south-west, while the steeper northern side is dominated by the Rio Genil, which starts near Mulhacén. The rock is chiefly soft micaceous schist. The climate is Mediterranean at lower levels and subarctic above 2,500 metres, so summer and winter daytime temperatures are some 12 degrees lower than in Granada, in an area otherwise known for high temperatures and abundant sunshine.

Parts of the range are included in the Sierra Nevada National Park, and the range has also been declared a biosphere reserve. It is one of the foremost plant biodiversity hotspots in the Western Mediterranean: 2,100 species of vascular plants have been recorded, of which 80 are endemic, including about 40 per cent of the high-elevation species. Evergreen oaks and maquis shrubland grow on dry, south-facing slopes, deciduous and conifer forests at higher elevations, and subalpine shrublands and grasslands at the highest. Wet grasslands on peat soils and around springs fed by snowmelt include many endemic species.

The high peaks make skiing possible at one of the most southerly ski resorts in Europe. The Sierra Nevada Observatory, the Calar Alto Observatory and the IRAM 30m telescope stand on the northern slopes at an elevation of 2,800 metres.
sierre: Sierre was first mentioned around 800 as Sidrium. The hill of Gerunden and the surrounding area were settled very early, and finds include neolithic objects, Bronze Age weapons and jewellery and Roman inscriptions. In the Roman period there seems to have been no major population centre but several scattered upper-class dwellings, and the duumvir of the Civitas Vallensium, Caius Cominus Chiu, lived there. In 515 King Sigismund of Burgundy gave the estate to the Abbey of Saint-Maurice as a fief, and by the 11th century it belonged to the Bishop of Sion.

The aristocratic families and residents lived on three hills, each with a castle serving as the residence of the bishop's representatives and as a refuge. The castles were razed in the middle of the 14th century when the noble families stood with the bishop in his war with the Zenden of the Upper Valais and the Counts of Savoy, and most residents settled farther north in Plan-Sierre.

The Contrée of Sierre began as a group that managed the common land, took on a larger political role in the 14th and 15th centuries and became the core of the Zenden of Sierre. As the capital of a Zenden, Sierre fought the French in the invasion of 1798 and 1799, and in 1799 French and Vaudois troops occupied it.

Sierre lies in the middle Rhône valley, on the right bank of the river, and is the capital of the district of Sierre. It is the last official French-speaking town in the canton before the language border, which is marked by the Raspille mountain stream and the forest of Finges. About 8 percent of its people speak German. It is nicknamed the City of the Sun for its average of 300 days of sunshine a year, and its coat of arms is a golden sun on red.

After 1848 the villages of the Noble Contrée became municipalities and the Zenden became the District of Sierre. At the beginning of the 20th century aluminium smelting, enabled by hydroelectricity, made the town economically important. Sierre is a starting point for the Val d'Anniviers and is linked to Crans-Montana by a funicular railway.
sigismund-holy-roman-emperor: Sigismund was the son of Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor, and his fourth and final wife, Elizabeth of Pomerania. His place and exact date of birth are disputed: his mother's letter points to 14 February 1368, and in 1892 Theodor Lindner gave 15 February and Nuremberg. In the Bohemian Crown lands he was nicknamed the ginger fox because of his hair. He was betrothed in 1374 to Mary, eldest daughter of King Louis I of Hungary, to augment the lands of the House of Luxembourg. After his father's death in 1378 he became Margrave of Brandenburg and was sent to the Hungarian court, where he learned the language, and in 1381 he was sent to Kraków to learn Polish.

Mary became queen of Hungary in 1382, and Sigismund married her in 1385. In 1396 he led the Crusade of Nicopolis, and was decisively defeated by the Ottoman Empire. Afterwards he founded the Order of the Dragon to fight the Turks. After King Rupert's death in 1410 three electors chose him as king of Germany, but a rival election made Jobst of Moravia king too; Jobst died on 18 January 1411, and Sigismund was elected again on 21 July 1411 and crowned at Aachen on 8 November 1414.

He took a leading part in the Council of Constance, which ended the Western Schism. It also had Jan Hus burned at the stake in July 1415, and historians debate Sigismund's complicity: he had granted Hus a safe conduct and protested against his imprisonment, and Hus was condemned by a Church court in his absence. When Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia died in 1419, Sigismund became titular king, but the Czech Estates, who distrusted him as the betrayer of Hus, did not acknowledge him for seventeen years. Three campaigns against the Hussites ended in disaster. He received the Iron Crown at Milan on 25 November 1431 and was crowned emperor in Rome on 31 May 1433.

Sigismund died on 9 December 1437 at Znojmo in Moravia and was buried at Nagyvárad, next to the tomb of King Saint Ladislaus I of Hungary. He was the last male member of the House of Luxembourg, and his only surviving legitimate child was Elisabeth of Luxembourg, so the succession passed on. Historian Thomas Brady Jr. remarks that he possessed a breadth of vision and a sense of grandeur unseen in a German monarch since the thirteenth century. His difficulties with the Hussites are now generally seen as the result of a lack of financial resources and other constraints, not of personal failings.
sigismund-i-the-old: Sigismund was born on 1 January 1467 at Kozienice, the fifth son of Casimir IV Jagiellon, and was not expected to rule. When Casimir died in 1492 he was the only son without titles or land. His efforts to get land from his brother Alexander and an Austrian throne failed, as did an invasion of Moldavia in 1497. His eldest brother Vladislaus II, king of Bohemia and Hungary, then granted him the duchies of Głogów in 1499 and Opava in 1501, and in 1504 he became governor of Silesia and Lower Lusatia.

After Alexander I died in 1506, the Lithuanian Ducal Council elected Sigismund grand duke on 20 September, and the Polish Senate at Piotrków elected him king on 8 December. He was crowned at Wawel Cathedral on 24 January 1507. He summoned annual sessions of the Sejm and issued statutes between 1530 and 1538 that fixed the free election of the monarch. His reforms included a permanent conscription army in 1527 and the recovery of royal properties that had been pawned to nobles, which provoked the Chicken War of 1537, a revolt of the lesser nobility at Lwów. Sigismund rejected most of the demands and accepted only the principle that one person could not hold two offices.

War against Muscovy brought the loss of Smolensk in 1514 but a Polish and Lithuanian victory at Orsha on 8 September 1514, and the commander Jan Amor Tarnowski stopped a Muscovite invasion at Starodub in 1535. The Treaty of Kraków of 1525 ended two centuries of wars with the Teutonic Knights: the Order was secularised and his nephew Albert, who had become a Lutheran, became Duke of Prussia and paid homage to Poland. After the death of Janusz III of Masovia in 1526 Sigismund united that duchy and Warsaw with the kingdom.

Sigismund married first Barbara Zápolya and then Bona Sforza, daughter of the Duke of Milan, who supported his purchase of land and improvements of the royal estates. Under her influence Italian styles dominated at the height of the Polish Renaissance.
