His only surviving legitimate son, Sigismund Augustus, was made co-king in 1529 and took the throne when his father died on 1 April 1548.
sigismund-ii-augustus: Sigismund Augustus was born in Kraków on 1 August 1520, the elder of two sons of Sigismund I the Old and Bona Sforza of Milan, and the only one to survive infancy. He was educated by the leading scholars in the country. His mother wished to name him Augustus, either for the month of his birth or after the first Roman Emperor.

Because the Polish crown was elective, his parents secured his succession by having him chosen king in his father's lifetime. He was inaugurated as Grand Duke of Lithuania on 18 October 1529, named King of Poland alongside his father on 18 December and crowned at the age of nine on 20 February 1530 by Primate Jan Łaski. The nobles criticised this election, which became one of the reasons for the Lwów Rokosz in 1537. He began his reign as active Grand Duke in 1544 and at first opposed the Polish–Lithuanian union, hoping to leave his throne to heirs, since the Lithuanian throne was hereditary and the Polish was not.

He married Elizabeth of Austria on 5 May 1543, when she was 16 and he 22. Queen Bona plotted against her, and the couple settled in Vilnius. Elizabeth died in 1545 at 18. In July or August 1547 he secretly married Barbara Radziwiłł, who was despised by Bona. The deputies of his first Sejm, on 31 October 1548, threatened to renounce their allegiance unless he repudiated her, and he even considered abdicating. After his father's death on 1 April 1548 he declared her Queen on 17 April, and she died five months after her coronation. His third wife was Catherine of Austria. Neither marriage produced living children.

His reign saw the bloodless introduction of the Protestant Reformation into Poland and Lithuania, and the collapse of the Knights of the Sword in the north, which led to the Commonwealth's acquisition of Livonia as a Lutheran duchy. He kept a policy of tolerance towards minorities and peaceful relations with neighbours, except for the Northern Seven Years' War, fought to secure Baltic trade. He established the first regular Polish navy and the first regular postal service in Poland, and in 1569 oversaw the signing of the Union of Lublin, which formed the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Culture flourished under his patronage, and he collected tapestries from the Low Countries.

Sigismund Augustus died on 7 July 1572, the last male monarch of the Jagiellonian dynasty. The dynasty ended with the death of his sister Anna in 1596. His rule is widely considered the apex of the Polish Golden Age.
sigismund-iii-vasa: Sigismund was born on 20 June 1566 at Gripsholm Castle, the second child and only son of Catherine Jagiellon and Grand Duke John III of Sweden. The couple had been held prisoner there since 1563, after John staged a failed rebellion against his brother Eric XIV of Sweden. Catherine was a daughter of King Sigismund I the Old of Poland, and Sigismund was raised as a Catholic, although his younger sister Anna Vasa of Sweden was a Lutheran.

In 1587 he stood for election to the Polish throne after the death of Stephen Báthory. Queen Dowager Anna and several magnates backed him as a descendant of the Jagiellons, while nobles associated with the Zborowski family opposed him. He was elected on 19 August 1587.

Chancellor Jan Zamoyski was hostile to the king almost from his arrival, criticising his liking for Habsburg culture and his cold character. The king's friends came largely from the higher clergy and the Jesuits, and religious freedoms guaranteed by the Warsaw Confederation of 1573 came under pressure. When mob violence against non-Catholics broke out in Vilnius and Kraków in 1591, dissidents gathered in conventions and Sigismund had to yield to their demands. In 1606 his efforts to strengthen royal authority provoked the Zebrzydowski rebellion, an armed rising of nobles and magnates.

After succeeding his father in 1592 he also ruled Sweden, where the Uppsala Resolution of 1594 had promised to uphold the Lutheran faith. He placed his own commanders in the castles and appointed Catholics to high office, which angered many Swedes. A civil war began in 1597 under his uncle Duke Charles, who took most of the castles. Sigismund accepted a peace at Linköping, then fled to Poland with his sister, and Charles deposed him in 1599.

In the east he used the Russian Time of Troubles to invade from 1609, and the campaign ended with the seizure of Smolensk and the occupation of Moscow. A Polish–Ottoman war followed in 1620–1621 over Moldavia. In 1626 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden invaded and later annexed parts of Polish Livonia.

Towards the end of his reign Sigismund withdrew from politics and devoted himself to family matters and the performing arts. In his last days he was bedridden with gout and joint pain. His rule of nearly 45 years is seen as controversial: it brought considerable developments in architecture, the arts and culture, but also conspiracies, religious conflict and the long war with Sweden. His policies began the Counter-Reformation in Poland–Lithuania and weakened Protestantism there. Szymon Starowolski ranked him above his predecessors, while opponents thought he had lived too long. His son Władysław IV Vasa succeeded him and later commissioned the column in Warsaw that bears his name.
sigmaringen: Sigmaringen lies in the Danube valley, surrounded by wooded hills, south of the Swabian Alps and about 40 km north of Lake Constance. It is the capital of the Sigmaringen district. The town is known for its castle, Schloss Sigmaringen, which was the seat of the principality of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen until 1850 and is still owned by the Hohenzollern family.

The first castle was built in the 11th century on the rock that protects the valley. The first written reference dates from 1077, when King Rudolf of Rheinfelden tried in vain to conquer it. The town was officially founded in 1250, and in 1325 it was sold to Ulrich III, Count of Württemberg. The castle was rebuilt into a chateau in 1460 and 1500. In 1535 Sigmaringen came into the hands of the Hohenzollern through the county of Werdenberg, and it belonged to the principality of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen from 1576. The Swedes occupied the castle in 1632 during the Thirty Years' War.

From 1806 to 1849 Sigmaringen was the capital of the sovereign principality and the residence of the princes of Hohenzollern. After the Sigmaringen Revolution of 1848 the princes of Hechingen and Sigmaringen abdicated, and both principalities fell to Prussia in 1850. Until 1945 the town was the seat of the Prussian government of the Province of Hohenzollern, and Karl Anton von Hohenzollern was Prime Minister of Prussia from 1858 to 1862. Carol I of Romania, born there in 1839, was king of Romania from 1866 to 1914, and Ferdinand I, born there in 1865, reigned from 1914 to 1927.

On 7 September 1944, after the Allied invasion of France, Philippe Pétain and members of the Vichy cabinet were relocated to Germany, against Pétain's fierce resistance. A government in exile headed by Fernand de Brinon was set up at Sigmaringen, with embassies of Germany, Italy and Japan. The writers Louis-Ferdinand Céline and Lucien Rebatet fled there with it, and Céline's novel D'un château l'autre describes its fall. Free French forces took the town on 22 April 1945.

Three railways meet in Sigmaringen: the Ulm to Sigmaringen line, the Tübingen to Sigmaringen line, and the line from Engstingen operated by the Hohenzollerische Landesbahn. Among the people born there are the Capuchin martyr Fidelis of Sigmaringen, born in 1577, and the physician Theodor Bilharz, who made discoveries in parasitology.
sigmund-freud: Sigmund Freud was born Sigismund Schlomo Freud on 6 May 1856 in the Moravian town of Freiberg, in the Austrian Empire, now Příbor in the Czech Republic. He was the first of eight children of Ashkenazi Jewish parents who both came from Galicia. His father, Jakob Freud, was a wool merchant, and his mother, Amalia Nathansohn, was Jakob's third wife. The family was struggling financially and living in a rented room when he was born. He was born with a caul, which his mother saw as a good omen.

Freud took almost nine years to finish his medical studies, because of his interest in neurophysiological research, including the sexual anatomy of eels, and in philosophy under Franz Brentano. He entered private practice in neurology for financial reasons and received his doctorate in medicine in 1881, aged 25. In the 1880s he worked chiefly on the anatomy of the brain. In 1891 his monograph Zur Auffassung der Aphasien entered the debates about aphasia, coined the term agnosia and counselled against too locationist a view of neurological deficits.

He was also an early researcher of cerebral palsy, then called cerebral paralysis, and showed that the disease existed long before other researchers studied it. He suggested that William John Little, who first identified it, was wrong that lack of oxygen at birth was a cause, and proposed instead that birth complications were a symptom. Freud died on 23 September 1939.

Freud founded psychoanalysis, a clinical method that treats conflicts in the psyche through dialogue between patient and analyst. He introduced free association, the interpretation of dreams and the analysis of transference. He widened the idea of sexuality to include infantile stages, which led to the Oedipus complex, and developed a theory of the unconscious and a model of the mind with id, ego and superego. His later work offered an interpretation and critique of religion and culture.

His books include The Interpretation of Dreams (1899), Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), Totem and Taboo (1913), The Ego and the Id (1923), The Future of an Illusion (1927), Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) and Moses and Monotheism (1939). His talking cure gave the basic format for later psychotherapy. The neo-Freudians, among them Alfred Adler and Karen Horney, rejected his theory of instinctual drive, and Jacques Lacan approached psychoanalysis through linguistics and literature. His legacy remains controversial.
sigtuna: Sigtuna lies in Stockholm County on Skarven, a bay of Lake Mälaren. The present harbour town developed about 4 kilometres east of Old Sigtuna, which, according to Old Norse religion, was once the home of the widely revered god Odin. The name is closely linked with the higher land to the north, Signhildsberg, and its second element means a settlement. The first element may come from dialect words for seeping water or swamp, since the estate was surrounded by marshy terrain, or the name may be an old prestigious name meaning strong fortress, from a word for victory.

Sigtuna was founded on what was then the shore of Lake Mälaren just over a thousand years ago and took its name from an ancient royal estate several kilometres to the west. Some sources name King Eric the Victorious as founder and others King Olof Skötkonung. It operated as a royal and commercial centre for some 250 years and was one of the most important cities of Sweden. At the end of the 10th century and the beginning of the 11th, Sweden's first coins were minted there.

The Dominican monastery played an important role in the Swedish Middle Ages and produced many important church officials, among them many Swedish archbishops. Its church, St Mary's, built in the 13th century, remains largely intact. In 1187 raiders from across the Baltic Sea attacked and pillaged Sigtuna, possibly from Curonia, from the island of Saaremaa, or Karelians and Novgorodians, though excavations have not verified the tradition of destruction. The town began slowly to lose its importance in the 13th century because post-glacial rebound caused navigability problems. Its first known seal dates from 1311, and in the late 19th century it had only about 600 people, the smallest town in Sweden.

Sigtuna is a locality in Sigtuna Municipality, still often called a stad for historical reasons. It has a medieval-style town centre with the old main street, Stora gatan, the small old town hall, Viking runestones and several church ruins, among them St Per's Church from the 1100s, St Olof's Church from around the middle of the 11th century and St Lars's Church from the middle of the 13th. Its population growth in the second half of the 20th century is related to Stockholm Arlanda Airport, 10 kilometres away.
sikasso: Sikasso was a small village until Tieba Traoré, whose mother came from there, became faama, or ruler, of the Kénédougou Kingdom and moved the capital to it. He established his palace on the sacred Mamelon hill and built a massive tata, a defensive wall, against attacks by the Malinke conqueror Samori Ture and by the French colonial army. This made Sikasso the largest fortified city ever built in West Africa.

The city withstood a siege by Samori Ture that lasted fifteen months, from 1887 to 1888, before the French, who were allies of Kénédougou against him, relieved it. The French nevertheless contrived a diplomatic crisis to attack in 1898. They began a major artillery barrage against the tata on 15 April 1898, and the city fell on 1 May amid furious house-to-house fighting. It then had around 30,000 inhabitants.

Babemba Traoré, Tieba's brother and successor as faama, ordered his bodyguards to kill him rather than let him fall into French hands. He is remembered for upholding a Bambara saying, usually rendered as death is preferable to shame. About 4,000 captives were taken in the sack and shared out as slaves among the French and their African auxiliaries. They were marched west to the Niger, and many, too weak or starved to continue, died or were killed on the way.

Sikasso lies 375 kilometres south-east of Bamako, 100 kilometres north of Côte d'Ivoire and 45 kilometres west of Burkina Faso, and acts as a crossroads between the coastal countries and landlocked Mali and Burkina Faso. It is the capital of the Sikasso Cercle and the Sikasso Region and the second largest city of Mali, with 225,753 residents in the 2009 census. Its ethnic groups include the Senufo, the Bobo and the Minianka.

The surrounding country has abundant agriculture, and the city produces enough fruit and vegetables to feed itself. Its attractions include the large market, the Mamelon hill, the remains of Tieba Traoré's tata and the nearby Missirikoro Grotto. A festival of the balafon, a traditional Malian instrument, is held each June.
sikh-empire: By the mid-18th century a confederation of twelve Sikh states, the misls, was established in central and eastern Punjab, and their Dal Khalsa armies fought the Mughals and the invading Afghans under Ahmad Shah Abdali. Ranjit Singh was born in 1780 into the ruling family of the Sukerchakia misl and succeeded his father at the age of thirteen. After Zaman Shah Durrani invaded the Punjab and withdrew in 1797–98, Ranjit Singh captured Lahore, and in 1799 he moved his capital there from Gujranwala. He was formally crowned on 12 April 1801 by Sahib Singh Bedi, a descendant of Guru Nanak.

Ranjit Singh annexed the other misls, beginning with Amritsar in 1802, and by 1813 all were under his rule. Afghan influence east of the Indus ended with the fall of Multan in 1818, and Kashmir and Peshawar were later lost by the Durrani Afghans to the Sikhs. By 1840 Ladakh and Baltistan had come under Sikh suzerainty through Gulab Singh. At its height the empire reached from Gilgit in the north to the Sindh deserts in the south and from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej. Ranjit Singh modernised his army with new training, weapons and artillery. The British policy of confining him to the north of the Sutlej led to the river becoming the boundary between the two states.

After Ranjit Singh's death in 1839 the empire was weakened by internal divisions, which the British East India Company is said to have stoked, and by political mismanagement. It was dissolved in 1849 after its defeat in the Second Anglo-Sikh War, and it was the last major region of the subcontinent to be conquered by the British.

The court at Lahore was known as the Lahore Darbar or Khalsa Darbar, and the state itself in its own chronicles as the Sarkar Khalsaji. In theory it rested on the ideals of the Khalsa, but in practice it was secular, with Sikhs, Hindus, Muslims and Christians serving at court. The Fakir brothers, Muslims who served as advisers, included Fakir Azizuddin, foreign minister and translator, who advised Ranjit Singh against war with the British in 1808. Land revenue provided about 70 percent of income, and the court observed Vaisakhi, Dussehra, Basant, Holi and Diwali. Estimates of the population vary widely, and most of its people were Muslims.
sikhism: Sikhism, also called Sikhi, developed from the teachings of Guru Nanak (1469–1539), the first guru, and the nine gurus who followed him. Nanak was born in the village now called Nankana Sahib, in present-day Pakistan, to Punjabi Khatri Hindu parents. The hagiography Puratan Janamsakhi, composed more than two centuries after his death, says that after a disappearance of three days he declared, "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim". In 1526 he started a small commune at Kartarpur, and his disciples came to be known as Sikhs, a word meaning students or disciples.

In 1539 Nanak chose his disciple Lahiṇā, who became Guru Angad, as successor rather than either of his sons. The Mughal emperors tortured and executed two gurus, Guru Arjan (1563–1606) and Guru Tegh Bahadur (1621–1675), who refused to convert to Islam. In 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, an order meant to protect freedom of conscience, whose members express the qualities of the sant-sipāhī, the saint-soldier.

Sikhs hold that only one God exists, present in everything, a oneness expressed in the phrase Ik Onkar. The word for God is Waheguru. Central practices are remembrance of the divine name (simran), selfless service (sevā), honest work and sharing with those in need. Nanak is quoted as saying, "Truth is the highest virtue, but higher still is truthful living." Sikhism rejects the claim that any religious tradition has a monopoly on truth, and Sikhs do not actively proselytise, though voluntary converts are generally accepted.

The Khalsa is the name Guru Gobind Singh gave to Sikhs fully initiated in the ceremony of ammrit sañcār, in which sweetened water is stirred with a double-edged sword. Baptised Sikhs wear the five Ks, which include the kesh, uncut hair, so that most religious Sikh men wear a turban. Gurdwaras are open to all.

The central scripture is the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh decreed in 1708 that it would be the final and perpetual guru, closing the line of human gurus, and Sikhs regard it as the eleventh and eternally living guru. Its earlier form, the Ādi Granth, was compiled primarily by Bhai Gurdas under Guru Arjan in 1603 and 1604. It contains the hymns of the gurus and of thirteen Hindu and two Muslim bhagats of the Bhakti tradition, among them Kabir and the Sufi saint Farid. It is written as poetry for recitation in thirty-one ragas. The Dasam Granth, containing texts attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, does not have the same authority.
sikhs: The word Sikh comes from the Sanskrit word for seeker, disciple or student. Guru Nanak, who lived from 1469 to 1539, was born into a Hindu Khatri family in the village of Talwandi, near Lahore, now Nankana Sahib. According to the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a Sikh is a person who faithfully believes in one immortal being, the Gurus from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh, the Guru Granth Sahib and the teachings of the Gurus, and in the initiation called Amrit Sanchar, and who owes allegiance to no other religion. Early followers were mostly Khatris, and many Jats joined later.

Sikh political history may be said to begin in 1606, with the death of the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan. On 30 March 1699 Guru Gobind Singh initiated five people from varied social backgrounds, known as the Panj Piare, to form the Khalsa, the collective body of initiated Sikhs. In the 18th and 19th centuries the Punjab was ruled by Sikhs for significant periods, and Mughal and Afghan persecution in the 17th and 18th centuries left little room for art, which changed under Ranjit Singh and the Sikh rule at Lahore.

After the British annexed the Sikh kingdom, large numbers of Sikhs were recruited into the British Army, and the Sikhs stayed loyal during the 1857 mutiny. The Singh Sabha movements of 1873 and 1879 worked to define Sikh identity, and the Akali movement of the 1920s led to the Sikh Gurdwara Bill of 1925, which placed historic shrines under the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. In 1947 the partition of the Punjab was marked by conflict, and Sikhs and Hindus moved east as Muslims moved west. Sikh migration abroad began in earnest in the second half of the 19th century.

Initiated Sikhs, known as Khalsa, wear five articles of faith: uncut hair, usually covered by a turban, a steel bracelet, a short sword, a cotton undergarment and a small wooden comb. Male Sikhs generally take the last name Singh, meaning lion, and female Sikhs Kaur, meaning princess, names given by the Gurus partly as a rejection of caste. Sikh devotional music, Gurmat Sangeet, sets the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib to ragas. About 25 to 30 million Sikhs live in the world, most of them in India.
silent-night: The carol was composed in 1818 by Franz Xaver Gruber, schoolmaster and organist in the nearby village of Arnsdorf, to words by Father Joseph Mohr. On Christmas Eve 1818 Mohr brought the poem to Gruber and asked him to write a melody and guitar accompaniment for that night's mass, after river flooding had possibly damaged the church organ. The church was later destroyed by repeated flooding and replaced by the Silent-Night-Chapel. "Stille Nacht" was first performed on Christmas Eve 1818 at the Nikolauskirche, the parish church of Oberndorf. Several films repeat the story of a broken organ, which appeared in a fictional account published in the U.S. in the 1930s.

A manuscript in Mohr's handwriting, found in 1995 and dated by researchers to about 1820, shows that he wrote the words in 1816 at the pilgrim church of Mariapfarr and that Gruber composed the music in 1818. It is the earliest manuscript known. Before its discovery the carol was often attributed to better-known composers such as Haydn, Mozart and Schubert.

Mohr's poem had six verses. The melody Gruber wrote was a moderato tune in 6/8 time with a siciliana rhythm. The melody changed slightly in the early decades of its spread, and the slow, meditative lullaby or pastorale sung today differs from Gruber's original, especially in its final strain. In 1859 the Episcopal priest John Freeman Young, then at Trinity Church in New York City, published the English translation sung most often today, made from three of the original six verses. The carol has been translated into about 300 languages. Its words and melody are in the public domain.

Karl Mauracher, an organ builder who serviced the Oberndorf organ, took the song home to the Zillertal, where two families of travelling folk singers, the Strassers and the Rainers, added it to their shows. The Rainers were singing it by about Christmas 1819 and performed it before Franz I of Austria and Alexander I of Russia. They gave its first performance in the U.S., in New York City in 1839. By the 1840s it was known in Lower Saxony and was reported to be a favourite of Frederick William IV of Prussia. The first edition appeared in 1833 in a collection of Four Genuine Tyrolean Songs.

The carol was first recorded in 1905, and more than 137,000 recordings are known. Composers who have arranged it include Carl Reinecke, John Rutter and David Willcocks, and UNESCO declared it an intangible cultural heritage in 2011.
silistra: Silistra lies on the southern bank of the lower Danube in the Bulgarian part of the historical region of Dobruja, at the point where the border with Romania stops following the river. It is the administrative centre of Silistra Province. The name is possibly derived from the root of Istrum, the old Thracian name of the lower Danube. Landmarks include a richly decorated Late Roman tomb, remains of the medieval fortress and an Ottoman fort.

After the Roman province of Moesia was founded in 12 CE, the Romans built a fort in 29 on the site of an earlier Thracian settlement and kept its name, Durostorum. After Trajan's Dacian Wars it was enlarged into a legionary fortress for the Legio XI Claudia, which stayed there from before 114 until about 400, and it grew into a city at the time of Marcus Aurelius.

Durostorum became a bishopric and a centre of Christianity in the region. The earliest saints of Bulgaria are Roman soldiers executed there in the Diocletian Persecution, among them Saint Dasius, and the Roman general Flavius Aëtius was born in the town in 396.

Around the end of the 7th century the town was incorporated into the First Bulgarian Empire, as Drastar, and its bishop was proclaimed the first patriarch of Bulgaria. In 895 Simeon I the Great held the fortress against besieging Hungarians. Sviatoslav I of Kiev captured it in 969, and the Byzantines took it two years later in the Battle of Dorostolon.

Tsar Samuel restored Bulgarian rule in 976, and the Byzantines regained the town in 1001. It joined the Second Bulgarian Empire after the rebellion of Asen and Peter in 1186 and withstood a three-month Mongol siege in 1279. It remained Bulgarian until the Ottoman conquest of the Balkans around 1400.

Under Ottoman rule Silistre was the centre of a sanjak and later of a large province. It was besieged between 14 April and 23 June 1854 during the Crimean War, an event that inspired Namık Kemal's play Vatan Yahut Silistre. Silistra joined Bulgaria in 1878. It passed to Romania in 1913, was held by Bulgaria from 1916, returned to Romania by the Treaty of Neuilly in 1919 and became Bulgarian again in 1940, a transfer confirmed in 1947.

Silistra is a cultural, industrial, transport and educational centre of north-eastern Bulgaria. The grave of the rabbi Eliezer Papo, who served the Jewish community from 1819 to 1826, is a place of pilgrimage. The Roman general Flavius Aëtius, who defeated Attila the Hun, is the town's best-known native.
silk: Silk is a natural protein fibre, composed mainly of fibroin with a smaller coating of sericin, most commonly made from the cocoons of insect larvae. The best-known silk comes from the mulberry silkworm, Bombyx mori, reared in captivity in a process called sericulture. The production of silk originated in central China in the Neolithic period. The earliest evidence is the silk protein fibroin found in soil from two tombs at Jiahu in Henan, about 8,500 years old, and the earliest surviving silk fabric, from about 3630 BCE, wrapped the body of a child at a Yangshao culture site in Henan.

Silk production remained confined to China until the Silk Road opened, at some point in the latter part of the 1st millennium BCE, and China kept a virtual monopoly on it for another thousand years. Wild silks were spun in China, South Asia and Europe from ancient times, but always on a far smaller scale.

The Roman Empire knew of silk and traded in it, and Chinese silk was the most highly priced luxury good it imported. Under the emperor Tiberius, sumptuary laws forbade men to wear silk, but they proved ineffectual. The secret of silk-making reached Europe only around 550, by way of the Byzantine Empire; contemporary accounts say monks working for the emperor Justinian I smuggled silkworm eggs from China to Constantinople inside hollow canes. The best looms and weavers worked inside the Great Palace there, and the cloth was used for imperial robes and as diplomatic gifts.

Italy was the leading producer in the medieval period, beginning at Catanzaro in the 11th century. Bengal was the leading exporter of silk between the 16th and 19th centuries, and silkworms were brought to Oaxaca from Spain in the 1530s.

Silk is not spun like other natural fibres. The cocoons are soaked in boiling water to remove the sericin and free the end of the filament, which is then reeled off in one continuous length. A caterpillar spins about one mile (1.6 km) of filament in two or three days, and since one thread is too fine for commercial use, three to ten strands are twisted together. The flat surfaces of the fibrils reflect light at many angles, which gives silk its natural sheen. It was used for clothing and furnishings, and also in parachutes and bicycle tyres.
silver: Silver was known in prehistoric times. Copper, silver and gold occur in elemental form in nature and were probably the first primitive forms of money, replacing simple barter. Unlike copper, silver did not lead to the growth of metallurgy, because of its low structural strength; it was used mostly for ornament or as money. Native silver was much scarcer than native gold, and in Egypt silver was more expensive than gold until about the fifteenth century BCE.

The discovery of cupellation, which extracts silver from its ores, changed this. Slag heaps in Asia Minor and on the Aegean islands show silver being separated from lead as early as the 4th millennium BCE, and Sardinia was one of the earliest extraction centres in Europe, in the early Chalcolithic. The techniques spread widely only later.

Silver is a soft, ductile and malleable metal, slightly less malleable than gold, with a brilliant white lustre that takes a high polish; the name of the metal has become the name of a colour. It is one of the seven metals of antiquity and sits in group 11 of the periodic table with copper and gold. Because pure silver is so soft, silver used for jewellery, coinage and household objects is usually alloyed with copper.

The English word comes from Old English seolfor and siolfor, with cognates in Old High German silabar, Gothic silubr and Old Norse silfr. The chemical symbol Ag comes from the Latin argentum, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'white' or 'shining'.

The earliest known coins were minted in the kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor around 600 BCE, of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver. Silver standards, in which the unit of account is a fixed weight of silver, were then widespread until the 20th century. Notable silver coins include the Greek drachma, the Roman denarius, the Islamic dirham, the karshapana of ancient India, the rupee of the Mughal Empire and the Spanish dollar.

Apart from coinage, the major use throughout most of history was in jewellery and general-use items such as table silver. In Hesiod's Works and Days the successive ages of humanity are named after metals, among them silver, and Ovid, in the Metamorphoses, describes a silver age that excels bronze but is excelled by gold.
sima-qian: Sima Qian was born at Xiayang in Zuopingyi, near present-day Hancheng in Shaanxi. His father, Sima Tan, was appointed grand historian at the imperial court, a relatively low-ranking post whose main duty was to draw up the yearly calendar, identifying ritually auspicious and inauspicious days, and which also involved recording events at court and across the country.

In 126 BCE, at about the age of twenty, he made an extensive tour of Han China. Starting from Chang'an, he went south across the Yangtze to the Changsha Kingdom, where he visited the Miluo River, traditionally the place where the poet Qu Yuan drowned himself. He visited the grave of the general Han Xin at Huaiyin and Qufu, the hometown of Confucius, where he studied ritual.

After his travels Sima became a Palace Attendant to Emperor Wu of Han. His father had conceived a complete history of China but left only preparatory sketches, and summoned his son to continue it. Sima Qian succeeded him as grand historian and in 105 BCE was among the scholars chosen to reform the calendar. The resulting Taichu calendar, promulgated in 104 BCE, is the first Chinese calendar whose full method of calculation has been preserved.

In 99 BCE he became embroiled in the Li Ling affair. The general Li Ling had been defeated and captured in a campaign against the Xiongnu, and every official condemned him. Sima alone defended him, though Li had never been his friend. Emperor Wu took this as an attack on his brother-in-law Li Guangli and sentenced Sima to death. Execution could be commuted by money or by castration; lacking the money, Sima chose castration and spent three years in prison. On his release he lived on as a palace eunuch to finish his history, rather than die as a disgraced gentleman-scholar was expected to.

The Shiji, or Records of the Grand Historian, runs to over 500,000 characters in 130 chapters and covers more than two thousand years, from the Yellow Emperor to the reign of Emperor Wu. It combined basic annals of sovereigns, tables, treatises on music, ritual and economics, house chronicles and ordered biographies. Earlier histories had recounted particular events or regions. Sima treated the known world and was the first Chinese historian to treat the Xiongnu as human beings implicitly the equals of the Han. His Letter to Ren An is admired as prose. His grandson Yang Yun released the work during the reign of Emperor Xuan.
simeon-i-of-bulgaria: Simeon was born in 864 or 865, the third son of Prince Boris I, who made Bulgaria Christian. Boris intended him for the church and sent him to Constantinople at thirteen or fourteen, where he spent about a decade and became so fluent in Greek that Byzantine chronicles called him the half-Greek. About 888 he returned to the royal monastery at Preslav and translated religious works from Greek into Medieval Bulgarian. When his elder brother Vladimir tried to reintroduce paganism, Boris had him imprisoned and blinded and appointed Simeon. An assembly at Preslav made Bulgarian the only language of state and church and moved the capital from Pliska to Preslav.

The long peace with Byzantium ended when Emperor Leo VI moved the market for Bulgarian goods from Constantinople to Thessaloniki, where merchants were heavily taxed. The Byzantines induced the Magyars to attack Bulgaria in 895, but in 896 Simeon, with Pecheneg allies, defeated them at the Battle of Southern Buh, and he then destroyed a Byzantine army at Bulgarophygon. Peace brought an annual tribute from Byzantium. After Leo's death in 912, Simeon reached Constantinople in 913 and was recognised as Emperor of the Bulgarians by Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos, though Zoe, mother of the young Constantine VII, disowned the recognition in 914.

On 20 August 917, at the river Achelous, the Bulgarians routed a Byzantine army, in one of the largest battles in medieval history. Simeon annexed Serbia in 924 after a revolt there. He met Romanos Lekapenos on the Golden Horn on 9 September 924, and about 925 raised the Bulgarian Church to a patriarchate; Pope John X recognised his imperial title. In 926 his troops were defeated by King Tomislav of Croatia at the Battle of the Bosnian Highlands. Simeon died of heart failure in Preslav on 27 May 927 and was succeeded by his son Peter I.

Simeon's reign saw the first and most productive period of medieval Bulgarian literature. The Preslav Literary School and the Ohrid Literary School, where the Cyrillic alphabet was developed, produced translations of the Bible and of works by John Chrysostom and Basil of Caesarea, and original works such as John Exarch's Six Days and Černorizec Hrabǎr's An Account of Letters. Disciples of Cyril and Methodius, among them Naum and Constantine of Preslav, took part. Preslav had more than twenty cross-domed churches and a Golden Church, and it was Simeon's imperial capital.
simferopol: Simferopol lies in the south-central Crimean Peninsula on the Salhir River, near the artificial Simferopol Reservoir, which supplies the city's drinking water and has the biggest earth dam in Europe. It has a humid subtropical climate. The city is a political, economic and transport hub of the peninsula and has a major railway station.

Its name comes from the Greek Sympheropoli, meaning city of common good or usefulness. In Crimean Tatar the city is Aqmescit, the white mosque. The colour does not describe a building: Turkic peoples give a colour to each cardinal point, and white is the west, so the name means the Western Mosque.

The Crimean Scythians lived in the area from the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE, and the remnants of their capital, Scythian Neapolis, lie within the city. The Crimean Tatars later founded Aqmescit, which was for a time the residence of the Qalğa-Sultan, the second most important office in the Crimean Khanate after the Khan.

After Catherine II annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1784, the new city of Simferopol was founded on the site of Aqmescit, in line with her Greek Plan of Greek place names for the new southern lands. It became the administrative centre of the Taurida Governorate in 1802. After the Crimean War of 1854-1856 more than 30,000 Russian soldiers were buried near the city. In 1870 about 57 per cent of the population were Eastern Orthodox, with Jewish, Karaite, Catholic and other communities beside them.

The Red Army took the city on 13 November 1920, and it became capital of the Crimean Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic in 1921. German forces occupied it from 1 November 1941 to 13 April 1944 and killed over 22,000 local people, mostly Jews, Russians, Krymchaks and Romani, including an estimated 14,300 from 9 December 1941. On 18 May 1944 the city's Crimean Tatars were deported with their whole nation to Central Asia. Crimea was transferred to the Ukrainian SSR on 26 April 1954. After 1991 Simferopol was capital of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014; the city is internationally recognised as part of Ukraine.
simon-bolivar: Simón Bolívar was born on 24 July 1783 in Caracas, the youngest of four children of Juan Vicente Bolívar y Ponte and María de la Concepción Palacios y Blanco, in a wealthy creole family. His father died of tuberculosis in 1786 and his mother in 1792, and he was raised partly by an enslaved woman named Hipólita, whom he viewed as both a motherly and a fatherly figure. In 1799 he was sent to Madrid, where he married María Teresa Rodríguez del Toro y Alaysa in 1802; she died of yellow fever in 1803. On a second journey to Europe he reached Rome, where he swore to end Spanish rule in the Americas.

After Napoleon's invasion of the Iberian peninsula, Venezuelan creoles sought their own government, and Bolívar helped secure Francisco de Miranda's election to the congress that declared Venezuela independent on 5 July 1811, creating the first Republic of Venezuela. The republic fell in 1812, and Bolívar went into exile in Curaçao and Cartagena. After Spanish forces subdued New Granada, he wrote the Jamaica Letter in 1815 in Kingston, laying out his ideology and vision of the future of the Americas.

In Haiti Alexandre Pétion, after Bolívar pledged to free every slave in the areas he occupied, gave him money and military supplies. In February 1819 the congress at Angostura elected him president. In May he marched over the Andes with more than 2,000 soldiers, and on 7 August 1819 the Royalists were routed at the Battle of Boyacá. Allies and Bolívar defeated the Spanish in Venezuela and Panama in 1821, Ecuador in 1822, Peru in 1824 and Bolivia in 1825, and Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador and Panama were merged into Gran Colombia.

In his final years Bolívar became disillusioned with the republics and was successively removed from his offices. He left Bogotá on 8 May 1830 intending to go into exile in England, but with his health failing and no ship available he was taken to the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino near Santa Marta, where he died of tuberculosis on 17 December 1830, aged 47. In 1842 his remains were returned to Caracas, and in 1876 they were moved to the National Pantheon of Venezuela. He is regarded as a hero and national and cultural icon throughout Latin America, and Bolivia and Venezuela, as the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, are named after him.
simon-stevin: Very little is known with certainty about Stevin's life. He is assumed to have been born in Bruges, since he enrolled at Leiden University as Simon Stevinus Brugensis, into a family likely to have been Calvinist. He left Bruges in 1571, perhaps to escape the persecution of Protestants by the Spanish rulers, and began a career as a merchant's clerk in Antwerp. He served as city clerk of Bruges from 1577 to 1581, then moved to Leiden, where he attended the Latin school and enrolled at the university on 16 February 1583. There he befriended Prince Maurice of Nassau, the second son of William the Silent.

After William's assassination, Stevin became the principal adviser and tutor of Maurice. He directed the waterstaet, the authority for public works and water management, from 1592 and later served as quartermaster-general of the army of the States-General. Maurice asked him to found an engineering school within the University of Leiden. His work on sluices and spillways to control flooding included improvements to windmills that raised their efficiency in pumping water from the polders threefold, for which he received a patent in 1586. Around 1600 he used a land yacht, a carriage with sails, on the beach between Scheveningen and Petten, with Maurice and twenty-six others, and it outran horses.

Stevin wrote De Thiende, a 35-page booklet first published in Dutch in 1585, which taught calculation without fractions by using decimal fractions. It was addressed to stargazers, surveyors and tradespeople. Decimal fractions had been introduced earlier by medieval Islamic scholars, and his notation was unwieldy. He derived the balance of forces on inclined planes, discovered the hydrostatic paradox, distinguished stable from unstable equilibria and in 1586 demonstrated that bodies of different weight fall with the same acceleration. He was the first to explain the tides by the attraction of the moon.

He believed Dutch ideal for scientific writing and wrote all his works in it, so that people who lacked Latin could use them. He coined Dutch terms such as wiskunde for mathematics, natuurkunde for physics and scheikunde for chemistry. He died in 1620 in Leiden or The Hague, leaving a widow and two children.
simone-de-beauvoir: Beauvoir was born on 9 January 1908 in Montparnasse, in Paris. Her father, Georges Bertrand de Beauvoir, was initially a lawyer but aspired to be an actor, and her mother, Françoise, was a devout Catholic and a banker's daughter. The promised dowry was lost when Françoise's father was jailed. Her parents were often absent, and she was raised chiefly by a nanny, Louise. She had a younger sister, Hélène, born on 6 June 1910. Intellectually precocious and encouraged by her father, she wrote that the contrast between her father's individualism and pagan standards and her mother's rigid conventional morality made her life an endless disputation, the main reason she became an intellectual.

After her studies Beauvoir saw teaching as a way to earn her own living. She did her practice teaching at the same secondary school as Maurice Merleau-Ponty and Claude Lévi-Strauss, and from 1929 to 1943 she taught at lycées in Marseille, Rouen and Paris until she could live on her writing. She then became a public intellectual. Her first novel, She Came to Stay, appeared in 1943, followed by The Blood of Others (1945), which tells a love story between two young students in the French Resistance during the Second World War.

With Jean-Paul Sartre and Maurice Merleau-Ponty she co-founded Les Temps Modernes, a monthly political journal that carried communists, Catholics, Gaullists and socialists, whose first issue appeared on 1 October 1945. Sartre and Merleau-Ponty later quarrelled, and Beauvoir sided with Sartre. She remained an editor until her death and in later years held the editorial meetings in her flat.

Her first philosophical essay, Pyrrhus et Cinéas (1944), was followed by The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), in which she argues that the freedom of the self requires the freedom of others. The Second Sex (1949) turned the existentialist principle that existence precedes essence into a feminist one: One is not born, but rather becomes, woman. It articulated the distinction between biological sex and the social construction of gender, and showed how sexual difference is used to trap women in the role of the Other. The Mandarins (1954), a roman à clef about Sartre's and Beauvoir's circle after the war, won the Prix Goncourt.

Beauvoir at first denied being a feminist but later admitted it. The Second Sex opened the way for second-wave feminism, and Kate Millett, Shulamith Firestone, Juliet Mitchell, Ann Oakley and Germaine Greer read it in translation and acknowledged their debt to her. Betty Friedan said that reading it in the early 1950s led to her own analysis of women's existence.
simone-martini: Simone Martini was born in Siena around 1284. It is thought that he was a pupil of Duccio di Buoninsegna, the leading Sienese painter of his time, although the Renaissance biographer Giorgio Vasari instead made him a pupil of Giotto di Bondone, with whom he went to Rome. His brother-in-law was the artist Lippo Memmi. Very little documentation of his life survives, and many attributions to him are debated by art historians.

Among his first documented works is the Maestà of 1315 in the Palazzo Pubblico in Siena. Lippo Memmi painted a similar Maestà for the Palazzo Comunale in San Gimignano soon afterwards, an example of the lasting influence of his models. During a stay in Naples at the request of the king he painted Saint Louis of Toulouse Crowning His Brother Robert of Anjou in 1317, now in the Museo di Capodimonte, and he painted a polyptych of Saint Catherine of Alexandria in Pisa in 1319.

He also painted the Annunciation with St. Margaret and St. Ansanus of 1333, now in the Uffizi in Florence, and frescoes in the San Martino Chapel in the lower church of the Basilica of San Francesco in Assisi. A Christ Discovered in the Temple of 1342 is in the Walker Art Gallery in Liverpool.

His Sienese style contrasts with the sobriety and monumentality of Florentine art and is noted for soft, stylised, decorative features, sinuous line and courtly elegance. His art owes much to French manuscript illumination and ivory carving, examples of which reached Siena along the Via Francigena, a main pilgrimage and trade route. He greatly influenced the International Gothic style.

He likely moved to Avignon in 1334 or 1335 and died there in July 1344 in the service of the papal court. He was commissioned to paint frescoes for the porch of Avignon Cathedral, of which only faint sinopia outlines remain. According to Vasari, he painted a portrait of Laura de Noves for his friend Petrarch, who refers to it in two sonnets of the Canzoniere.
simonides-of-ceos: Few clear facts about Simonides' life have survived, and ancient sources are uncertain even about his date of birth. Modern scholars generally accept 556 to 468 BCE, though this would make him about fifty years older than his nephew Bacchylides. He was the son of Leoprepes and was born in Ioulis on Ceos, an island with a rich musical culture, where choirs were trained at a school in Carthaea, and a tradition of athletic competition that made it fertile ground for the victory ode, a genre of choral lyric he pioneered. About the age of thirty he was drawn to Athens by the court of the tyrant Hipparchus, where his rivalry with the chorus-trainer Lasus of Hermione later became a joke.

After the assassination of Hipparchus in 514 BCE Simonides withdrew to Thessaly, under the patronage of the Scopadae and Aleuadae. A tradition related by Cicero and Quintilian says that Scopas refused to pay him in full for an ode that spoke too much of Castor and Pollux, and that the poet was called out of the banquet hall just before it collapsed, which was said to have led him to devise a system of mnemonics based on places. Quintilian dismisses the story as fiction.

He returned to Athens during the Persian Wars and became a prominent international figure as the author of commemorative verses. After the defeat of the second Persian invasion he composed epitaphs for Athenians, Spartans and Corinthians, a song for Leonidas and his men, and poems on the battles of Artemisium, Salamis and Plataea. His last years were spent in Sicily as a friend of Hieron of Syracuse, and he is said to have made peace between Hieron and Theron of Acragas. Callimachus records that he was buried outside Acragas.

Simonides wrote choral lyrics, elegiac verses, dirges, paeans and dithyrambs, and an epigram credits him with 57 victories in dithyrambic competitions. He is generally credited with popularising the victory ode, an extension of the hymn, and with establishing the choral dirge as a recognised form. Only a small part of his poetry survives, in papyrus fragments and quotations, and modern scholars consider just one of the epigrams attributed to him unquestionably authentic, an inscription for the seer Megistius, which places even the Thermopylae epitaph in doubt.

His style is clear and simple, with restraint and balance, and Quintilian praised his power to excite pity. Aristophanes made him a type of the miser, and a tradition holds that he was the first poet to charge fees. Plato quotes his poem on the difficulty of being truly good, which holds that only a god can be perfect and that a man is good enough if he does nothing shameful willingly.
simurgh: The Persian word sīmurğ derives from Middle Persian sēnmurw, which comes from Avestan mərəγō Saēnō, the bird Saēna, originally a raptor, likely an eagle, falcon or sparrowhawk. In Persian the phrase sī murğ also means thirty birds, a play on words used by Attar of Nishapur.

The figure appears in all periods of Iranian art and literature, and in the iconography of Georgia, medieval Armenia and the Eastern Roman Empire. The Sasanians used it heavily, as a tribal emblem and in their art and propaganda. Through Persian influence it reached the Arabic-speaking world, where it was conflated with other mythical birds such as the ghoghnus and developed into the rukh, the origin of the English word roc. Representations were adopted in early Umayyad art and coinage.

In Iranian art the simurgh is a winged creature in the shape of a bird, gigantic enough to carry off an elephant or a whale. It appears as a peacock with the head of a dog and the claws of a lion, and sometimes with a human face. It is inherently benevolent, and being part mammal it suckles its young.

The simurgh was thought to purify land and water and so bestow fertility, and it mediated between earth and sky. It roosted in Gaokerena, the Hōm tree of life in the middle of the sea Vourukasha, whose all-healing seeds it scattered when it took flight. It is also linked with farr, divine glory, the mandate underlying a king's authority; it appears resting on the head or shoulder of would-be kings and clerics as a sign that Ormuzd accepts them.

In Ferdowsi's Shahnameh the simurgh raises Zal, son of Saam, who was born albino and abandoned on the mountain Alborz. She gives him three golden feathers to burn if he needs her help. When his wife Rudaba is near death in labour, Zal burns a feather and the simurgh instructs him in performing a caesarean section, so that Rostam is born. The simurgh later heals Rostam and his horse Rakhsh after Esfandiyar's arrows and tells Rostam how to make the double-headed arrow that blinds Esfandiyar. In the fifth trial of Esfandiyar, a different simurgh is killed.

In Persian Sufi poetry it is a metaphor for God. In Attar's 12th-century Conference of the Birds, a group of pilgrim birds led by the hoopoe seeks the simurgh and at last finds only a lake in which they see their own reflection, a pun on thirty birds.
sinaloa: Sinaloa is one of the 31 states that, with Mexico City, make up the Federal Entities of Mexico. It covers 58,328 square kilometres and is divided into 20 municipalities. It borders Sonora, Chihuahua, Durango and Nayarit, and faces Baja California Sur across the Gulf of California. The Sierra Madre Occidental dominates the east, and many rivers flow from it to the gulf through fertile valleys and a narrow coastal plain. The most popular explanation of the name, attributed to Eustaquio Buelna, combines the Cahita words sina, the pitahaya plant, and lobola, rounded.

Sinaloa belongs to the northern limit of Mesoamerica, and the Fuerte River marks the start of Aridoamerica to the north. Before European contact it was inhabited by groups such as the Cahitas, the Tahues, the Acaxees and the Xiximes. In 1531 Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán, with a force of over 10,000 men, established a Spanish and allied Indian outpost at San Miguel de Culiacán. Over the next decade the Cahíta suffered severe depopulation from conquest and from smallpox and other diseases brought by Europeans.

Starting in 1599 Jesuit missionaries spread out from a base at what is now Sinaloa de Leyva, and by 1610 Spanish influence reached the northern edge of the territory. Their movement into the east prompted the Acaxee Rebellion of 1601; the Spanish executed 48 Acaxee leaders. After independence Sinaloa was joined with Sonora as the Estado de Occidente, and in 1830 it separated to become the 20th state of the First Mexican Republic, with Culiacán as its capital. Los Mochis was founded in 1893 by American settlers led by Albert K. Owen as the Topolobampo colony, inspired by utopian socialism.

The capital and largest city is Culiacán; other large cities include Mazatlán, a tourist resort, and Los Mochis. Irrigation projects built after the revolution turned arid land into farmland and earned Sinaloa the name granary of Mexico. Banda music, popularized there in the late 19th century, is its best-known cultural tradition, and ulama, a form of the ancient Mesoamerican ballgame, is still played in a few rural communities near Mazatlán.
sindh: Sindh lies in the south-east of Pakistan and is bounded by the Arabian Sea to the south, Balochistan to the west and Punjab to the north; to the east it shares a border with the Indian states of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Its landscape is mostly alluvial plain on either side of the Indus River, with the Thar Desert in the east and the Kirthar Mountains in the west. The name Sind is a Persian derivative of the Sanskrit sindhu, meaning river, and the Greeks under Alexander the Great called the Indus Indos. The spelling Sindh replaced the older Sind in 1988.

Settled life began around Sindh and Punjab some 9,000 years ago and developed into the Indus Valley Civilisation. Mohenjo-daro, built around 2500 BCE, was one of the largest settlements of that civilisation, with standardised bricks, street grids and covered sewerage. It was abandoned in the 19th century BCE as the civilisation declined, and was not rediscovered until the 1920s. Around 1000 BCE the Indo-Aryan kingdom of Sindhu-Sauvira emerged and lasted until the Achaemenids captured the region in 518 BCE, after whom came the Macedonians, Mauryans, Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians, Guptas and Sasanians.

The first Muslim naval raids came in 636 under the caliph Umar. Arab forces conquered Sindh in 712 under the Umayyad Caliphate and made it a province, which laid the foundations of the Muslim period in South Asia. The Habbari Emirate emerged in the 9th century, and between the 11th and 16th centuries the Soomra, Samma and Arghun dynasties ruled, mostly as vassals of the Delhi Sultanate. Akbar, himself born at Umerkot in Sindh, sent an army in 1591 to 1593 to take lower Sindh from the Tarkhan dynasty. Mughal rule ran from the provincial capital Thatta, while the Kalhora dynasty held upper Sindh from Khudabad. The Talpur dynasty ruled from 1783, and the East India Company later captured the province.

Sindh became a separate province in 1936. After the Lahore Resolution of 1940 it was the first province to endorse the Pakistan Movement, and it joined the Dominion of Pakistan in 1947. It was merged into West Pakistan in 1955 and restored as a province in 1970.

Karachi, on the southern coast, is the provincial capital and the largest city. Sindhi, spoken by about 60 per cent of the population at the 2023 census, is the most widely spoken language, and about 90 per cent of residents are Muslim. Sufism is an important marker of Sindhi identity for Muslims and Hindus alike, and the poet Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai lived here. Two World Heritage Sites lie in the province, Mohenjo-daro and the Makli Necropolis near Thatta.
singapore: Singapore lies about one degree of latitude, 137 kilometres, north of the equator, off the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. Its territory is a main island, also known as Pulau Ujong, over 60 satellite islands and one outlying islet, and two man-made connections, the Johor–Singapore Causeway and the Tuas Second Link, join it to Johor in Malaysia. The highest natural point is Bukit Timah Hill, at 163.63 metres. Land reclamation has raised the land area from roughly 580 km2 in the 1960s to 770 km2. The name is an anglicisation of the Malay Singapura, from the Sanskrit for 'lion city', and the island was earlier known as Temasek.

According to the Malay Annals, the Kingdom of Singapura was founded in 1299 by Sang Nila Utama, although historians debate the accounts. In the 14th century, as Temasek, Singapore was a trading port under the influence of both the Majapahit Empire and the Siamese kingdoms. Around the end of that century its ruler Parameswara was attacked, by either the Majapahit or the Siamese, and moved to Malacca, where he founded the Sultanate of Malacca. Portuguese raiders burned the settlement in 1613, and the island then faded into obscurity for two centuries, nominally part of the Johor Sultanate.

Stamford Raffles arrived on 28 January 1819, when around 150 people lived on the island, 120 of them Malays. With the help of the Temenggong of Johor, he brought Tengku Long back from exile and recognised him as Sultan Hussein, and in the Treaty of Singapore of 6 February 1819 the Sultan granted the British the right to establish a trading post. Singapore came under direct British control in 1867 as part of the Straits Settlements, was occupied by Japan in 1942, gained self-governance in 1959 and joined Malaysia in 1963. It was expelled from the federation two years later and became independent in 1965.

Singapore is a parliamentary republic based on the Westminster system. Its population was 6,110,200 in 2025, of whom 3,660,200 were citizens. The 2020 census reported 74.3% of residents of Chinese descent, 13.5% Malay and 9.0% Indian. English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil are the four official languages, and 78.7% of resident households live in public housing developed by the Housing and Development Board.
sinn-fein: The name is Irish for Ourselves or We Ourselves, frequently mistranslated as ourselves alone, from the early 20th-century slogan Sinn Féin Amháin. It asserts Irish national sovereignty and self-determination rather than political union with Great Britain under the Westminster Parliament. The party was founded on 28 November 1905 when Arthur Griffith, at the first annual Convention of the National Council, outlined a policy to establish in Ireland's capital a national legislature endowed with the moral authority of the Irish nation. Its first platform was conservative and monarchist, advocating an Anglo-Irish dual monarchy modelled on the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867. It won 27 per cent of the vote in the 1908 North Leitrim by-election, after which support and membership fell.

Its members founded the revolutionary Irish Republic and its parliament, the First Dáil, and many were active in the Irish War of Independence, when the party was associated with the Irish Republican Army. The party split before the Irish Civil War and again afterwards. Pro-Treaty deputies formed Cumann na nGaedheal in 1923, which governed the Irish Free State for nine years and merged with other groups to form Fine Gael in 1933. In 1926 Éamon de Valera, after losing a motion to let elected members take their seats if the Oath of Allegiance were removed, resigned and founded Fianna Fáil, taking most of the party's deputies with him. The remaining party was small, and for decades often without parliamentary representation.

A split in 1970, at the start of the Troubles, produced the modern party, linked in that conflict with the Provisional Irish Republican Army, and for most of it affected by broadcasting bans. Under Gerry Adams, leader from 1983, electoral politics became more important. The party dropped abstention from the Dáil in 1986, and some members formed Republican Sinn Féin in protest. In the 1990s Adams and Martin McGuinness took part in the Northern Ireland peace process leading to the Good Friday Agreement, and in 2006 the party signed the St Andrews Agreement and agreed to support the Police Service of Northern Ireland.

Sinn Féin operates under democratic centralism, and describes itself as an Irish republican and democratic socialist party. It is active in both the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, and its main political goal is a united Ireland. It continues a policy of abstaining from the House of Commons at Westminster. Caoimhghín Ó Caoláin, elected to the Dáil in 1997, was the first person under the Sinn Féin name to take a seat there since 1922. Mary Lou McDonald succeeded Gerry Adams as president in 2018.
sino-indian-war: China and India shared a long border with several disputed regions. At its western end lies Aksai Chin, about 38,000 square kilometres, which India considered part of Ladakh and China part of Xinjiang. At its eastern end China claimed the North-East Frontier Agency, about 90,000 square kilometres, administered by India. The two fronts lay roughly 1,000 kilometres apart. India recognised the Johnson Line in the west and the McMahon Line in the east, and China did not. The western boundary goes back to the conquest of Ladakh by Raja Gulab Singh in 1834 and the British transfer of Jammu and Kashmir in 1846. China built a road through Aksai Chin linking Tibet and Xinjiang, which was one of the triggers of the conflict.

After the Tibetan uprising of 1959, when India granted asylum to the 14th Dalai Lama, border skirmishes increased. Talks between officials in 1960, following an agreement between Nehru and Zhou Enlai, failed. In 1961 China began patrolling along the McMahon Line, and India answered with a forward policy of setting up outposts behind Chinese troops. In June 1962 India set up the Dhola Post below Thagla Ridge, and in August China began occupying positions on the ridge.

China abandoned attempts at a peaceful settlement on 20 October 1962 and launched simultaneous offensives on both fronts. In the east, Chinese forces overran Indian positions at Namka Chu and Tawang. In the west they took the Chip Chap Valley and Pangong Lake. After a lull of three weeks, they resumed the offensive on 14 November and captured Se La, Bomdila and Gurung Hill in the east, while the battle of Rezang La in the west cost both sides heavy casualties.

The fighting was mountain warfare, with large-scale combat at altitudes above 5,000 metres. It took place entirely on land, with no naval or air assets, and neither side declared war or broke off diplomatic relations. China declared a unilateral ceasefire on 20 November 1962 and announced a withdrawal to its pre-war position, the effective China–India border.

The war was a major military and political setback in India. India rapidly modernised and expanded its armed forces and strengthened its border defences, and it reassessed its policy towards China. The conflict permanently damaged relations between the two states. As the Sino-Soviet split deepened, the Soviet Union supported India with the sale of military hardware, and India turned to the Soviets for aid because the United States and the United Kingdom refused to sell it advanced weapons.
sino-soviet-split: During the Second Sino-Japanese War, Joseph Stalin ordered Mao Zedong to cooperate with Chiang Kai-shek against Japan, and after Japan's surrender the Chinese civil war resumed and the communists won by 1949. In 1950 Mao and Stalin signed the Treaty of Friendship, Alliance and Mutual Assistance. Stalin gave a loan of 300 million dollars, promised military aid should Japan attack, and handed over the Chinese Eastern Railway, Port Arthur and Dalian; in return the People's Republic recognised the independence of the Mongolian People's Republic. Unlike the satellite states of Eastern Europe, China was not controlled by the Soviet Union.

In early 1956 relations began to deteriorate after Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin in his speech On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences. His turn from confrontation with the West to peaceful coexistence posed problems of credibility and authority for Mao, who had modelled his leadership on Stalin's. Mao called the Soviet policy revisionism.

In 1958 Chinese domestic politics took on an anti-Soviet tone, and China became more sensitive about sovereignty and foreign policy, especially over Taiwan. In 1959 Khrushchev met US President Dwight Eisenhower, the Soviet Union reneged on an agreement for technical aid for China's atomic bomb project, and it sided with India in the border dispute. In 1960 Mao expected Khrushchev to hold Eisenhower to account over a shot-down U-2 spy plane, and when Khrushchev did not win an apology at the Paris summit, the Chinese held rallies demanding military confrontation. By 1961 China formally denounced Soviet communism as the work of revisionist traitors.

From then communications were written. In June 1963 the Chinese Communist Party published its proposal on the general line of the international communist movement, attacking the Soviet Union by name, and the Soviets replied with an Open Letter. Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966, and Red Guards harassed the Soviet embassy in Beijing. After the Zhenbao Island border incident of 1969 the Soviet Union reportedly considered a large-scale nuclear strike against China, and the Chinese leadership was evacuated from Beijing before both sides returned to negotiations.

Talks over border issues began in October 1969 and lasted a decade. Both sides built up forces along the frontier, with an estimated 1 million to 1.2 million Soviet troops and as many as 1.5 million Chinese. The split turned the bipolar Cold War into a tripolar one and helped make possible President Richard Nixon's visit to China in 1972. It also weakened the Western idea of monolithic communism. In the 1970s the two states competed for influence in Africa, Asia and the Middle East, though both supported North Vietnam.
sino-vietnamese-war: The Chinese Communist Party and the Viet Minh had a long history, and communist China aided the Viet Minh against France. After Stalin's death in 1953 relations between the Soviet Union and China deteriorated into the Sino-Soviet split, and Vietnam did not support China against the Soviets. China viewed the growing Soviet-Vietnamese relationship with alarm and feared encirclement. Tensions by the mid-1970s also involved Vietnam's treatment of ethnic Chinese, border conflicts and Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia.

China supported the Maoist Khmer Rouge, who came to power under Pol Pot in 1975. After numerous border clashes, Vietnam invaded Cambodia on 25 December 1978, and by 7 January 1979 its forces had entered Phnom Penh. Border skirmishes rose from 125 in 1974 to 2,175 in 1978.

On 17 February 1979 a People's Liberation Army force of about 200,000 troops with about 200 tanks entered northern Vietnam, in the army's first major combat operation since the China-India War of 1962. It advanced in two directions, the eastern commanded by Xu Shiyou towards Cao Bằng, Lạng Sơn and Quảng Ninh, and the western commanded by Yang Dezhi towards Ha Tuyen, Hoang Lien Son and Lai Châu. Chinese forces quickly captured several cities near the border.

The Soviet Union took no direct military action but supplied intelligence and equipment and airlifted Vietnamese troops from Cambodia to the north. It also deployed troops on the Sino-Soviet and Mongolian-Chinese borders, though it refused to defend its ally directly. China had to keep most of its forces along its northern frontier as a deterrent. On 6 March China declared its punitive mission accomplished and withdrew.

Casualty figures are disputed. A Vietnamese agency claimed over 44,000 Chinese casualties, which Western analysts thought greatly inflated, and leaks from Chinese military sources indicate 6,954 Chinese dead. China held 1,636 Vietnamese prisoners and Vietnam 238 Chinese, and they were exchanged in May and June 1979. Vietnam continued to occupy Cambodia until 1989, so China did not achieve one of its stated aims, though it showed that the Soviet Union could not protect its Vietnamese ally.

In Vietnam the authorities expelled about 8,000 Hoa people from Hanoi to southern New Economic Zones in spring 1979 and expelled 20,468 members from the Communist Party. Border skirmishes continued through the 1980s, including a naval battle over the Spratly Islands in 1988. Relations were normalized in November 1991, and a border pact was signed in 1999.
sintra: Sintra is a town and municipality in the Greater Lisbon region, on the Portuguese Riviera. The Sintra Mountains, a granite massif ten kilometres long, rise abruptly between a plain to the north and the Tagus estuary and wind towards the Atlantic and Cabo da Roca, the most westerly point of continental Europe. Local tradition of astral cults called them the Mountain of the Moon, Promontorium Lunae. A micro-climate, fertile soils and the nearness of the estuary drew considerable early settlement, and the mountains support a park of dense foliage with a rich botanical diversity.

The earliest traces of human occupation, at Penha Verde, date to the early Paleolithic. Neolithic remains with decorated ceramics and microlithic flint tools from the 5th millennium BCE were found beside the chapel of the Moorish Castle. In July 1109 Count Henry reconquered the Castle of Sintra. A year before, Prince Sigurd the Crusader, son of Magnus III of Norway, had tried to take it on his way to the Holy Land, but failed. The castle surrendered definitively in November 1147, after Afonso Henriques, supported by Crusaders, conquered Lisbon in October, and he founded the Church of São Pedro de Canaferrim within its walls.

The royal palace was until the end of the 17th century one of the principal residences and summer estates of the court. John I decided there to conquer Ceuta in 1415, Afonso V was born and died there, and John II was acclaimed king in the palace in 1481. Royal visits declined during the war with Spain from 1640 to 1668 and as Mafra and Queluz rose in the 18th century. After the proclamation of the Portuguese Republic in 1910, development was promoted, wine growing at Colares was regulated, and parts of the medieval village were destroyed in 1911. The early decades of the 20th century were the time of Sintra's fastest urbanisation, helped by the rail link to Lisbon.

The municipality had 385,654 inhabitants in 2021 and covers 319.23 square kilometres. The historic centre of Sintra is known for its 19th-century Romanticist architecture, estates, gardens and royal palaces, and the town is classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its landmarks include the medieval Castle of the Moors, the Romanticist Pena National Palace and the Portuguese Renaissance Sintra National Palace. The area includes the Sintra-Cascais Nature Park.
sion-switzerland: Sion is a municipality in the Rhône valley and the capital of the canton of Valais and of the district of Sion. Its German name is Sitten and its Latin name was Sedunum. Landmarks include the Basilique de Valère and the Château de Tourbillon. Several neighbouring municipalities have merged into it: Bramois in 1968, Salins in 2013 and Les Agettes in 2017. It is one of the driest and sunniest areas of Switzerland.

Sion is one of the most important prehistoric sites in Europe. The oldest trace of settlement dates from about 6200 BCE, in the late Mesolithic, and early Neolithic farmers from the Mediterranean settled there around 5800 BCE. Their descendants buried the dead in stone cists with engraved stelae and later in large dry stone communal tombs such as the Dolmen of Le Petit-Chasseur. At the end of the 1st century BCE it was the capital of the Seduni, one of four Celtic tribes of the Valais, and the Romans conquered them in the 10s BCE.

The Roman Catholic diocese of Sion is the oldest in Switzerland. In the Middle Ages the citizens gained a limited independence through privileges granted by the bishop. An agreement of 1217 was the first written charter of freedom for the city, and in 1269 the burghers had their own council. In 1339 Emperor Louis the Bavarian raised Sion to a free imperial city. From the middle of the 14th century to 1475 the city was repeatedly attacked: it was pillaged by an army from Savoy in 1352, attacked in 1384 and 1418, and attacked again during the Burgundian Wars in 1475.

After the French invasion of Switzerland on 5 March 1798 the town was divided between supporters of the revolution, who raised a liberty pole on 10 March, and conservatives. A counter-revolutionary rising in the upper Valais was crushed by French and Vaudois troops on 17 May 1798, and Sion was plundered.

Archaeologists found six aligned standing stones in the Petit-Chasseur district in July 2019, near where about thirty such stones and the dolmens were found in 1960. Three were carved, and the largest, of about two tonnes, appears to represent a male figure in geometrically decorated clothing. Most residents speak French as their first language. Sion has an airfield for civilian and military use that serves as a base for air rescue.
sirimavo-bandaranaike: Sirimavo Bandaranaike was born Sirima Ratwatte on 17 April 1916 at Ratnapura in British Ceylon, into a Sinhalese Kandyan aristocratic family. Her father, Barnes Ratwatte, was a native headman and politician, and her mother, Rosalind Hilda Mahawalatenne Kumarihamy, was an informal Ayurvedic physician. She was educated in Anglican, English-medium schools but remained a Buddhist and spoke Sinhala as well as English.

On 2 October 1940 she married S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike, in a wedding the press called the wedding of the century. They had two daughters, Sunethra and Chandrika, and a son, Anura. As the wife of the founder of the Sri Lanka Freedom Party, she acted as hostess and informal adviser and worked on the welfare of rural women and girls. After his assassination in 1959 she was persuaded to lead the party.

The Freedom Party won the July 1960 election by a landslide, and on 21 July 1960 she was sworn in as prime minister, the first woman to hold the post anywhere. As she was not a member of Parliament, she was appointed to the Senate. In her first term she nationalised banking, foreign trade, insurance, the petroleum industry and funded parochial schools, and she took control of seven newspapers. Her government survived a plot by military officers in 1962. She followed a policy of non-alignment, attended the first four summits of the Non-Aligned Movement and chaired it in 1976–1977.

The 1965 election made her Leader of the Opposition, and the United Front won a large majority in 1970. Her second government faced an insurrection by the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna in 1971, and in May 1972 a new constitution replaced Ceylon with the Republic of Sri Lanka. It recognised the supremacy of Buddhism, made Sinhala the only official language and abolished the Senate. In 1975 she created an agency on women's issues, later the Ministry of Women and Child Affairs. She lost heavily in 1977. A 1978 constitution introduced a presidential system, and she returned as prime minister in 1994 under her daughter Chandrika Kumaratunga, who had become president.
Bandaranaike died on 10 October 2000 of a heart attack, on the day of a parliamentary election in which she had been casting her vote. Two days of national mourning were declared.

She served more than seventeen years as prime minister across three terms. Her policies of nationalisation and of Sinhala as the official language remained points of dispute, and her language policy aggravated discontent among the Tamil population. Her children also held prominent public positions, and the Bandaranaike family became one of the leading political families of the country.
sisak: Sisak lies in central Croatia, 57 km south-east of Zagreb, where the Kupa, Sava and Odra rivers meet, and is usually considered the point where the Posavina, the Sava basin, begins. It is the administrative centre of Sisak-Moslavina County, Croatia's biggest river port and a centre of river shipping. Before Roman rule the region was Celtic and Illyrian, and the settlement was called Segestica or Segesta. Roman rule gave it the name Siscia. Roman writers describe it as a great town on an island formed by the Sava and two other rivers, the Colapis and the Odra, which a canal dug by Tiberius completed.

Siscia was strongly fortified from the first. After Tiberius captured it, in the reign of Augustus, it became one of the most important places in Pannonia, a centre of commerce and the base from which Augustus and Tiberius carried out their undertakings against the Pannonians and Illyrians. Under Septimius Severus it received fresh colonists. The town held an imperial mint that struck coins under a series of emperors between 262 and 383 CE. The Christian martyr Quirinus of Sescia, the presumed first bishop, was tortured in Diocletian's persecution and is the patron saint of Sisak. When Diocletian divided Pannonia, Siscia became capital of Pannonia Savia.

In the Middle Ages Braslav of Lower Pannonia reigned from Sisak until he was killed in the Hungarian invasion around 898, and Duke Tomislav reclaimed it soon after. In 1593 Croats, Austrians and Carniolans defeated the Ottomans there at the Battle of Sisak, led by the Croatian Ban Thomas Erdődy. Even so, the Ottomans took the town on 24 August 1593, and on 11 August 1594 they fled and set the fortress on fire as a Habsburg and Croat army approached. Until the late 19th century the Kupa divided the town into Civil Sisak, part of the Kingdom of Croatia, and Military Sisak, part of the Croatian Military Frontier.

During World War II the Ustaše government of Croatia set up the Sisak children's concentration camp for Serbian, Jewish and Romani children, where an estimated 1,160 to 1,600 children died. On 22 June 1941 the 1st Sisak Partisan Detachment, with 79 members, was formed in the Brezovica Forest, the first Partisan armed anti-fascist unit in occupied Yugoslavia.

The well-preserved 16th-century triangular fortress of the Old Town, now a museum, is the main destination for visitors. Other landmarks are the Baroque palace of Mali Kaptol, the classicist Veliki Kaptol and the brick Old Bridge over the Kupa. Croatia's largest oil refinery stands in Sisak.
sisteron: Sisteron stands on the banks of the Durance just below the point where the Buëch and the Sasse join it, in a narrow gap between two long mountain ridges. This position has earned it the name Gateway to Provence, and although the town is small it is signed as a navigation point as far away as Grenoble.
