socialist-realism: Socialist realism grew out of earlier Russian realism, such as the work of the Peredvizhniki and Ilya Yefimovich Repin, which lacked the later political connotation. After the Bolsheviks took power on 25 October 1917 there was a marked shift in artistic styles, following a short period of artistic exploration. The term is attributed to the writer Maxim Gorky, who introduced the concept in 1933 in a literary rather than a visual context. The First Congress of Soviet Writers in 1934 proclaimed it the only acceptable method for Soviet cultural production in all media. Its formal objective was to depict reality in its revolutionary development, though no definitive guidelines on style or subject matter were given.

Works were usually characterised by unambiguous narratives or iconography relating to Marxist-Leninist ideology, such as the emancipation of the proletariat. In the visual arts the style often relied on the conventions of academic art and classical sculpture. Key concepts that were to assure loyalty to the party included partiinost (party-mindedness), ideinost (ideological content), klassovost (class content) and pravdivost (truthfulness). Content counted for more than form, which allowed works to be condemned as formalism. Optimism was required: the present and the future were idealised, and tragedy and negativity were not permitted unless shown in a different time or place. The Soviet mass song, including Isaakovsky's Katiusha and Aleksandrov's Sacred War, was a leading genre in music of the 1930s and the war.

Leon Trotsky, Stalin's adversary, criticised the approach, regarding it as an arbitrary construct of the Stalinist bureaucracy and holding that literary schools had been strangled one after the other. After the Russian Revolution socialist realism became an international literary movement, and it was taken up in East Germany, China and Indonesia, where the group Lekra pushed artists to follow it. In art, from the mid-1960s more relaxed and decorative styles became acceptable in the Warsaw Pact bloc. In the non-communist world it had little mainstream impact and was widely seen as a means of imposing state control on artists.
socialist-revolutionary-party: The party's ideas rested on the Narodnik populist movement of the 1860s and 1870s, revived by the neo-populists, especially Viktor Chernov, who entered a dialogue with Marxism to attract the growing urban workforce to a programme that was traditionally peasant-oriented. The party was established in 1902 out of the Northern Union of Socialist Revolutionaries, founded in 1896, and local groups such as the Workers' Party of Political Liberation of Russia, created by Catherine Breshkovsky and Grigory Gershuni in 1899.

The Socialist Revolutionaries, or SRs, were agrarian socialists and supporters of a democratic socialist republic. They won a mass following among the peasantry by endorsing the overthrow of the Tsar and the socialization of land, its division among peasant tenants, as against the Bolshevik programme of nationalization.

Until about 1909 the party relied heavily on assassinations of officials, carried out by its Combat Organisation, which killed two Ministers of the Interior, Dmitry Sipyagin and Vyacheslav von Plehve, and Grand Duke Sergei Aleksandrovich. Its leader after 1903, Yevno Azef, was an agent of the Okhrana secret police. When he was exposed in 1908 the Central Committee resigned, and the party then renounced individual terror.

After the February Revolution of 1917 the SRs returned to active politics. Alexander Kerensky, a nominal member, became head of the Provisional Government in July, and Chernov served as Minister of Agriculture but found his land reforms blocked. A split over the war and land redistribution produced the Left SRs in the autumn, and it became final on 25 October when the Left SRs stayed at the Congress of Soviets while the mainstream party walked out. In the Constituent Assembly election two weeks after the Bolsheviks took power, the SRs won 37.6% of the vote against the Bolsheviks' 24%; the Bolsheviks dissolved the Assembly by force in January 1918.

The Left SRs governed with the Bolsheviks from late November 1917 and resigned their positions after the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. Two Left SR Chekists assassinated the German ambassador Count Wilhelm Mirbach on 6 July 1918, and the Left SRs' attempted rising failed, leading to arrests and executions. Fanny Kaplan, a former SR, tried to kill Lenin on 30 August. A trial of SRs in Moscow in 1922 drew protests from Eugene V. Debs, H. G. Wells, Karl Kautsky and Albert Einstein. A small remnant operated in exile, with a delegation in Prague, and belonged to the Labour and Socialist International from 1923 to 1940.
socotra: Socotra is the largest of six islands in its archipelago and makes up about 95 per cent of its land. It lies 380 kilometres south of the Arabian Peninsula and 232 kilometres east of the Horn of Africa. It is culturally and administratively part of Yemen but geographically belongs to Africa, since it is a continental fragment linked to the Somali plate. The archipelago was once part of Gondwana and detached in the Miocene.

The island has coastal plains with dunes, limestone plateaus where goats and sheep were herded for centuries, and the granite Hajhir Mountains, which rise to 1,503 metres. About 37 per cent of its plant species and 90 per cent of its reptile species are found nowhere else. The inhabitants speak Arabic and Soqotri, a Semitic language related to Mehri.

Oldowan stone tools were found near Hadibo in 2008. In antiquity the island played a part in international trade and appears in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek navigation aid of the first century CE, as the island of Dioscurides. Sailors who visited between the first century BCE and the sixth century CE left nearly 250 inscriptions and drawings in Hoq Cave, in South Arabian, Ethiopic, Brāhmī, Greek, Palmyrene and Bactrian. They are a main source for Indian Ocean trade at that time. Christians lived there in the 6th century.

In 880 an Aksumite force conquered the island, and it was later dislodged by an armada from Oman. The geographer Ibn al-Mujawir, who arrived from India in 1222, described indigenous mountain dwellers and foreign coastal dwellers, among them large settlements of Indian traders. In 1507 a Portuguese fleet under Tristão da Cunha and Afonso de Albuquerque captured the port of Suq after a hard fight with the Mahra Sultanate, hoping for a base on the route to India. Famine and sickness struck the garrison, and the Portuguese left in 1511. The Mahra sultans regained control and the inhabitants were converted to Islam.

The East India Company kept a garrison on Socotra in 1834 and 1835, but the sultan refused to sell the island. In 1886 the British government made a protectorate treaty with him. The Mahra Sultanate was abolished in October 1967, and on 30 November 1967 Socotra became part of South Yemen.

Socotra is a Yemeni island, and its principal town, Hadibu, lies on the north coast. The Dragon's Blood Tree, Dracaena cinnabari, which has an umbrella-like crown and a red sap, is the best-known of its endemic plants. UNESCO recognised the archipelago as a World Heritage Site in 2008.
socrates: Socrates left no writings, and what is known of him comes from others: his pupils Plato and Xenophon, the comic dramatist Aristophanes, and Aristotle, who was born after his death. These accounts often contradict one another, a difficulty scholars call the Socratic problem. Xenophon wrote about him in the Memorabilia, the Oeconomicus, the Symposium and the Apology. How far Plato's dialogues portray the historical Socrates is debated, and some scholars distinguish an earlier, more faithful portrait from a later one carrying Plato's own views.

Socrates was born in 470 or 469 BCE in the Athenian deme of Alopece, to Sophroniscus, a stoneworker, and Phaenarete, a midwife. He had the usual education of a well-off Athenian and served in three campaigns of the Peloponnesian War, according to Plato. He married Xanthippe, with whom he had three sons, and also a daughter of the statesman Aristides. He was indifferent to comfort, owned one ragged coat and walked barefoot, and he criticised both the democrats and the oligarchs of Athens.

The method named for him, the elenchus, is shown mainly in Plato's early dialogues. Socrates asks an apparent expert for a definition, and further questions lead the expert to contradict it. A new definition is then tested in the same way. The discussion usually ends in an impasse, with the interlocutor unable to define what he thought he understood. Socrates frequently proclaimed his ignorance, saying he was sure only that he did not know.

Scholars dispute what the method achieves. In 1982 Gregory Vlastos argued that it could show only that an interlocutor's beliefs were inconsistent. Because Socrates taught no fixed doctrine, later schools drew different conclusions.

In 399 BCE Socrates was accused of impiety and of corrupting the youth. The accusation was brought by a poet, Meletus, with Anytus and Lycon. The trial came after the defeat of Athens by Sparta at the Battle of Aegospotami in 404 BCE and the rule of the Thirty Tyrants, and it probably lasted most of a day. A jury of hundreds of citizens found him guilty. He proposed free meals from the state, or alternatively a fine of one mina of silver, and the jurors ordered his death. Plato relates that he was put to death with hemlock after refusing offers to help him escape.

Almost every philosophical current after Socrates traced its roots to him, among them Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, the Cynics and the Stoics, except the Epicureans and the Pyrrhonists. He was considered to have shifted philosophy from the natural world to human affairs.
sodom-and-gomorrah: In Genesis, Sodom and Gomorrah are two of the cities of the plain. Lot, the nephew of the patriarch Abraham, settled in the Jordan Valley and moved his tent as far as Sodom. Genesis 14:2 names Bera as king of Sodom and Birsha as king of Gomorrah. The two cities rebelled against Chedorlaomer of Elam, to whom they were subject, and he defeated them at the Battle of Siddim and took many captives, including Lot. Abraham gathered his men, rescued Lot and freed the cities.

The Genesis account then tells that God resolved to destroy Sodom because of its reputation for wickedness. Abraham asked whether the righteous would be swept away with the wicked, and obtained God's agreement to spare the city if ten righteous people could be found. Two angels came to Lot's house in the evening. The men of the town surrounded it and demanded that Lot surrender the visitors so that they might know them, and the angels struck the crowd blind. Lot and his daughters were spared, while Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt for looking back.

Genesis names no single sin as the cause. Other texts attribute various sins, sexual and nonsexual, and Ezekiel, Isaiah and Jeremiah describe the crimes of Sodom as concerning the poor treatment of the less fortunate, as well as adultery and lies. Since 1955 scholars have increasingly read the central sin as inhospitality to guests, while debate turns on the Hebrew verb yada, to know, in Genesis 19:5. The reading that the sin was homosexuality is traced to Philo of Alexandria, and became accepted Church teaching in the 12th century. The Quran refers to the people of Lut and their destruction, associated primarily with idolatrous practices.

The cities may have been based on real places along the Dead Sea, and Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira have been suggested as candidates, though the archaeological evidence is inconclusive. Strabo placed Sodom at a hill of limestone and salt at the south-western tip of the Dead Sea, near Mount Sodom, and some scholars believe the cities lie flooded beneath the southern basin of the sea. One proposal is an earthquake between 2100 and 1900 BCE along the Jordan Rift Valley, but no contemporary account of seismic activity supports it, and volcanic and meteor explanations have been dismissed as unlikely. The names became a byword for destruction and desolation in the prophets and the New Testament.
sofia: Sofia lies in western Bulgaria in the Sofia Valley, at the northern foot of the Vitosha mountain, on an average altitude of 550 metres. It is surrounded by mountains: Vitosha to the south, Lyulin to the west and the Balkan Mountains to the north. It is built west of the Iskar. Its development as a settlement owes much to its central position in the Balkans: three mountain passes lead to the city and have been key roads since antiquity, and Vitosha is the watershed between the Black and Aegean seas. Hot water springs still flow abundantly in the centre.

The area has a history of nearly 7,000 years. A Neolithic village at Slatina is documented. The earliest tribes were the Thracian Tilataei, and in the 500s BCE the area joined the Odrysian kingdom. In 339 BCE Philip II of Macedon destroyed and ravaged the town for the first time. The Celtic tribe Serdi gave the city its name, Serdica; the earliest mention is an Athenian inscription of the 1st century BCE, and according to Dio Cassius the Roman general Crassus subdued the Serdi. The emperor Marcus Ulpius Traianus gave it the name Ulpia Serdica.

During the decline of the Roman Empire the city was raided by Huns, Visigoths, Avars and Slavs. In 809 Khan Krum incorporated it into the First Bulgarian Empire, and it became known as Sredets. In 1018 the Byzantines ended Bulgarian rule until 1194, when the Second Bulgarian Empire took it back. Sredets was a major administrative, economic, cultural and literary hub until the Ottoman conquest in 1382. From 1530 to 1836 Sofia was the regional capital of Rumelia Eyalet, the Ottoman Empire's largest and most important province.

Its population fell from 70,000 in the late 18th century to 19,000 in 1870 and 11,649 in 1878. Bulgarian rule was restored in 1878, and Sofia was selected as the capital of the Third Bulgarian State the next year, beginning a period of intense demographic and economic growth. After the Liberation War, knyaz Alexander Battenberg invited architects from Austria-Hungary to shape the new capital.

Sofia is the capital and largest city of Bulgaria. Ancient Roman, Byzantine and medieval Bulgarian buildings survive in the centre, among them the 4th-century Rotunda of St. George, the walls of the Serdica fortress and part of the Amphitheatre of Serdica. The Boyana Church was included on the World Heritage List in 1979.
sogdians: Sogdia, or Sogdiana, lay between the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, including the fertile valley of the Zeravshan, in what is now Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Its Bronze Age urban culture appears at Sarazm in Tajikistan, as early as the 4th millennium BCE. The Sogdian city-states, centred on Samarkand, were never politically united. Sogdian is an Eastern Iranian language, no longer spoken, although Yaghnobi, a descendant of one of its dialects, is still spoken by the Yaghnobis of Tajikistan. Sogdiana was a province of the Achaemenid Empire, named on the Behistun Inscription of Darius I, and Cyrus the Great conquered it in 546 to 539 BCE.

Alexander the Great's forces captured the Sogdian Rock in 327 BCE, and Roxana, daughter of the Sogdian nobleman Oxyartes, married Alexander. Sogdia later passed to the Seleucid Empire, the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, the Sakas and the Yuezhi, and the Sasanian Empire conquered it in 260 CE.

The Hephthalites took it around 479, and the First Turkic Khaganate and the Sasanians defeated them perhaps in 557, after which the Turks kept the land north of the Oxus. Qutayba ibn Muslim began the Muslim conquest of Sogdia in the early 8th century, and Sogdians, aided by the Turgesh, expelled the Umayyad garrison from Samarkand.

Conversion to Islam was virtually complete by the end of the Samanid Empire in 999, and Sogdian was largely supplanted by New Persian. Genghis Khan later destroyed Bukhara and Samarkand, but in 1370 Samarkand revived as the capital of the Timurid Empire.

The Sogdians turned their energies to trade so thoroughly that the Saka of Khotan called all merchants suli, Sogdian. They learned trade from the Kushans and became the main Silk Road middlemen after the Kushan collapse, establishing a trading network across the 1,500 miles from Sogdiana to China. In 568 a Sogdian diplomat, Maniah, persuaded Istämi, ruler of the First Turkic Khaganate, to send an embassy to Constantinople, where Justin II agreed to an alliance against Sasanian Persia and a direct silk trade.

Other Sogdians settled in China for generations and rose to prominence in the military and government of the Tang dynasty. They first practised Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism, Buddhism and, to a lesser extent, the Church of the East. The 6th century is thought to be the peak of Sogdian culture, and the Afrasiab paintings of Samarkand and the murals of Panjakent are rare surviving examples of its art.
sognefjord: The Sognefjord, nicknamed the King of the Fjords, stretches 205 kilometres inland from the ocean to the small village of Skjolden in Luster Municipality. It gives its name to the surrounding district of Sogn; the name is related to the Norwegian word súg-, to suck, presumably from the surge of the tidal currents at the fjord's mouth. The fjord is up to six kilometres wide, and its main branch averages less than five. It reaches 1,308 metres below sea level, with the deepest parts near Høyanger, and is more than 1,000 metres deep for about 100 kilometres.

Cliffs rise almost sheer from the water to 1,000 metres and more. The inner end lies south-east of a mountain range covered by the Jostedalsbreen, continental Europe's largest glacier, so its climate is less wet than the outer coast. The whole system, with its branches, holds about 500 cubic kilometres of water. The main branches include the Aurlandsfjord, the Fjærlandsfjord and the Nærøyfjord, 18 km long, a World Heritage Site that is only 300 metres across at its narrowest. The innermost arm, the Lustrafjord, is 42 km long.

The valley predates the Quaternary glaciations. The fjords of western Norway formed in connection with the eastward tilting of much of Norway during the Cenozoic uplift of the Scandinavian Mountains, which let rivers cut deeply into the older landscape. An estimated 7,610 cubic kilometres of rock has eroded from the drainage basin since then. During the last glaciation the ice reached a maximum thickness of nearly 3,000 metres, and the confluence of tributary fjords excavated the deepest basin.

In earlier times, transport between Bergen and the Scandinavian inland went by boat between Bergen and Skjolden and from there over the highlands on a simple road, or by boat to Lærdal and through the mountain pass to Valdres. Around the inner end of the fjord three of Norway's stave churches have survived: Kaupanger and Urnes along the shoreline, and Borgund, 30 km into the Lærdal valley.

The fjord runs through ten municipalities, among them Solund, Sogndal, Aurland, Årdal and Luster, and boats and ferries connect the settlements along it and its side arms. Gudvangen lies by the Nærøyfjord, and from Flåm the Flåm Railway climbs 864 metres to Myrdal Station over 20 kilometres. The Nærøyfjord and the Geirangerfjord are listed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Summer tourists are an important part of the local economy.
soissons: Soissons is a commune in the department of Aisne in northern France, on the river Aisne about 100 kilometres north-east of Paris. It is one of the most ancient towns of France and is probably the ancient capital of the Suessiones. It has been the see of a Roman Catholic diocese since about 300, and a number of church synods, called the Council of Soissons, met there.

The town enters written history under its Celtic name Noviodunum, meaning new hillfort, as the capital of the Suessiones. Julius Caesar mentions it in 57 BCE: after leaving the Aisne he reached Noviodunum in one long day's march, found it surrounded by a high wall and a broad ditch, and received its surrender. From 457 to 486, under Aegidius and his son Syagrius, it was the capital of the Kingdom of Soissons, until it fell to the Frankish king Clovis I after the Battle of Soissons in 486.

As part of Neustria, the region and the Abbey of Saint-Médard, founded in the sixth century, played a political part under the Merovingian dynasty. After the death of Clovis I in 511 Soissons became the capital of one of the four kingdoms into which his lands were divided, until Chlothar II amalgamated the Frankish lands in 613. The Council of Soissons of 744 met at the instigation of Pepin the Short and Saint Boniface and condemned the bishop Adalbert and the missionary Clement of Ireland.

During the Hundred Years' War French forces committed a massacre of English archers in the town's garrison, in which many townsfolk were also killed. Henry V of England, noting that the town was dedicated to Saints Crispin and Crispinian, claimed to avenge their honour at Agincourt on Saint Crispin's Day 1415. Joan of Arc's forces liberated Soissons on 23 July 1429. The Congress of Soissons, held from June 1728 to July 1729, sought to settle disputes between Great Britain and Spain and led to the Treaty of Seville. The Prussians besieged the town for over a month in the Franco-Prussian War, and it surrendered in October 1870. It was heavily bombarded in World War I.

Soissons is a commercial and manufacturing centre. Its Gothic cathedral of Saint-Gervais-et-Saint-Protais was begun about 1177, and its choir was completed in 1211, earlier than Chartres Cathedral. The other principal sites are the ruins of the Abbey of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes and the crypt of the former Abbey of Saint-Médard. The Passerelle des Anglais, a footbridge over the Aisne, was rebuilt in 1914 by British soldiers and again in 1950.
sojourner-truth: Sojourner Truth was born Isabella Bomefree, later also given as Baumfree, and estimated that she was born between 1797 and 1800. She was one of ten or twelve children of James and Elizabeth Bomefree, who were held as slaves by the Hardenbergh family at Swartekill in the town of Esopus, New York. Her first language was Dutch, and she spoke with a Dutch accent for the rest of her life. When she was an infant, her brother and sister were sold to a different estate.

New York began to legislate the abolition of slavery in 1799, but emancipation was not complete until 4 July 1827. Her owner, Dumont, had promised to free her a year earlier if she did well, then changed his mind. Late in 1826 she walked away with her infant daughter Sophia, leaving her other children, who were not freed until they had served as bound servants. Isaac and Maria Van Wagenen of New Paltz took her in. In 1828 she went to court to recover her son and became the first Black woman to win such a case against a white man.

On 1 June 1843 she took the name Sojourner Truth, after hearing the Spirit of God calling her to preach the truth, and set out to travel and preach against slavery. In 1844 she joined the Northampton Association of Education and Industry in Florence, Massachusetts, a community founded by abolitionists, where she met William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass and gave her first anti-slavery speech.

In May 1851 she spoke at the Ohio Women's Rights Convention in Akron. The first report, by Marius Robinson in the Anti-Slavery Bugle, does not contain the question Ain't I a Woman. A version published twelve years later by Frances Dana Barker Gage, in a speech pattern associated with enslaved people in the South, became the most widely circulated, though Truth, raised in New York, is unlikely to have spoken so. During the Civil War she helped recruit Black men into the Union army, and afterwards she tried unsuccessfully to secure land grants for formerly enslaved people.

Truth died at her home in Battle Creek, Michigan, on 26 November 1883, and about a thousand people attended her funeral. A memorial bust was unveiled in 2009 in Emancipation Hall in the Capitol Visitor Center, making her the first African American woman with a statue in the Capitol.
solapur: Solapur lies on the Deccan Plateau in the south-western part of Maharashtra, close to the border with Karnataka, at an average elevation of 458 metres. It is about 410 km from Mumbai, 245 km from Pune and 305 km from Hyderabad, and it stands on a major highway and at a junction of railway lines between Mumbai, Pune, Bangalore and Hyderabad. The climate is dry, with three seasons, summer, monsoon and winter. The name is believed to come from the Marathi words sola, sixteen, and pura, village: the present city was considered to spread over sixteen villages, among them Ahmedpur, Fatehpur and Sonallagi.

The area was ruled by various dynasties, among them the Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Yadavas and Bahamanis. Inscriptions from the time of the Kalachuris of Kalyani show the town was called Sonnalage, an old Kannada name later pronounced Sonnalagi, and it was the main commercial hub of the Yadavas of Devagiri. A Sanskrit inscription found at Kamati in Mohol gives the name Sonalipur, and inscriptions in the fort give Sonalpur and Sandalpur.

The Solapur district was formed in stages in the 19th century: in 1838 it became a sub-district of Ahmednagar, and in 1871 it was reformed with subdivisions from Satara. After the reorganisation of 1956 Solapur belonged to Bombay State, and in 1960 it became a district of Maharashtra.

Weavers of the Padmashali community moved to Solapur and other places in search of work when imported English cloth undercut hand weaving. Many worked in cotton mills. The Manacha Shri Ajoba Ganpati temple began celebrating the Ganesh festival in 1885, and Lokmanya Tilak, who visited Solapur, started the Ganesh festival in Pune in 1893. During the independence movement the Solapur Municipal Council hoisted the Indian national flag on its building on 6 April 1930, in the spirit of Gandhi's Dandi March.

Residents enjoyed full freedom from 9 to 11 May 1930. Four men, Mallappa Dhanshetti, Abdul Rasool Qurban Hussein, Jagannath Bhagwan Shinde and Shrikisan Laxminarayan Sarada, were hanged by the British on 12 January 1931 at Pune, and the city became known as the City of Hutatmas, the City of Martyrs.

Solapur is a city of Marathi, Kannada and Telugu cultural influences. It has long been a centre of cotton mills, power looms and handlooms, and Solapuri chadars were the first product in Maharashtra to receive a Geographical Indication tag. It also leads Maharashtra in the production of beedi cigarettes. The chief deity of the city is Shri Shivyogi Siddheshwar, and the Gadda Yatra fair, with the Nandi-dhawaj procession at Makar Sankranti, is associated with his marriage. The Shri Siddheshwar Swami Temple and the Bhuikot Fort are its main sights.
solar-cell: Edmond Becquerel demonstrated the photovoltaic effect experimentally and in 1839, at the age of 19, built the first photovoltaic cell in his father's laboratory. In a 20 February 1873 issue of Nature, Willoughby Smith described the effect of light on selenium during the passage of an electric current. In 1876 William Grylls Adams and Richard Evans Day constructed the first solid-state photovoltaic cell, and in 1883 Charles Fritts built another by coating selenium with a thin layer of gold to form the junctions; his device was only about 1 per cent efficient.

A solar cell is an electronic device whose electrical characteristics change when it is exposed to light. Its operation needs three things: the absorption of light, the separation of charge carriers of opposite types and their separate extraction to an external circuit. Most cells are made of semiconducting material, usually silicon, fabricated into a p-n junction, formed by doping one side p-type and the other n-type with small amounts of boron or phosphorus. A single silicon cell produces an open-circuit voltage of about 0.5 to 0.6 volts, so cells are joined into modules, and strings of modules into arrays, which give direct current that an inverter often converts to alternating current.

Almost all commercial cells are of crystalline silicon, cut into wafers 160 to 240 micrometres thick. Thin-film cells, of which cadmium telluride is the main kind, use less material, while multi-junction cells stack layers that absorb different parts of the spectrum and were first developed for satellites.

The first prominent application was in space. Solar cells were proposed and flown on the Vanguard satellite in 1958 as an alternative to its battery, which allowed the mission to last longer without changes to the spacecraft. In 1959 the United States launched Explorer 6, with large wing-shaped arrays of 9600 Hoffman solar cells, and such arrays became a common feature of satellites.

Costs stayed high through the 1960s because space users would pay for the best cells, and in 1971 a cell cost some $100,000 per watt. Terrestrial research grew with a programme of the US National Science Foundation that ran from 1969 to 1977 and with the Cherry Hill Conference of 1973. Adjusted for inflation, a solar module cost $96 per watt in the mid-1970s and 30 cents per watt in 2018. Solar cells are also used to power calculators and watches.
solidarity-polish-trade-union: In the 1970s Poland's government raised food prices while wages stagnated, and protests in 1976 were followed by a crackdown on dissent. Groups such as KOR and ROPCiO began to form underground networks to monitor and oppose the government, with labour unions an important part of them. In 1979 the Polish economy shrank for the first time since World War II, and foreign debt reached around 18 billion dollars by 1980. The writings of the philosopher Leszek Kołakowski, banned in Poland, circulated in underground copies, and Pope John Paul II's 1979 visit to Poland was, in Lech Wałęsa's words, a significant factor in the creation of the union.

Anna Walentynowicz was dismissed from the Gdańsk Shipyard on 7 August 1980, five months before she was due to retire, for taking part in the illegal trade union. Workers struck in her defence on 14 August, and she and Alina Pienkowska turned a strike over bread and butter into a solidarity strike with other establishments. The government signed the agreement allowing the union to exist on 31 August 1980. On 17 September more than twenty founding committees merged into one national organisation, and it was registered on 10 November 1980.

Solidarity brought together people linked to the Catholic Church and members of the anti-Soviet left, and it advocated non-violence. In September 1981 its first national congress elected Wałęsa president and adopted a programme called the Self-governing Republic. The government imposed martial law on 13 December 1981 under General Wojciech Jaruzelski, arresting the regional delegates. The union survived underground with financial support from the Vatican and the United States.

The Round Table talks of 6 February to 5 April 1989 led to semi-free elections on 4 June 1989, in which the opposition won 99 of the 100 Senate seats and all 161 contestable seats in the Sejm. A Solidarity-led coalition government was formed by the end of August, with Tadeusz Mazowiecki as prime minister, and in December 1990 Wałęsa was elected President of Poland.

The union's survival was unprecedented in the Eastern bloc, where Soviet-led invasions had quelled the Hungarian Uprising of 1956 and the Prague Spring of 1968. Its electoral victory in 1989 set off a mostly bloodless chain of events across Central and Eastern Europe known as the Revolutions of 1989. Wałęsa was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983. Organised as one big union by region rather than by craft, the union reached about 10 million members in September 1981, a third of the working-age population. After 1989 it became a more traditional trade union, and a political arm, Solidarity Electoral Action, won the parliamentary election of 1997.
solidus: The solidus, from the Latin for solid, was a highly pure gold coin of the Later Roman and Byzantine empires. It replaced the aureus in the early 4th century, and Constantine the Great struck it for mass circulation from about 312. His coins were struck at 72 to a Roman pound of gold, about 326.6 g, so each weighed about 4.5 grams. The weight stayed relatively constant for seven centuries, and the solidus was also a unit of weight, one seventy-second of a Roman pound. In Western Europe it was the main gold coin of commerce from late Roman times to the Early Middle Ages. In the Greek-speaking world it was called the nomisma.

In theory it was pure gold, but the limits of refining meant coins were often about 23 carats, or 95.8% gold. It bore no face value throughout its manufacture. Fractions were produced, the semissis, a half, and the tremissis, a third, and these were especially popular in the West, where few purchases required a coin as large as the solidus.

From the 4th to the 11th centuries solidi were mostly minted at Constantinople. After 476 the Germanic successor kingdoms, such as the Ostrogothic Kingdom and the Franks, struck imitations bearing the portrait and title of the emperor in Constantinople. Justinian I's reconquests reopened mints such as Carthage, which struck great numbers until the Arab conquest in 698.

Although imperial law forbade merchants to export solidi, it was loosely enforced, and many have been found in Russia, Central Europe, Georgia and Syria. The word soldier is ultimately derived from solidus, referring to those paid in solidi.

Michael IV began debasing the coin in 1034. Its fineness fell to about 21 carats under Constantine IX Monomachos, 16 under Romanos IV Diogenes and, after the defeat at Manzikert, to 14 under Michael VII Doukas and between 0 and 8 carats in the first eleven years of Alexios I Komnenos. In 1092 Alexios abolished the solidus and introduced the hyperpyron, at about 20.5 carats, which stayed stable until the sack of Constantinople in 1204.

In medieval Europe, where the only coin in circulation was the silver penny, the solidus survived as a unit of account worth 12 deniers. Its name gave the French sou, the Italian soldo, the Spanish sueldo and the English shilling, whose abbreviation s. comes from solidus, and the word soldier is ultimately derived from it, referring to those paid in solidi.
solingen: Solingen lies 25 kilometres east of Düsseldorf along the northern edge of the Bergisches Land, south of the Ruhr, and after Wuppertal is the second-largest city of the Bergisches Land. The city covers 89.45 square kilometres, about half of it used for agriculture, horticulture or forestry. The Wupper, a right tributary of the Rhine, flows through it for 26 kilometres. Solingen is called the Klingenstadt, the City of Blades, and its local dialect, a variety of Limburgish, calls the city Solich.

A chronicler first mentioned the area in 1067 as Solonchon, and the modern form of the name seems to have been in use from the late 14th and early 15th centuries. Smelters of blacksmiths more than 2,000 years old have been found around the town. Swords from Solingen have turned up in the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of the British Isles and were traded across Europe. It was a tiny village for centuries and became a fortified town in the 15th century. In the late 17th century a group of Solingen swordsmiths broke their guild oaths and took their sword-making secrets to Shotley Bridge in County Durham, England.

Plague killed about 1,800 people in 1614 to 1619. In the Thirty Years' War Solingen was heavily fought over, repeatedly attacked and plundered, and Burg Castle was destroyed. Ohligs, whose chief products early in the 20th century were cutlery and hardware, became part of Solingen in 1929. A British air raid in 1944 destroyed the Old Town completely, killing 1,800 people and injuring over 1,500, so few pre-war sites remain in the centre. From 1945 to 1949 Solingen lay in the British occupation zone, and reconstruction of the old town began in 1949. The independent town of Burg an der Wupper was incorporated in 1975.

Solingen's firms still make swords, knives, scissors and razors. The German Blade Museum shows swords and cutlery of all periods, and the Rhineland Industrial Museum is in the Hendrichs Drop Forge. Burg Castle was the castle of the counts of Berg. The Müngsten Bridge, built in 1897 and originally named the Kaiser-Wilhelm-Brücke, carries a railway 107 metres above the ground between Solingen and Remscheid and is the tallest railway bridge in Germany.
solomon: Solomon was born in Jerusalem, the second child of David and his wife Bathsheba, the widow of Uriah the Hittite. The first child of the union, a son conceived while Uriah was alive, died seven days after birth, which the Hebrew Bible suggests was a judgment from God. Solomon had three named full brothers and six known older half-brothers. His two names, Solomon and Jedidiah, are traditionally taken to mean peaceful and friend of God. The conventional dates of his reign, about 970 to 931 BCE, derive from biblical chronology.

According to the Hebrew Bible, God appeared to Solomon in a dream and asked what he wanted. Solomon asked for wisdom in order to rule his people, and God, pleased that he had not asked for long life or the death of his enemies, promised it. The account describes a reign of forty years in which Israel reached a height of splendour and wealth. He allied himself with Hiram I, king of Tyre, who sent materials and an architect for the Temple that David had gathered materials to build. The account also gives him 700 wives and 300 concubines, many of them foreign princesses, and disapproves of his building temples to their gods. It tells of a visit by the Queen of Sheba.

Solomon died of natural causes at around 55 years of age. His son Rehoboam succeeded him, but ten of the tribes refused him and followed Jeroboam, splitting the monarchy into the northern Kingdom of Israel and the smaller southern Kingdom of Judah. The historicity of Solomon is much debated. Current scholarship generally allows that a historical Solomon is possible, but regards the biblical picture of his opulence as almost surely an anachronistic exaggeration. Tradition ascribes to him the books of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs. He is revered in Islam as the prophet Sulaiman ibn Dawud, and the Solomon Islands were named for him by Álvaro de Mendaña in 1568.
solon: Solon's family belonged to a noble Eupatrid clan of Attica. His father was probably Execestides, which would trace his lineage back to Codrus, the last king of Athens. According to Plutarch he was related to the later tyrant Pisistratus. When Athens and Megara contested possession of Salamis, Solon led the Athenian forces after repeated disasters and raised their morale with a patriotic poem. With the support of Pisistratus he defeated the Megarians around 595 BCE, and the Spartans, asked to settle the dispute, awarded the island to Athens.

According to Diogenes Laërtius, Solon was chosen archon in 594 BCE and repealed all of Draco's laws except those on homicide. His debt relief, later called the seisachtheia, the shaking off of burdens, addressed a system in which farmers who could not honour their obligations, and their families, could be sold into slavery. Aristotle's Athenian Constitution calls him the first people's champion, and says he admitted all citizens to the Ekklesia and formed a court, the Heliaia, from all citizens. His laws were inscribed on wooden axones kept in the Prytaneion.

Modern knowledge is limited. His laws survive only in fragments quoted by Plutarch and others, and fourth-century orators such as Aeschines tended to attribute to him every law of their own day. His poems also survive only in fragments.

After completing his reforms Solon surrendered his extraordinary authority and travelled abroad for ten years so that the Athenians could not press him to repeal any law. Within four years of his departure the old social rifts returned, and Pisistratus ended the factionalism by force and established a tyranny. Solon opposed him and died shortly after, around the age of 70. Pausanias lists him among the Seven Sages of Greece, and Demosthenes credited his reforms with starting a golden age.
somali-region: The Somali Region, officially the Somali Regional State, is a region of eastern Ethiopia and the second largest of the country by area. It borders Afar and Oromia to the west, Djibouti to the north, Somalia to the east and south, and Kenya to the southwest. Its capital is Jijiga. The region is divided into eleven administrative zones and several special zones, among them Fafan, Jarar, Korahe, Liben and Sitti. Its people are mainly pastoralists, and in 2005 the region was estimated to hold 96.2 percent of Ethiopia's camels.

The area was part of the conquests of Menelik II in the late 19th century. Until 1995 it formed a large part of the provinces of Hararghe, Bale and Sidamo. There have been attempts to incorporate the area into a Greater Somalia. In 1977 Somalia invaded Ethiopia, starting the Ogaden War, which Somalia lost after the Soviet Union and Cuba intervened; afterwards local groups continued to seek either union with Somalia or independence. The first district elections were held in February 2004, before which zone and woreda administrators had been appointed by the regional government.

The census of 2007 counted 4,439,147 people, of whom 14 percent lived in towns. Somali is the first language of nearly 96 percent of the population, and almost all are Muslim. The region is home to almost all major Somali clan families, the Ogaden clan of the Darod being the largest, while Dir subclans such as the Issa and Gadabuursi live mainly in the north.
somalia: Somalia is the easternmost country in continental Africa. It borders Ethiopia, Djibouti and Kenya, and has the longest coastline on the mainland, more than 3,333 kilometres, along the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Its land area is 637,657 square kilometres of plateaus, plains and highlands. In the north a semi-desert plain, the Guban, runs parallel to the Gulf of Aden coast, and the Cal Madow range contains the highest peak, Shimbiris, at about 2,416 metres. The country sits at the mouth of the Bab el Mandeb gateway to the Red Sea.

The oldest evidence of burial customs in the Horn of Africa comes from cemeteries in Somalia dating to the 4th millennium BCE. The Laas Geel rock art near Hargeisa is approximately 5,000 years old. Ancient stone ruins have been taken as evidence of a civilisation that traded with Egypt and Mycenaean Greece from the second millennium BCE, supporting the hypothesis that Somalia or adjacent regions were the Land of Punt. An Egyptian expedition to Punt sent by Queen Hatshepsut is recorded on the reliefs at Deir el-Bahari. Puntites traded myrrh, spices, gold, ebony, ivory and frankincense.

In the Middle Ages the Ajuran Sultanate, Adal Sultanate and Sultanate of the Geledi dominated regional trade. The Italian and British empires colonised the sultanates in the late 19th century, forming Italian Somaliland and British Somaliland, which united in 1960 as the Somali Republic. Siad Barre seized power in 1969, launched a failed invasion of Ethiopia and brutally attempted to quash the Somaliland War of Independence.

Barre's regime collapsed in 1991 with the onset of the Somali Civil War. A provisional constitution adopted on 1 August 2012 made Somalia a federation. About 85 per cent of residents are ethnic Somalis. Somali is the official language, Arabic is recognised as a second, and the overwhelming majority are Sunni Muslims. About 80 per cent of the population are nomadic or semi-nomadic pastoralists.
somalis: The origin of the name is debated. Tradition names Samaale as the common ancestor of several clans, and the ethnonym is generally regarded as derived from him. Other proposals derive it from soo and maal, meaning go and milk, or from an Arabic word for wealthy, both pointing to herding. Ancient rock paintings estimated at 5,000 years old, among them the Laas Geel complex in the Somaliland region, are among the earliest known rock art on the African continent and show pastoralist scenes. According to most scholars, the ancient Land of Punt, which had close relations with Egypt under Sahure and Hatshepsut, formed part of the ethnogenesis of the Somali people.

Somali society is traditionally clan-based and patrilineal. Most Somalis belong to one of five clan families, the Hawiye, Darod, Isaaq, Rahanweyn and Dir, and many can trace their ancestry back several generations. Pastoralism has long shaped life, and camel meat and milk are important in the diets of herders, whose portable aqal houses are built of wood.

The Somali language belongs to the Cushitic branch of the Afroasiatic family, and its nearest relatives are Afar and Saho. Its dialects fall into three groups, Northern, Benadiri and Maay, and Northern Somali forms the basis of the standard language. Somalis are with very few exceptions Muslims, mostly Sunni of the Shafi'i school. Scholars give two accounts of Islam's arrival: early, through refugees who crossed the Red Sea, or between the 7th and 10th centuries through Arab and Persian merchants. The geographer al-Yaqubi wrote in the late 9th century that Muslims lived along the northern coast.

Poetry plays a central part in Somali social and political life, and Somalia has often been called a nation of poets. Somalis live mainly in Somalia, Somaliland, Ethiopia, Kenya and Djibouti, a region often called Greater Somalia. The flag adopted at independence in 1960 was conceived in 1954 by Mohammed Awale Liban, and its five-pointed star stands for the five territories where Somalis live. The civil war that began in the early 1990s displaced many people and produced a widespread diaspora.
somapura-mahavihara: Somapura was one of five great Buddhist mahaviharas of the Pala period in Bengal and Magadha named in Tibetan sources, with Vikramashila, Nalanda, Odantapura and Jaggadala. They formed a network under state supervision, and scholars moved easily between them. Seals found at Paharpur bear an inscription naming Somapura and the Pala king Dharmapala, who ruled about 781–821 and is identified as its builder. Later inscriptions and Tibetan sources show it in use under Mahendrapala and repaired under Mahipala. Atisa resided there, and many Tibetan monks visited between the 9th and 12th centuries.

In the 11th century a part of the monastery was destroyed by fire set by the army of Jatvarma of the Varman dynasty. It declined for the last time under the Sena dynasty in the second half of the 12th century, with no clear signs of large-scale destruction at the ruins.

The monastery covers 11 hectares, and the complex of 8.5 hectares has a quadrangular court with 177 cells and a central temple. Outer walls carry ornamental terracotta plaques whose subjects show the influence of Buddhist, Jain and Hindu traditions. In area it was the largest of the mahaviharas.

The cruciform temple with its terraced, receding form resembles temples of Burma, Java and Cambodia, and scholars have compared its plan and superstructure to Chandi Loro Jongrang and Chandi Sevu of Prambanam in Central Java. The temple's missing superstructure has been reconstructed in different ways: as a stupa by Prudence Myer in 1969, as a shikhara-type stupa-shrine by a team from Khulna University in 1999, and as a crown like that of the Ananda temple at Pagan by Mohammad Habib Reza in 2012.

K. N. Dikshit's Paharpur, published in the Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India in 1938, remains the most authentic record. A copperplate dated to the Gupta year 159, or 479 CE, found in 1927 in the northeast corner, records a donation by a Brahmin couple to a Jain teacher. UNESCO named the site a World Heritage Site in 1985 and prepared a master plan costing US$5.6 million, and a museum was built nearby. The terracotta work has been damaged by poor drainage, salty soil, heavy rain and vegetation.
somerset: Somerset is a ceremonial county of South West England, bordered by the Bristol Channel, Bristol and Gloucestershire to the north, Wiltshire to the east, Dorset to the south-east and Devon to the south-west. The centre of the county is dominated by the Levels, a coastal plain and wetland drained by the Axe, Brue and Parrett. The Mendip Hills, the Quantock Hills and most of Exmoor lie within it. Its name most likely comes from the Old English Sumorsǣte, the people living at or dependent on Sumortūn, now Somerton. The first known use is in the law code of King Ine of Wessex, who reigned from 688 to 726.

The caves of the Mendip Hills were settled in the Palaeolithic. Bones from Gough's Cave at Cheddar Gorge have been dated to 12,000 BCE, and a complete skeleton known as Cheddar Man dates from 7150 BCE. The Sweet Track, one of the oldest known engineered roadways in the world, was built across the Levels in 3807 or 3806 BCE. The Second Legion Augusta invaded Somerset from the south-east in 47 CE, and the county remained Roman until about 409 CE. Roman remains include the baths that gave Bath its name.

After the Romans left, the Anglo-Saxons controlled much of England by 600 CE, but Somerset was still in British hands. It was later brought into the West Saxon kingdom, and the Saxon royal palace at Cheddar was used several times in the 10th century to host the Witenagemot. In the later Middle Ages the wealth of the county paid for grand rebuilding of its monasteries and parish churches. Glastonbury Abbey was particularly important and claimed to house the tomb of King Arthur and Guinevere.

Somerset was largely Parliamentarian in the English Civil War, with the Sieges of Taunton and the Battle of Langport among its engagements. In 1685 the Monmouth Rebellion ended at the Battle of Sedgemoor at Westonzoyland, the last pitched battle fought in England. Arthur Wellesley took his title of Duke of Wellington from the town of Wellington.

The county town is Taunton, which took the status from Somerton, which had taken it from Ilchester, about 1366. Somerset has two cities, Bath and Wells, and the largest settlement is Bath, a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its Georgian architecture. Its boundaries are largely unchanged since the Middle Ages. In 1373 Edward III made Bristol a county of its own, separate from Gloucestershire and Somerset.
somme-river: The Somme is 245 km long. It rises at Fonsomme near Saint-Quentin, on the high ground of the former Arrouaise Forest, and flows to the Bay of the Somme on the English Channel. Because it is fed by groundwater from a chalk basin, its gradient is gentle and its flow steady, and its valley floor is flat, with fens and pools. The traditional market gardens of Amiens, the Hortillonages, lie on this kind of land. The Canal de la Somme, 156 km long, was begun in 1770 and completed in 1843, and the St Quentin Canal and the Canal du Nord link the river to the Oise.

In antiquity the river was known as the Samara, which presumably means the summery or quiet river, from a Celtic root meaning summer. The Gallic town of Samarobriva, bridge on the Samara, was the chief town of the Ambiani by the early first century BCE and later became Amiens.

The Somme has been prominent in many military campaigns. In 1066 William the Conqueror's invasion fleet assembled in the Bay of the Somme at Saint-Valery-sur-Somme. In 1346 the army of Edward III of England forded the river at the Battle of Blanchetaque on the way to Crécy, and in 1415 crossing the river was part of the campaign that led to Agincourt. In 1636 a Spanish army under Thomas Francis, Prince of Carignano, crossed it during the Thirty Years War and defeated a French army, threatening Paris.

The Battle of the Somme, fought from July to November 1916, caused more than a million casualties. In the spring of 1918 the battles that stopped the German offensive were fought in the valley, at places such as Villers Bretonneux.

The river flows through the department that bears its name, past Saint-Quentin, Ham, Péronne, Corbie, Amiens, Abbeville and Saint-Valery-sur-Somme. Its valley still has fens used for fishing and shooting, and a nature reserve at Saint-Quentin.
sonderbund-war: In the early 1840s the radical Free Democratic Party of Switzerland, strong in the largely Protestant cantons and among the urban bourgeoisie, won a majority in the Federal Diet, the Tagsatzung, and proposed a new constitution that would draw the cantons closer together. The Diet had also acted against the Catholic Church, closing the monasteries and convents of Aargau in 1841 and seizing their property. When Lucerne recalled the Jesuits to head its education, bands of armed radicals known as Freischärler invaded the canton.

In 1845 Lucerne, Fribourg, Valais, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug, all predominantly Catholic and under conservative governments, formed the Sonderbund, or separate alliance. Ticino and Solothurn, Catholic but liberal, stayed out. On 21 October 1847 the Diet ordered the league dissolved as a breach of the Federal Treaty of 1815, which forbade such alliances. Austria sent the Sonderbund some money and munitions, but the great powers could not agree on intervention, which Lord Palmerston of Britain refused to support.

The Sonderbund's commander was Jean-Ulrich de Salis-Soglio of Grisons, himself a Protestant. The Diet's choice, Guillaume Henri Dufour of Geneva, was sworn in on 25 October after first declining the office. Neuchâtel and Appenzell Innerrhoden declared themselves neutral and sent no troops. The Sonderbund moved first: troops from Uri seized the St. Gotthard Pass in early November, and the first deaths came on 4 November.

Dufour turned first on isolated Fribourg, which surrendered on 14 November; its act of surrender became the template for the other cantons. Zug's parliament voted to give up on 21 November. On 23 November the federal divisions converged on Lucerne. At Gisikon a third assault, led in person by Colonel Eduard Ziegler, carried the Sonderbund position after two hours; thirty-seven men were killed and about 100 wounded. Federal troops entered Lucerne unopposed the next morning. Unterwalden, Schwyz and Uri yielded between 25 and 27 November, and Valais on 29 November.

The federal army reported 78 killed and 260 wounded; later research arrived at 60 dead and 386 wounded on the federal side and 33 killed and 124 wounded among the Sonderbund. Dufour had ordered his troops to care for the injured and declined to use Congreve rockets, so as not to give the war a violent character. The Sonderbund governments were forced to resign, and Liberals took power in Fribourg, Lucerne and Valais. Federal troops left the occupied cantons by February 1848. The constitution of that year banished the Jesuits from Switzerland, a provision lifted by a vote on 20 May 1973.
sondershausen: Sondershausen is the capital of the Kyffhäuserkreis district, about 50 kilometres north of Erfurt. It lies in a low mountain range between the Hainleite to the north and the Windleite to the south, and the highest hill is the Frauenberg to the west of the town. A small river, the Wipper, flows through it, and the surrounding forests are mixed and dominated by beech. Until 1918 the town belonged to the principality of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen. On 1 December 2007 the former municipality of Schernberg was merged into it.

The palace began as a fort and was built up as a Renaissance palace. It was later extended in the Baroque style between 1764 and 1771, and its Blue Hall and gardens are especially noted. An earlier Princes' Palace, built between 1721 and 1725, served as a residence of the princes from 1835 to 1851 and now houses the district administration office. The Baroque Trinitatiskirche is a Lutheran church with a mausoleum containing the graves of the last members of the princely family. The Crucis Church is the oldest building in the town, and St Matthias Church is considered one of the most beautiful churches of the region.

Sondershausen Palace houses a large museum with three exhibit areas. Among its special exhibits are a Golden Coach, the only one of its kind in Germany, and the bronze figurine known as the Püstrich von Sondershausen. Other places of interest include a former mine under the town and a Jewish bath from the 14th century. The town was the birthplace of the composers and music writers Ernst Christoph Dressler and Ernst Ludwig Gerber, of the poet Johann Karl Wezel and of the theologian Valentin Ernst Löscher. It is twinned with Rolla in Missouri, Pecquencourt in France and Kazlų Rūda in Lithuania.
song-dynasty: The dynasty was founded by Emperor Taizu of Song, who reigned from 960 to 976. He usurped the throne of the Later Zhou dynasty and spent sixteen years conquering the rest of China proper, ending the period of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. The Song often came into conflict with the Liao, Western Xia and Jin dynasties in the north. In 1127, after the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty took the northern half of Song territory, the court retreated south of the Yangtze and set up its capital at Lin'an, now Hangzhou. The two periods are called the Northern Song, 960 to 1127, and the Southern Song, 1127 to 1279.

The Mongols conquered the Jin in 1234 and kept uneasy relations with the Southern Song. Möngke Khan died in 1259 while besieging Diaoyucheng in Chongqing, and his brother Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271. After two decades of sporadic warfare, his armies defeated the Southern Song at the Battle of Yamen in 1279 and reunited China under the Yuan.

Civil service examinations had existed since the Sui dynasty, but under the Song they became virtually the only way into government. Candidates for the lower prefectural examinations rose from about 30,000 a year in the early 11th century to 400,000 by the late 13th century. The change favoured a scholar-bureaucratic elite over a military-aristocratic one. Historians disagree about how open the system was: some, using Song statistics, argue that an official ancestor did not guarantee office, while others criticise that model for ignoring the extended family. The army was organised so that it could not threaten the throne, and the court sometimes removed or executed successful generals such as Yue Fei.

The Northern Song census recorded 20 million households, and its population is estimated at 90 million. Expanded rice cultivation, including early-ripening Champa rice introduced in 1011, supported the growth. Kaifeng and Hangzhou each had over a million people. The state supported retirement homes, public clinics and paupers' graveyards, and its overseas trade passed through ports such as Quanzhou and Guangzhou.

The Wujing Zongyao of 1044 was the first book to give formulas for gunpowder and its uses in bombs. Shen Kuo was the first to discern magnetic declination while experimenting with a compass, and Bi Sheng's movable type was first described in Shen's Dream Pool Essays of 1088. The Song also issued the first true paper money and set up the first permanent standing navy of a Chinese government. Cheng Yi and Zhu Xi renewed Confucianism with new commentary, and their work established the doctrine of Neo-Confucianism.
song-of-songs: The Song of Songs, in Hebrew Shir ha-Shirim, is one of the five megillot, or scrolls, in the Ketuvim, the last section of the Tanakh. Unlike other books of the Hebrew Bible it is erotic poetry, in which lovers express desire, exchange compliments and invite one another to enjoy. It tells a love story between a woman and her lover through dialogues, dreams and metaphors, and the woman warns the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time.

Its title follows an idiom of biblical Hebrew that marks the supreme member of a class, as in Holy of Holies, and the name Song of Solomon means a song of, by, for or dedicated to Solomon. It has no plot, but links between its beginning and end form a framework, and scholars have not agreed how to divide it.

The text gives no explicit reference to its author, or to when, where or how it was composed. Its superscription calls it Solomon's, but modern scholarship argues that it may contain ancient material while there is no evidence that Solomon wrote it. Since the 1800s most scholars have dated it to the 3rd century BCE, chiefly on its language, whose vocabulary, morphology and syntax point to a date centuries after Solomon.

It has parallels with Mesopotamian and Egyptian love poetry and with the pastoral poems of Theocritus, and proposals range from the 10th to the 2nd century BCE; some scholars doubt that its language demands a date after the Babylonian exile. Scholars also debate whether it is a single poem or an anthology, and some connect it with the sacred marriage of Ishtar and Tammuz.

Most scholars now read the Song as erotic poetry celebrating human love, not as a divine metaphor. Judaism accepted it into the canon and long read it as an allegory of the love between God and Israel; canonicity was tied to its attribution to Solomon, and Rabbi Akiva is reported to have forbidden singing it in taverns while defending its place in scripture. Kabbalah later gave it a mystical reading.

Many Jews read it during Passover, a custom first recorded in the 8th century. In Christianity it is viewed as an allegory of Christ and his bride, the Church. It has inspired works by Marc Chagall, Carl Theodor Dreyer, Toni Morrison and John Steinbeck.
songhai-empire: Between the 9th and 3rd centuries BCE several groups formed the Songhai identity around Kukiya: the Sorko, who fished and carried goods by boat on the Niger, the Gao, who hunted river animals, and the Do, who farmed the fertile land. Before the 10th century horse-riding Songhai speakers subjugated them, and by the 10th century the Songhai chiefs had established Gao as a small kingdom controlling the trade routes. Mali conquered Gao around 1300 and held it until about the 1430s, and Ibn Battuta visited the town in 1353. As Mali weakened, the Songhai reasserted control and formalised their independence, probably under Sunni Muhammad Dao.

Sonni Ali took power in 1464, honouring the traditional religion his Dendi mother had taught him, which earned him the reputation of a tyrant among Islamic scholars. He annexed Timbuktu in 1468 and starved Djenné into surrender after a seven-year siege, and he repelled attacks by the Mossi and conquered the Dogon. Under him the Songhai surpassed Mali in area, wealth and power. His son Sonni Baru was overthrown by one of his father's generals, Muhammad Ture, known as Askia the Great.

Askia organised the conquered territory, kept a full-time corps of warriors, built mosques and schools, and made the pilgrimage to Mecca. He centralised the administration, built canals, and introduced a system of weights and measures. In 1528 his children revolted against him, and after 1531 the empire declined through plots and civil wars. In 1591 Sultan Ahmad I al-Mansur of the Saadi dynasty sent an army under Judar Pasha, with thousands of arquebusiers. The Songhai were routed at the Battle of Tondibi despite their numbers, and Judar sacked Gao, Timbuktu and Djenne. The Saadi dynasty soon let the region splinter, and Songhai nobles moved south to found smaller kingdoms.

The empire's wealth rested on overland trade in the Sahel and river trade along the Niger, above all gold from West Africa exchanged for salt, with ivory, ostrich feathers and slaves sent north for horses, camels and cloth. Under Sonni Ali dikes improved irrigation. Society was ordered by clans that decided occupations, with noblemen at the top, then freemen and traders, and prisoners of war and enslaved people at the bottom, working mainly in agriculture. Askia divided the territory into military zones under governors, and criminal justice followed Islamic principles, with qadis in towns such as Timbuktu and Djenne. Timbuktu was the educational capital, and a revival of Islamic scholarship took place at its university.
sonoma-california: When the first Spaniards arrived, the area lay near the north-eastern corner of the territory of the Coast Miwok, with the Southern Pomo to the north-west, the Wappo to the north-east and the Suisun and Patwin peoples to the east. Mission San Francisco Solano, founded in 1823 by the priest José Altimira, Giovanni Toscano and Giovanni Álvarez under Governor Luis Antonio Argüello, was the only mission built by the Mexican authorities rather than the Spanish. It formed part of a plan to fortify the area north of San Francisco Bay against Russian expansion southward from Russian America.

After the Mexican secularization act of 1833, Governor José Figueroa made Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo administrator of the mission and military commander of the Northern Frontier. In 1835, with the help of William A. Richardson, Vallejo laid out the streets, lots, central plaza and main avenue of the Pueblo de Sonoma on a grid prescribed by the Spanish Laws of the Indies. The Sonoma Barracks housed his troops. The pueblo remained under military control until a town council was established in 1844.

Before dawn on 14 June 1846 thirty-three Americans already in rebellion against the Mexican provincial government arrived in Sonoma, some of them from the camp of the army captain John C. Frémont. They met no resistance. They took Vallejo and three associates prisoner, though Vallejo had invited their leaders into his home to negotiate, and William Ide urged the rebels to stay and found a new republic. The remaining twenty-four made the Sonoma Barracks their headquarters and within days created their Bear Flag. The Californios called them Los Osos, the Bears. The Bear Flag Revolt ended and the California Republic ceased on 9 July 1846, when Lieutenant Joseph Warren Revere of the United States Navy raised the American flag before the barracks.

After California became a state in 1850, Sonoma was the first seat of Sonoma County, but an election of 1854 moved the seat to Santa Rosa. Disputes over land titles from Vallejo's grants took some thirty years of lawsuits to settle. The City Hall in the middle of the Plaza was dedicated in 1908.

Sonoma is a city in Sonoma County in the North Bay region of the San Francisco Bay Area, one of the principal cities of California's wine country and the centre of the Sonoma Valley wine region. It had 10,739 residents in the 2020 census. The Plaza, laid out by Vallejo, remains the centre of town.
sonora: Sonora is one of the 31 states that, with Mexico City, make up the Federal Entities of Mexico, and it is divided into 72 municipalities. With a territory of 184,934 square kilometres it is the second largest state of the country. It borders Chihuahua, Baja California and Sinaloa, and to the north it adjoins Arizona and New Mexico along a border 588 kilometres long. The east is dominated by the Sierra Madre Occidental, the centre is plains and rolling hills, and the southwest has a long coast on the Gulf of California. Most of the state is arid or semiarid.

Sonora is home to eight indigenous peoples, among them the Mayo, the O'odham, the Yaqui and the Seri. Evidence of human presence goes back over 10,000 years. The cultures of the region are considered a zone separate from Mesoamerica: they farmed in a dry climate and had no true cities, only small settlements clustered around water sources.

Little reliable information remains about the 16th century after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire. Francisco Vázquez de Coronado passed through in 1540 and called part of the area Valle de la Sonora, the first record of the name. Unlike in central Mexico, no central power existed for the Spaniards to take over, and the Yaqui resisted intrusion until the 17th century. Lasting Spanish settlement became possible only with the mission system.

Sonora became part of an independent Mexico in 1821. The former province of Sonora, Ostimuri, y Sinaloa was divided in 1823 into the states of Sonora and Sinaloa, reunited in 1824 and separated again in 1831, when Sonora wrote its first state constitution. With the Gadsden Purchase it lost more than a quarter of its territory. The Cananea miners' strike of 1906, a prelude to the Mexican Revolution, ended when federal troops put it down brutally.

The capital and largest city is Hermosillo; other large cities include Ciudad Obregón, Nogales and San Luis Río Colorado. Agriculture is the most important economic activity, with irrigation in valleys such as the Yaqui and the Mayo, and Sonora is one of Mexico's two largest wheat-producing states. Livestock and mining have mattered since the colonial period. The El Pinacate biosphere reserve protects a field of dormant volcanic craters.
sophocles: Sophocles was the son of Sophillus, a wealthy member of the rural deme of Hippeius Colonus in Attica, which later became the setting of his play Oedipus at Colonus. He was probably born there a few years before the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, and 496 or 497 BCE is the most likely year. His father manufactured armour, and he was highly educated.

In 480 BCE he was chosen to lead the paean, a choral chant to a god, for the Greek victory over the Persians at the Battle of Salamis. He lived through both the Persian Wars and the Peloponnesian War, and died at the age of 90 or 91 in the winter of 406/5 BCE.

His first artistic triumph came in 468 BCE, when he took first prize at the Dionysia and beat Aeschylus, the reigning master of Athenian drama. According to Plutarch, the archon departed from the custom of choosing judges by lot and asked Cimon and the other generals present to decide. His first production was probably in 470 BCE. For almost 50 years he was the most successful playwright in the dramatic competitions at the festivals of the Lenaea and the Dionysia. He competed 30 times and won 24, and was never placed lower than second. Aeschylus won 13 competitions and Euripides four.

He also served Athens in public office. In 443/2 BCE he was one of the Hellenotamiai, the treasurers of Athena, and in 441 BCE, according to the Vita Sophoclis, he was elected one of the ten generals as a junior colleague of Pericles and served in the campaign against Samos. In 411 BCE he was chosen as one of the commissioners, the probouloi, who responded to the destruction of the Athenian expedition in Sicily. Foreign rulers invited him to their courts, but he never accepted.

Sophocles wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete: Ajax, Antigone, Women of Trachis, Oedipus Rex, Electra, Philoctetes and Oedipus at Colonus. Only Philoctetes, of 409 BCE, and Oedipus at Colonus, staged in 401 BCE after his death by his grandson, can be dated securely. The three Theban plays, Oedipus Rex, Oedipus at Colonus and Antigone, were written for separate competitions many years apart, and they are not a trilogy, which explains some inconsistencies among them.

He is known for innovations in dramatic structure and a deeper development of character than earlier playwrights. Aristotle credits him with adding a third actor, which reduced the role of the chorus, though Themistius attributes this to Aeschylus. Aristotle also used Oedipus Rex in his Poetics as an example of the highest achievement in tragedy. Fragments of the satyr play Ichneutae were discovered in Egypt in 1907, and fragments of the Epigoni in 2005.
sopron: An Iron Age hilltop settlement with a burial ground lay near Sopron-Várhely. Under Roman rule the city of Scarbantia stood here, and the site of its forum is now the main square. By the time Hungarians arrived the city was in ruins. From the 9th to the 11th centuries they strengthened the old Roman walls and built a castle, and the city takes its Hungarian name from a castle steward named Suprun. The city was mentioned as important in 1153. In 1273 King Otakar II of Bohemia occupied the castle, but the city opened its gates to King Ladislaus IV of Hungary, who raised it to the rank of free royal town.

The Ottomans ravaged the city in 1529 without occupying it, and many Hungarians fled there from occupied areas. A fire destroyed the city in 1676, and Baroque buildings replaced the medieval ones over the following decades. After the compromise of 1867 until 1918 it was part of the Habsburg-ruled Kingdom of Hungary, with the dual name Sopron and Ödenburg. In 1910 its 33,931 inhabitants were 51 per cent German and 44.3 per cent Hungarian.

After the breakup of the Austro-Hungarian Empire the German-inhabited parts of four western Hungarian counties were first awarded to Austria by the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in 1919. After local unrest and Italian mediation in the Venice Protocol, a controversial plebiscite on 14 December 1921 decided the status of Sopron and eight surrounding villages, and 65 per cent voted for Hungary. Since then the city has been called Civitas Fidelissima, the Most Loyal City, and the anniversary is a city holiday. The western parts of the counties formed the Austrian state of Burgenland.

Sopron was bombed several times in World War II, and the Red Army captured it on 1 April 1945. On 19 August 1989 it was the site of the Pan-European Picnic on the border with Austria, which over 600 East Germans used to escape to the West and which helped pave the way for the mass flight that preceded the fall of the Berlin Wall.

Walls and foundations from Roman times remain in the old town, together with Medieval, Renaissance and Baroque buildings, among them the Esterházy Palace and the Firewatch Tower. Sopron is also a wine-producing region, known for Kékfrankos red and Traminer white wines, and its street signs are in Hungarian and German.
sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz: Juana Inés de Asbaje y Ramírez de Santillana was born at San Miguel Nepantla, near Mexico City, the illegitimate daughter of Don Pedro Manuel de Asuaje y Vargas-Machuca, a Spanish navy captain from the Canary Islands involved in transatlantic shipping and trade, and Doña Isabel Ramírez de Santillana y Rendón, a criolla whose father leased the Hacienda de Panoayan.

In 1667 she entered the Monastery of St. Joseph, a community of Discalced Carmelite nuns, but stayed only a few months. In 1669 she entered the Hieronymite convent, whose rules were more relaxed, and took the name Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz. She chose the convent so that she could study as she wished, wanting in her words no fixed occupation that might curtail her freedom to study. Octavio Paz and Diane Marting hold that she also refused marriage, and that the convent gave her authority and freedom without it.

First Dream is a long philosophical and descriptive silva, a poetic form combining verses of seven and eleven syllables. It describes the shadow of night, the sleep of a person and the soul's vision of itself at the summit of its own intellect. Her poem Hombres Necios, written in the 1680s, explores the double standards of men and is among the first proto-feminist literary works in the Americas. Her comedies, among them Pawns of a House, first performed on 4 October 1683, are read by some scholars as questioning the relations of men and women through humour.

She was also interested in science, mathematics and music, and wrote a treatise, El Caracol, now lost, that sought to simplify musical notation and to solve problems of Pythagorean tuning. One surviving musical work attributed to her is the four-part villancico Madre, la de los primores. Her contemporaries nicknamed her The Tenth Muse and The Phoenix of America.

Sor Juana died on 17 April 1695. She wrote most of her work in the convent of San Jerónimo; its buildings in the historic centre of Mexico City now house the University of the Cloister of Sor Juana, founded by the Mexican government in 1979. Her works were rediscovered after her death, and Octavio Paz did much to restore her importance in his 1982 book on her life and times. Scholars have presented her as a candidate for Catholic sainthood, a symbol of Mexican nationalism and, in recent decades, a feminist before the time of feminism.
sora-lazio: Sora lies in the province of Frosinone, built on a plain on the banks of the Liri. It is 115 km from the centre of Rome and 138 km from the centre of Naples, and its municipality borders Abruzzo. Above the town, on a precipitous rock 540 metres high that guards the valley of the Liri and the entrance to the Abruzzi, stand remains of polygonal walls, where possibly the citadel of the original Volscian town lay, together with remains of medieval fortifications.

The Romans captured Sora in 345, 314 and 305 BCE before they confirmed its annexation by a colony 4,000 strong in 303 BCE. In 209 BCE it was one of the colonies that refused further contributions to the war against Hannibal. By the lex Julia it became a municipium, and under Augustus it was colonised by soldiers of the legio IV Sorana, which had mainly been enrolled there.

In the early Middle Ages Sora lay in the Ducatus Romanus under the authority of the pope, and the Lombards of Gisulf I of Benevento captured it in 705. The castle of Sorella on the rocky height above the town was a stronghold of some note. In 1229, during the War of the Keys, Sora submitted to the Papacy and was then sacked by Emperor Frederick II, who had its inhabitants hanged.

In 1443 King Alfonso of Naples made Sora the seat of an independent duchy. Pope Pius II seized it, but Pope Sixtus IV restored it to the Cantelmi, and it ultimately passed to the duke Giovanni della Rovere. Francesco Maria I della Rovere defended the city against Cesare Borgia. Pope Gregory XIII bought it for 11,000 ducats and placed it under his son Giacomo Boncompagni, the first duke of Sora of that family.

Sora is a town and comune of Lazio and the seat of some important manufacturing, especially paper mills. The original cathedral, consecrated by Pope Adrian IV in 1155, was destroyed by the earthquake of 1634. Among the town's churches are the Sanctuary of the Madonna della Figura and San Silvestro Papa. Caesar Baronius, the cardinal and ecclesiastical historian, was born there, as was the film director Vittorio De Sica.
sorbs: The name Sorbs, in Upper Sorbian Serbja and in Lower Sorbian Serby, derives from medieval groups called Surbi or Sorabi, and the Sorbs are also known as Lusatian Serbs. By the 6th century Slavs occupied the area west of the Oder formerly inhabited by Germanic peoples. The Sorbs are first mentioned in the 6th or 7th century. According to the 7th-century Chronicle of Fredegar, the Surbi lived in the Saale-Elbe valley and were vassals of the Merovingian dynasty. In the Early Middle Ages they formed their own principality, which for a short time became part of Samo's Empire and of Great Moravia, and was ultimately conquered by East Francia and the Holy Roman Empire.

In 1002 Bolesław I of Poland took over Lusatia, and the Peace of Bautzen confirmed it as part of Poland, but it returned to German rule in 1031. In the 1070s southern Lusatia passed to the Czechs within the Duchy of Bohemia. From 1376 to 1469 and from 1490 to 1635 Lusatia belonged to the Lands of the Bohemian Crown, and under Bohemian rule the Sorbs were allowed to return to cities, offices and crafts and to use their language in public. From the beginning of the 16th century the rest of the Sorbian-inhabited area underwent Germanization.

The Congress of Vienna in 1815 divided Lusatia between Prussia and Saxony.
