It has more than one hundred institutions of higher education and is the home of Gadjah Mada University, the first state university established in Indonesia.
spoleto: Spoleto lies in east-central Umbria, in the province of Perugia, on a foothill of the Apennines. It is 63 kilometres south-east of Perugia and 126 kilometres north of Rome. The town rises in tiers up a hill resting against Monte Luco, which reaches 453 metres at the fortress. In antiquity the territory was fertile, and its wine was particularly esteemed. Monte Luco, covered with holm oaks, was a sacred wood in the Roman period, and from the 5th century hermits fleeing Syria settled there, founding a network of hermitages.

Spoleto was founded by the Umbri in the 10th century BCE and taken by the Etruscans in the 7th century BCE. A Roman colony was founded at Spoletium in 241 BCE, shortly after the First Punic War, and the city was expanded and fortified with polygonal walls. In the 5th century it suffered barbarian invasions connected with Theodoric, Belisarius, Totila and Narses. Faroald I made it the seat of the Duchy of Spoleto, a key Lombard duchy, which included Umbria, Sabina, Picenum as far as Pescara and the lands of the Marrucini, Marsi and Peligni.

In 1155 Frederick Barbarossa ordered Spoleto destroyed, after the duchy refused tribute and the inhabitants acted against his envoy Guido Guerra; the city was captured, burned and destroyed. With the death of Henry VI the line of dukes ended, and he ordered in his testament that the duchy be restored to the Holy See. Pope Innocent III reclaimed it, expelling Conrad of Swabia. In 1319 the Ghibellines of Spoleto, led by Federico of Montefeltro, expelled the Guelphs. Plague struck in 1414 and 1436, and in 1418 Martin V appointed Guido Antonio, count of Urbino, as duke. Later popes, among them Gregory XIII, who in 1577 had the iron mines exploited, kept the territory under papal rule.

The Cathedral of Spoleto, dating to the first half of the 11th century on the site of an earlier church, was destroyed in 1155 and consecrated again in 1198 by Innocent III. The Basilica of San Salvatore, built between the late 4th and early 5th centuries, stands outside the medieval walls. The Rocca albornoziana, begun in 1359 for Pope Innocent VI and named after Cardinal Albornoz, crowns the hill of Sant'Elia. The Ponte delle Torri, a limestone bridge about 230 metres long and 80 metres high, links that hill with Monteluco and was given its present appearance in the mid-14th century.
sputnik-1: On 17 December 1954 the Soviet rocket scientist Sergei Korolev proposed a plan for an artificial satellite to the Minister of the Defense Industry, Dimitri Ustinov. In July 1955 the United States announced that it would launch a satellite during the International Geophysical Year, and four days later the Soviet physicist Leonid Sedov said the Soviet Union would do the same. The Politburo approved the proposal on 8 August 1955. The launch vehicle was the R-7, designed as an intercontinental ballistic missile. A much heavier satellite, Object D, was planned first, but the lighter Object PS, which became Sputnik 1, was launched ahead of it.

Sputnik 1 was a polished sphere 58 centimetres across, assembled from two hemispheres sealed with O-rings and joined by 36 bolts, with a mass of 83.6 kilograms. Its chief constructor at OKB-1 was Mikhail Khomyakov. Four whip antennas gave it an almost spherical radiation pattern. It could not be controlled, only observed. A spherical body let scientists work out the density of the upper atmosphere from the satellite's lifetime in orbit, and its radio signals were meant to give data on how radio waves travel through the atmosphere.

It was launched from Tyuratam in the Kazakh SSR on 4 October 1957 at 19:28:34 UTC, which was 5 October at the launch site. Several engines did not fire on time, which nearly aborted the mission, and the satellite entered an orbit with an apogee about 500 kilometres lower than intended. It circled the Earth every 96.20 minutes at a peak speed of about 8 kilometres a second. It transmitted on 20.005 and 40.002 MHz for 22 days until the batteries ran out on 26 October. On 4 January 1958 it burned up on re-entering the atmosphere, after 1,440 orbits.

Radio operators around the world picked up the beeping signal, and the first recording in the United States was made by RCA engineers on Long Island. Groups of observers at 150 stations in Operation Moonwatch looked for the satellite in the sky. What most people actually saw was the much more visible core stage of the rocket. The Soviets did not at once use the launch for propaganda, but later stressed the achievement as a sign of their superiority.

President Dwight Eisenhower was not surprised, having been forewarned of the R-7's capabilities, but he underestimated the reaction of the American public, who were shocked by the launch and by the televised failure of the Vanguard rocket. The anxiety was sometimes called the Sputnik craze, and the launch began the Space Race. Two physicists at Johns Hopkins University, William Guier and George Weiffenbach, used the Doppler effect in Sputnik's signal to fix its position, which led to the TRANSIT navigation system, a forerunner of the Global Positioning System.
srebrenica: Srebrenica is a small mountain town and municipality in eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Republika Srpska entity. Its name means place or land of silver, the same sense as its old Latin name Argentaria. Illyrians mined silver nearby, and silver was a main reason for the Roman invasion of the area. A Roman settlement called Domavia stood near a mine, and ore was carried along the Via Argentaria to the mints at Salona and Sirmium. Mineral springs, notably the Crni Guber, later supported a spa, which drew tourists in the Yugoslav period and brought the town an annual income of about three million dollars.

In the 13th and 14th centuries the region belonged to the Banate of Bosnia and then the Bosnian Kingdom. The name first appears in 1376, when Srebrenica was already an important trading centre. Merchants of the Republic of Ragusa controlled the silver trade and its export through Dubrovnik, and many German miners settled there in the 14th century. Armed conflicts over the mines were frequent: according to the historian Konstantin Josef Jireček, between 1411 and 1463 the town changed hands several times among Hungary, Serbia, Bosnia and the Ottomans.

Under Ottoman rule its economic importance declined, and a Franciscan church was converted into the White Mosque. Austria-Hungary occupied the town in 1878, after the Congress of Berlin, and introduced modern administration, schools and a postal service.

During the Bosnian War, Serb forces occupied the town in April 1992, and Bosniak resistance groups retook it. Refugees from the Drina valley gathered there, and it was besieged. On 16 April 1993 the United Nations declared the enclave a safe area, guarded by a small Dutch unit with no permission to use force. In July 1995 the Army of Republika Srpska under General Ratko Mladić captured it.

Men of fighting age and teenage boys who fell into Bosnian Serb hands were killed in a systematically organised series of summary executions, 8,372 men and boys in all, while women, boys under 12 and men over 65 were taken by bus to Tuzla.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia ruled in 2001 that this was genocide, confirmed on appeal in 2004, and the International Court of Justice upheld the finding in 2007.

Under the 1995 Dayton Agreement Srebrenica was placed in the Republika Srpska. Its population is roughly half Muslim and half Orthodox, and most of the 23 mosques destroyed in the war have been rebuilt. The White Mosque dates to the 17th century, and the Sase Monastery is a Serbian Orthodox monastery dating back to the 13th century. The Church of the Intercession of the Holy Virgin dates to 1903.
sri-jayawardenepura-kotte: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte lies next to the urban area of Colombo, which is Sri Lanka's de facto economic capital. The municipal area is bounded on the west by Colombo, on the south-west by Dehiwala-Mount Lavinia and on the south-east by Maharagama. The older village of Darugama lay at the confluence of two streams, the Diyawanna Oya and the Kolonnawa Oya. It was a naturally secure place that enemies could not easily enter, and in the 13th century a local chieftain, Nissanka Alagakkonara, built a kotte, or fortress, there.

Kotte was a jala durgha, a water fortress, in the shape of a triangle, with the marshes of the Diyawanna Oya and Kolonnawa Oya forming two long sides and a large inner moat dug along the shorter land side. It covered nearly 2.5 square kilometres and was fortified with ramparts of laterite 2.5 metres high and 10.7 metres broad. Alagakkonara held the army of Arya Chakravarthy in front of Kotte, while he defeated the enemy's invasion fleet at Panadura. In 1391, after Prince Sapumal conquered the Kingdom of Jaffna, Kotte was given the epithet Sri Jayawardenepura, meaning resplendent city of growing victory. It remained the capital of the ancient Kingdom of Kotte until the end of the 16th century.

The city had a king's palace with walls of quartz and a golden spire, a three-storeyed temple housing the Buddha's tooth relic, a five-storeyed arama where sixty monks lived under a high priest, and a royal cemetery at Beddagana. The Portuguese arrived on the island in 1505 and were initially welcomed by the king, but they had militaristic and monopolistic intentions and gained control of the city by 1565. Unable to withstand repeated assaults by the neighbouring Kingdom of Sitawaka, they abandoned it and made Colombo their capital. Urbanisation restarted in the 19th century, and the archaeological remains were torn up for building materials, some of them ending up in the Victoria Bridge across the Kelani River.

Sri Lanka designated Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte as its new capital in 1977 to relieve congestion in Colombo. The official move was marked on 29 April 1982 by the inauguration of the new Parliament building, which stands on reclaimed land on an island of 50,000 square metres in a lake formed by dredging the marshlands around the Diyawanna Oya. President J. R. Jayewardene declared it open. The Kotte Urban Council became the Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte Municipal Council in 1997. Traces of the old moat and rampart are still visible in places, and the city is the seat of the Education Ministry and the University of Sri Jayewardenepura at Nugegoda.
sri-lanka: Sri Lanka lies in the Indian Ocean between latitudes 5° and 10° N, separated from the Indian subcontinent by the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait. According to Hindu mythology a land bridge once joined the island to India. It now amounts to a chain of limestone shoals, and legends claim it was passable on foot until 1480 CE, when cyclones deepened the channel. The island consists mostly of flat to rolling coastal plains, with mountains rising only in the south-central part. The highest point is Pidurutalagala at 2,524 metres, and the longest river is the Mahaweli, at 335 kilometres. The coastline is 1,585 kilometres long.

Prehistory on the island goes back 125,000 years and possibly 500,000. In caves such as Pahiyangala, Batadombalena and Belilena archaeologists found the remains of anatomically modern humans, named Balangoda Man. The earliest inhabitants were likely ancestors of the Vedda people. During the protohistoric period, 1000 to 500 BCE, the island was culturally united with southern India and shared its megalithic burials, pottery, iron technology and farming techniques.

According to the Mahāvaṃsa, a Pāḷi chronicle written in the 5th century CE, the original inhabitants were the Yakshas and Nagas, and Sinhalese history traditionally begins in 543 BCE with the arrival of the semi-historical Prince Vijaya, who sailed with 700 followers after being expelled from Vanga, present-day Bengal. Vijaya is the first of about 189 monarchs described in chronicles such as the Dīpavaṃsa, Mahāvaṃsa and Cūḷavaṃsa.

The earliest known Buddhist writings on the island, the Pali Canon, date back to 29 BCE. The island was known to explorers as early as the Anuradhapura period. The Portuguese reached it in 1505 and established a colony in the sixteenth century, the Dutch later controlled the coastal areas, and the British established a colony by the early 19th century. Independence came in 1948 as the Dominion of Ceylon, and the country became a republic in 1972. A civil war between Tamil separatists and the armed forces lasted from 1983 to 2009.

Colombo is the executive and judicial capital and the largest city, and Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the legislative capital. The island has been called by many names: Taprobanā by Greek geographers, Sarandīb by Arabs and Persians, and Ceilão by the Portuguese, which became Ceylon in English. Sinhala and Tamil are the official languages. The Sinhalese form about 74% of the population and Sri Lankan Tamils about 12%, with Moors, Indian Tamils, Burghers, Malays and Veddas among smaller communities. Buddhism is the largest religion, and Sinhalese culture, centred in Kandy and Anuradhapura, and Tamil culture, centred in Jaffna, are the two main traditions.
srinagar: Srinagar lies in the Kashmir Valley along the banks of the Jhelum River and on the shores of Dal Lake and the Anchar Lake, between the Hari Parbat and Shankaracharya hills. Nine old bridges connect the two parts of the city. The earliest record of the name is in Kalhana's Sanskrit chronicle Rajatarangini, as Śrīnagarī, meaning city of Lakshmi. The name first belonged to an older capital nearby; between the 14th and 19th centuries the city was also called simply Kashmir or Shahr-i-Kashmir.

According to the Rajatarangini, an older capital called Srinagari was built in the valley by an Ashoka whom historians identify with the Mauryan emperor, at what is now Pandrethan. A new capital was built by King Pravarasena of the Gonanda dynasty in the 6th century CE at the base of the Hari Parbat, where modern Srinagar stands. In the 14th century Rinchana, a Buddhist convert to Islam, built the first mosque in Kashmir, and the Sultans after him set their capitals in what is now the old city. Sultan Sikandar built the Khanqah-e-Moula in 1397 and the Jamia Mosque in 1402.

The Mughals annexed Kashmir in 1586. Jahangir, fond of the valley, brought prosperity to the city; the Shalimar and Nishat gardens were built around the Dal Lake in his reign and that of Shah Jahan. The Afghan Durrani Empire took Kashmir in 1753 and the Sikh Empire in 1819. After the 1846 Treaty of Amritsar Srinagar became the capital of the Dogra princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, and in 1872 the Darbar Move shifted the capital to Jammu for six months in winter. Srinagar became the summer capital of the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir in 1952.

Srinagar is the largest city and summer capital of the Indian-administered union territory of Jammu and Kashmir. It is known for gardens, houseboats on Dal Lake and traditional Kashmiri crafts such as the Kashmir shawl, papier-mâché, wood carving and carpet weaving. Its religious buildings include the Khanqah-e-Moula, the Jamia Mosque, the Hazratbal Shrine and the Shankaracharya temple. The University of Kashmir dates from 1948.
srivijaya: The earliest reference to Srivijaya dates from the 7th century. The Tang dynasty Chinese monk Yijing wrote that he visited it for six months in 671. The earliest known inscription naming it is the Kedukan Bukit inscription, found near Palembang and dated 605 Saka, which corresponds to 682 or 683. It tells of Dapunta Hyang Sri Jayanasa, who set out on a sacred siddhayatra journey with 20,000 troops from Minanga Tamwan to Jambi and Palembang and founded a kadatuan, a kingdom or polity.

The name itself is Sanskrit, meaning something like glorious or shining victory. Early 20th-century scholars thought it was a king's name, until the French historian George Cœdès postulated the empire's existence in 1918. Its history had been forgotten, and Indonesians, even around Palembang, had not heard of it until the 1920s, when Cœdès published his findings in Dutch and Malay newspapers.

The kingdom first had to consolidate its position in south-eastern Sumatra, which consisted of several quasi-independent polities ruled by local chieftains, and many of its forces were sea peoples, the orang laut. During the 7th century Langkasuka on the Malay Peninsula became part of it, and Pan Pan and Tambralinga came under its influence. In the second half of the 8th century its mandala seems to have been ruled by the Sailendra dynasty of Central Java, although it is not known whether the capital moved to Java or Srivijaya became subordinate to it. Between the late 7th and early 11th century it was a hegemon in Southeast Asia and a centre for the expansion of Buddhism.

Rajendra Chola, the Chola king from Tamil Nadu, launched naval raids on its ports in 1025. His fleet sailed with the monsoon winds and took Srivijaya by surprise, first ransacking Palembang and then moving on to other ports, including Kadaram. An inscription of Rajendra says he captured its king, Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman, and plundered treasures such as the jewelled war gate. The kingdom may have disintegrated after 1025, though Chinese sources continued to refer to a polity called Sanfoqi for some centuries, which some historians identify with Jambi after that date.

In its formation the empire had three zones: the capital region around Palembang, the Musi River basin as a source of valuable goods, and rival river-mouth areas, such as the Batang Hari in Jambi, held under its power by raids and conquests. Its main foreign aim was a lucrative trade agreement with China, kept through tribute missions from the Tang to the Song dynasty, and it controlled the Sunda and Malacca straits between India and China. Historians debate whether it was chiefly a sea power or a land-based polity.
st-andrews: St Andrews lies on the east coast of Fife, 16 kilometres south-east of Dundee and 50 kilometres north-east of Edinburgh. It is named after Saint Andrew the Apostle, and the settlement grew to the west of the cathedral, between the Scores to the north and the Kinness Burn to the south. Its earliest recorded name occurs in 747, when an Irish annal noted the death of Tuathalán, abbot of Kinrymonth. The name combines the Old Gaelic cenn, head or peninsula, with Rigmonad, containing the words for king and moor, later rendered in Lowland Scots as King's Muir.

The first settlers on the estuaries of the Tay and the Eden arrived in the Mesolithic, and farmers settled around the modern town about 4,500 BCE. In the Iron Age a fortified enclosure, possibly a hillfort, stood on East Balrymonth hill a mile to the south, and it is the oldest surviving structure in the area. The burgh became the ecclesiastical capital of Scotland, and held that position until the Scottish Reformation. Its cathedral, the largest in Scotland, is now a ruin. The Martyrs Memorial, at the west end of the Scores, honours Patrick Hamilton, George Wishart and other martyrs of the Reformation.

The town was once bounded by gates called ports, of which West Port, rebuilt between 1843 and 1845, and the Sea Yett survive. The Lade Braes Walk follows a medieval mill lade that may have been built before 1144. Fishing declined before the First World War, and the St Andrews Railway link to Leuchars ended in 1969.

St Andrews had a population of 16,460 in 2022, and its economy rests heavily on tourism and education. It is home to the University of St Andrews, the oldest university in Scotland, and is known worldwide as the home of golf. The earliest surviving document, from 1552, records permission from Archbishop Hamilton to play golf on the links beside the water of Eden.

The Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews was founded in 1754 and until 2004 held legislative authority over the game outside the United States and Mexico. The town bought the Old Course in 1894, and it is the most frequent venue of the Open Championship, staged from 1873. The film Chariots of Fire used West Sands beach for its opening scene.
st-bartholomews-day-massacre: The Peace of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 8 August 1570 ended three years of civil war between Catholics and Protestants, but intransigent Catholics refused to accept it. The queen mother Catherine de' Medici and her son King Charles IX supported peace and the Huguenot leader Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, who had returned to the king's council in September 1571, because of the kingdom's financial difficulties and the Huguenots' strong defensive position. To cement the peace, Catherine arranged the marriage of her daughter Margaret to the Protestant Henry of Navarre on 18 August 1572. The Pope and Philip II of Spain condemned her policy, and many well-born Protestants gathered in Paris, a violently anti-Huguenot city already strained by poor harvests, higher taxes and rising food prices.

On 22 August Coligny was shot from an upstairs window as he returned from the Louvre, and seriously wounded. The Guise family, the Duke of Alba and Catherine have each been suspected. The king and court visited him, but fears of Huguenot reprisals grew. On the evening of 23 August Catherine met her advisers and then the king, and Charles IX and his mother apparently decided to eliminate the Protestant leaders. The killing began that night, on the eve of the Feast of Saint Bartholomew. Coligny was killed, and the slaughter spread through Paris as mob violence.

Charles sent orders on 24 August to his provincial governors to prevent violence, but from August to October similar massacres took place in twelve other cities, among them Toulouse, Bordeaux, Lyon, Rouen and Orléans. Mack P. Holt notes that all were cities with Catholic majorities and former Protestant minorities. It seems unlikely that orders came from the king. Estimates of the dead vary widely: modern figures for all France run from 5,000 to 30,000.

The massacre was a turning point in the French Wars of Religion. The Huguenot political movement was crippled by the loss of many aristocratic leaders, many rank-and-file members converted, and those who remained became increasingly radicalised. A historian has called it the worst of the century's religious massacres, and it printed on Protestant minds throughout Europe the conviction that Catholicism was a bloody and treacherous religion.
st-georges-grenada: St. George's is the capital and largest city of Grenada and its main port. It stands on the south-west coast of the island, on a horseshoe-shaped harbour, and is surrounded by a hillside that is the rim of an old volcano crater. The climate is humid and tropical, with a wet season from June to December and a dry season from January to May, which favours the spice crops on which the island's economy rests. Nutmeg is the key crop, followed by cocoa, mace, cloves, vanilla, cinnamon and ginger.

The French colonised the island, then called La Grenade, under Jacques Dyel du Parquet, governor of Martinique, and began with skirmishes that virtually exterminated its native Carib population. In 1666 French colonists built a wooden fortification, Fort Royale, on a promontory overlooking the natural harbour. Work began in 1705 on a star fort on the same site, with four stone bastions, to the design of Jean de Giou de Caylus, chief engineer of the French West Indies, and was completed in 1710. The first settlement, at the eastern edge of the harbour, was named Saint Louis after King Louis IX but suffered from flooding and malaria, so a new town, the Ville de Fort Royal, was built.

When the island passed to Britain the town was renamed Saint George's Town after the patron saint of England, and Fort Royal became Fort George. After the mid-1880s St. George's was the capital of the British Windward Islands. Grenada became independent in 1974, and after a leftist coup in 1983 the island was invaded by US troops. In 2004 Hurricane Ivan damaged some 90 per cent of the island's homes.

Fort George still stands on the promontory west of the harbour, and its buildings are used by the police. The Grenada National Museum occupies French barracks dating from 1704, which later served as a prison and as the island's first hotel; it displays Carib and Arawak artefacts and Josephine Bonaparte's marble bath. The tower of St. George's Cathedral was built in 1818 and St. George's Anglican Church in 1825. York House houses the House of Representatives, the Senate and the Supreme Court.
st-johns-antigua-and-barbuda: St. John's lies in the western part of Antigua, around St. John's Harbour, on a gentle slope east of the harbour. It is the main city of the Central Plain region. Before the town was founded, a small group of houses lined the harbour, then known as the Cove. The flat land around it allowed a large network of roads to converge on the city, and its low coastline is prone to flooding.

St. John's was laid out after the French invasion of 1666, because of the strategic position of the harbour, and an act to build a town there was passed in April 1668. On 16 September 1675 the island's legislature, sitting at Old Road, established six places of trade, one of them St. John's, where the island had traditionally had two. By 1689 the town was as large as Falmouth, which it later replaced as the island's dominant city.

The town was largely spared armed conflict. In 1736 a plan by a St. John's resident, Prince Klaas, to turn Antigua into an independent African kingdom was discovered; he was killed and 132 other conspirators were punished. The scare led to the building of barracks on Rat Island in 1741 and in the centre of the town in 1753. A major fire struck in 1768, a hurricane in 1772 damaged its shipping, and another fire in 1782 broke out in one of the most densely populated districts. In 1784 a night watch was established, and building rules required most public buildings to have brick walls and tiled or slate roofs.

St. John's was the seat of government of the British Leeward Islands until the colony was abolished in 1959. The present Government House was built in the early 1800s. In the late 1800s and early 1900s the city had an elected council, which no longer exists.

St. John's is the largest city of Antigua and Barbuda, with a population of 22,219, and houses the Parliament and the other branches of government. Landmarks include the white baroque towers of St. John's Cathedral, Fort James at the harbour entrance, the Museum of Antigua and Barbuda and the Antigua Recreation Ground, the national stadium. Cruise ships dock at Heritage Quay and Redcliffe Quay.
st-johns-newfoundland-and-labrador: St. John's lies on the eastern tip of the Avalon Peninsula, on the island of Newfoundland, and is the easternmost city in North America apart from Greenland. The city covers 446.04 square kilometres, more than Montreal, though most of that area is still undeveloped woodland. Its downtown stands to the west and north of St. John's Harbour and the rest of the city spreads out from it. The climate is humid continental, but with smaller seasonal variation than is usual at its latitude, because of the moderating influence of the Gulf Stream.

Fishermen set up seasonal camps at St. John's in the early 1500s. A series of Portuguese expeditions from the Azores took place in the early 16th century, and by 1540 French, Spanish and Portuguese ships crossed the Atlantic every year to fish the waters off the Avalon Peninsula. A Portuguese map of 1519 marks the place as São João.

The origin of the name is disputed. Sebastian Cabot wrote on his map of 1545 that he and his father, John Cabot, sailed into the harbour on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, 24 June, which he dated to 1494 and British and French historians date to 1497; the locations of Cabot's landfalls are themselves disputed. In the Basque Country a common belief holds that Basque fishermen named it after a similar bay at home.

On 24 April 1800 nineteen Irish soldiers of the British garrison mutinied in what is called the United Irish Uprising. They were suspected of belonging to the Society of United Irishmen. The mutiny failed, and the men fled into the countryside and were caught within weeks. Of the seventeen captured, eight were executed, four were released and five were sentenced to transportation. The Great Fire of 1892 destroyed most of the downtown core, and most of the surviving wood-frame buildings date from the rebuilding after it. The city was incorporated in 1888, and from 1898 until 1988 it was the eastern terminus of the Newfoundland Railway.

St. John's is the capital and largest city of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. It is the eastern end of the Trans-Canada Highway. Its economy has long rested on the sea, first the cod fishery, which collapsed in the 1990s, and then offshore oil and gas. Guglielmo Marconi received the first transatlantic wireless signal at St. John's. Memorial University of Newfoundland and the Rooms, which houses the provincial museum, art gallery and archives, are among its institutions.
st-peters-basilica: Old St. Peter's Basilica was the fourth-century church begun by the Emperor Constantine the Great between 319 and 333. It had a wide nave, two aisles on each side and an apsidal end, and it was over 103 metres long, with a large colonnaded atrium. It was built over a small shrine believed to mark the burial place of Saint Peter, and it held most of the popes from Peter to the 15th century. By the end of the 15th century, after neglect during the Avignon Papacy, it had fallen into disrepair.

Pope Nicholas V, who reigned from 1447 to 1455, was the first to consider rebuilding, but little was achieved before his death. Pope Julius II then held a competition, and the design of Donato Bramante was chosen: a Greek cross crowned by a dome inspired by the Pantheon. Construction began on 18 April 1506. One method of financing it was granting indulgences in return for contributions, promoted by Albrecht, Archbishop of Mainz and Magdeburg, who appointed the Dominican preacher Johann Tetzel; his salesmanship provoked a scandal and led to the Protestant Reformation.

Michelangelo took over a building site where four enormous piers were rising behind the remaining nave of the old basilica. The dome rises to a total height of 136.57 metres from the floor to the top of the external cross, with an internal diameter of 41.47 metres. On 18 February 1606, under Pope Paul V, the dismantling of the remaining parts of the Constantinian basilica began. Carlo Maderno added the nave and façade, as the Counter-Reformation increasingly saw the Latin cross as the true symbol of Christianity. The basilica was completed on 18 November 1626.

Gian Lorenzo Bernini received the patronage of Pope Urban VIII in 1626 and worked on the basilica for 50 years; his works include the baldachin and the chair of Saint Peter, and he designed St. Peter's Square, built between 1656 and 1667. Catholic tradition holds that the tomb of Saint Peter lies directly below the high altar. The dome greatly influenced church architecture in Western Christendom, from Sant'Andrea della Valle in Rome to Christopher Wren's dome at St Paul's Cathedral in London.
st-vitus-cathedral: The present cathedral is the third church on its site in Prague Castle, all dedicated to Saint Vitus. The first was an early Romanesque rotunda founded by Wenceslaus I, Duke of Bohemia, in 930, after he obtained a relic of the saint's arm from Emperor Henry I. In 1060 Prince Spytihněv II began a larger Romanesque basilica, which incorporated the rotunda's apse housing the tomb of Saint Wenceslaus. The present Gothic building was begun on 21 November 1344, when Prague was raised to an archbishopric and King John of Bohemia laid the foundation stone. Charles IV intended it as a coronation church, a family crypt and a treasury of relics.

The first master builder was Matthias of Arras, a Frenchman summoned from Avignon, who planned a French Gothic basilica but lived to build only the easternmost parts of the choir. After his death in 1352 the 23-year-old Peter Parler took over and developed his own style, with net vaults, varied window tracery and sculpted busts of the royal family, saints and the two master builders. At Parler's death only the choir and parts of the transept were finished. His sons continued, completing the south tower and the Golden Gate, through which kings entered for coronations.

The cathedral is 124 metres long and 60 metres wide, and its main tower is 102.8 metres high. The Chapel of Saint Wenceslaus, built by Peter Parler between 1356 and 1364, has walls decorated with over 1,300 semi-precious stones, and a small door with seven locks leads to the chamber holding the Bohemian crown jewels. Since 1997 the cathedral has been dedicated to Saints Vitus, Wenceslaus and Adalbert.

The Hussite War halted construction, and Hussite iconoclasm damaged the furnishings. A fire in 1541 caused heavy damage. For centuries the cathedral stood half-finished, and a baroque spire was added to the south tower between 1753 and 1775. A society formed in 1844 to complete it, and work began on a new nave in 1870 under Josef Mocker, who designed the west facade, with Kamil Hilbert completing it. Alfons Mucha designed windows in the nave, and by the jubilee of Saint Wenceslaus in 1929 the cathedral was finished, nearly 600 years after it was begun.
staffordshire: Staffordshire is a ceremonial county in the West Midlands of England, bordering Cheshire, Derbyshire, Leicestershire, Warwickshire, Worcestershire, Shropshire and the West Midlands county. It covers 1,713 square kilometres, with Stoke-on-Trent in the north as its largest settlement and Stafford in the centre. The north is hilly, with the southern end of the Pennines and part of the Peak District National Park, and Cannock Chase lies in the south. The River Trent and its tributaries drain most of the county. The village of Flash, at 463 metres, is the highest in Britain.

The county contains Iron Age tumuli and Roman camps. The Angles settled it in the sixth century, and the oldest example of the Stafford knot, the county's symbol, appears on an Anglian cross in the churchyard of Stoke Minster. The county was formed in the early tenth century, when Stafford became the capital of Mercia. In July 2009 the largest hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold ever found in Britain was discovered in a field near Lichfield. The Staffordshire Hoard has been tentatively dated to the 7th or 8th centuries, in the time of the Kingdom of Mercia.

In 1553 Queen Mary made Lichfield a county corporate, which kept it administered separately until 1888. The county industrialised rapidly in the Industrial Revolution, when the North Staffordshire coalfield was exploited and fuelled iron and motor industries in the south. Pottery became its most best-known product, and in 1910 the six towns of the Staffordshire Potteries became the single county borough of Stoke-on-Trent. Hugh Bourne, a native of Stoke-on-Trent, founded Primitive Methodism at a gathering at Mow Cop, and by 1811 he and his brother had founded the first chapel in the Tunstall area.

The historic county included much of the present West Midlands, including Walsall, West Bromwich and Wolverhampton. On 1 April 1974 under the Local Government Act 1972 the Black Country county boroughs and the Aldridge-Brownhills urban district became part of the new metropolitan county of West Midlands. On 1 April 1997 Stoke-on-Trent became a unitary authority independent of Staffordshire.

The county's only cathedral is Lichfield Cathedral, in the city of Lichfield. Burton upon Trent is known for brewing, and Stoke-on-Trent still produces a limited amount of pottery, including the work of Wedgwood and Royal Doulton. Keele University and the University of Staffordshire are in the county. The Trent and Mersey Canal and the other canals of the county form an extensive network, and the West Coast Main Line passes through Stafford.
stamford-connecticut: Stamford lies in Fairfield County, about 55 km from New York City and roughly halfway between Manhattan and New Haven. It covers about 135 square kilometres, of which about 97 are land, which makes it the largest city in Connecticut by area. Its climate is temperate, with long hot summers and cool to cold winters, and it lies in the transition zone between the colder continental climates to the north and the warmer climates to the south.

The Siwanoy people who lived in the region called the place Rippowam, and the first European settlers used the same name. The present name comes from the town of Stamford in Lincolnshire, England. A deed to the land was signed between Captain Turner of the New Haven Colony and Chief Ponus. By the 18th century one of the town's main industries was trade by water, which its closeness to New York made possible. In 1692 Stamford had a witch trial, smaller and less well known than the one at Salem in the same year; the accusations grew through gossip.

Stamford had 135,470 inhabitants at the census of 2020 and is the second most populous city in Connecticut after Bridgeport. It is part of the New York City metropolitan area and has become a cluster of corporate headquarters, with the largest financial district in the region outside New York City. It is governed by a strong mayor and a Board of Representatives of forty members. Its railway station on the New Haven Line of the Metro-North Railroad is the second busiest on that system.

The Stamford Museum and Nature Center holds works by the sculptor Gutzon Borglum, who lived in the town for a decade. The Palace Theatre opened as a vaudeville house in 1927 and reopened as a nonprofit theatre in 1983, and the Fairfield County Astronomical Society, founded in 1954, runs the Stamford Observatory. UConn Stamford has its main building in a former department store in the downtown.
standard-chinese: Chinese has long had considerable dialectal variation, along with prestige dialects and linguae francae. Confucius is thought to have used a dialect known as yayan rather than regional speech, and Han dynasty texts refer to a common language, tongyu. For the educated elite the language was unified in Literary Chinese, a form that was primarily written. During the Ming and Qing dynasties the term Guanhua, official speech, named the lingua franca of the imperial courts. The English word Mandarin comes from the Portuguese mandarim, from the Sanskrit mantrin, minister, and was first used for scholar-officials; the Portuguese then called Guanhua the language of the mandarins.

In the 17th century the state set up orthoepy academies to bring officials' speech to a standard, with little success: as late as the 19th century the emperor had difficulty understanding some of his ministers.

After the Republic of China was established in 1912 a Commission on the Unification of Pronunciation was convened, and a Dictionary of National Pronunciation published in 1919 defined a hybrid pronunciation that matched no existing speech. The commission gradually settled on the prestigious Beijing dialect, and in 1932 its Vocabulary of National Pronunciation for Everyday Use normalised the pronunciation of all characters to it. Standard Chinese is therefore defined by the pronunciation of the Beijing dialect, though it is no longer synonymous with it.

It is an analytic language with almost no inflection, subject-verb-object word order and five phonemic tones, four classic ones and a neutral tone. It is written with characters that mostly represent a morpheme and usually descend from those of Classical Chinese. Words with no classical counterpart were written either with a borrowed character of similar sound, as with zhe, this, or with a newly created compound character.

Standard Chinese is the official lingua franca of the People's Republic of China, one of the six official languages of the United Nations, a national language of Taiwan and one of the four official languages of Singapore, with English, Malay and Tamil. It is called Putonghua, common speech, on the mainland and Guoyu, national language, in Taiwan. The word Guoyu was first used in the late Qing dynasty for Manchu, and its modern sense was borrowed from Japan in the early 20th century. In Taiwan Standard Chinese spread widely after 1949, when the Kuomintang and many refugees arrived from the mainland. In both places it is taught by immersion from elementary school.
stanislaw-leszczynski: Stanisław Leszczyński was born in Lwów (now Lviv) in 1677, the son of Rafał Leszczyński, voivode of Poznań Voivodeship, and Princess Anna Leszczyńska. He married Katarzyna Opalińska, and their daughter Maria became Queen of France as the wife of Louis XV.

In 1697, as Cup-bearer of Poland, he signed the confirmation of the articles of election of Augustus II the Strong. In 1703 he joined the Lithuanian Confederation, which the Sapiehas, with the aid of Sweden, had formed against Augustus.

After a successful Swedish invasion of Poland, Charles XII of Sweden chose Stanisław to replace Augustus II. With a bribing fund and an army corps, the Swedes secured his election on 12 July 1704 by a small assembly of castellans and a few score of noblemen.

He was crowned on 24 September 1705 with a new crown and sceptre supplied by Charles, since Augustus had carried the ancient regalia off to Saxony. His first act was an alliance with Charles against the Russian tsar, and he induced the Cossack hetman Ivan Mazepa to desert Peter the Great. After the Battle of Poltava in 1709 his authority vanished, and he abdicated the crown, though he kept the royal title, in exchange for the principality of Palatine Zweibrücken.

After Charles's death in 1719 he moved to Wissembourg in Alsace, and from 1725 to 1733 he lived at the Château de Chambord. When Augustus II died in 1733, Louis XV supported his claim. Stanisław reached Warsaw on 11 September 1733 disguised as a coachman and was elected the next day, but Russia backed Augustus's son, and the War of the Polish Succession followed. A Russian army besieged him at Danzig. The city capitulated on 30 June 1735 after 135 days, and he escaped in peasant disguise two days earlier.

On 26 January 1736 Stanisław abdicated again. In compensation he was later given the duchies of Lorraine and Bar, which were to revert to France on his death. He held court at the Château de Lunéville, which drew Enlightenment figures such as Madame Émilie du Châtelet. In Nancy in 1750 he founded the Académie de Stanislas and the Bibliothèque municipale, and he argued with Jean-Jacques Rousseau. His Głos wolny wolność ubezpieczający is counted among the important political treatises of the Polish Enlightenment.

He died on 23 February 1766, aged 88, after his silk clothing caught fire from a spark while he slept near the fireplace at Lunéville. His titles passed to Louis XV. Buried first in Nancy, his remains were taken to Poland after the French Revolution and laid in the royal tomb at Wawel Cathedral in Kraków. Nancy's Place Stanislas bears his name.
stans: Stans is one of the oldest settlements in the Nidwalden valley, with the first traces of human settlement dating to the second century BCE. The Roman era left little evidence except some funeral pyres and the Latin root of its name, stagnum, meaning a pool. The Alamanni settled the region in the seventh or eighth century, and the Christian Alamanni built the first church in Stans around 750, which served as parish church for the whole Engelberg Valley until the church of St Peter and Paul replaced it in 1647. The town covers 11.08 square kilometres, its highest point on the Stanserhorn.

Stans was first mentioned in 1124. By 1291, when Unterwalden joined Uri and Schwyz in what became the Swiss Confederation, it was already the capital of Unterwalden below the forest, which became the half canton of Nidwalden. Tradition places a soldier from Stans, Arnold von Winkelried, at the Battle of Sempach in 1386, where he is said to have thrown himself on the Habsburg pikes. It is doubtful that he existed, since the first mention of the act comes over 150 years later, but the legend is firmly kept in Stans, with a monument and a house bearing his name.

After the Burgundian Wars the Confederation was nearly torn apart when the city cantons claimed the larger share of the proceeds. In 1481 the Tagsatzung met in Stans, and the hermit Niklaus von der Flüe sent a message whose contents remain unknown. It calmed tempers and led to the Stanser Verkommnis, under which Fribourg and Solothurn were admitted to the Confederation. In 1713 a fire destroyed two thirds of the town, and the square was rebuilt in 1715 with baroque houses.

In 1798 French troops stormed Stans after Nidwalden refused the constitution of the Helvetic Republic, and Pestalozzi gathered the orphaned children in the Convent of St Klara, until the army needed the building the following year. Stans and Nidwalden joined the Sonderbund in 1845 and took part in the Sonderbund War of 1847. The open-air Landsgemeinde was held there annually until 1997.

Stans is the capital of the canton of Nidwalden, and its official language is German, though the main spoken language is the local Alemannic Swiss German. Its sights include the Dorfplatz with the Winkelried monument of 1865, the Capuchin monastery founded in 1583 by Melchior Lussy, and the Winkelriedhaus, which houses a museum. The Stanserhornbahn, built in 1893, is one of the oldest mountain railways in Switzerland.
state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs: The South Slavic peoples of Austria-Hungary were divided among several administrative units. The Austrian Littoral, the Duchy of Carniola and the Kingdom of Dalmatia lay under Austrian jurisdiction, while the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia and Fiume were under Hungarian jurisdiction, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was a condominium. On 30 May 1917 the Yugoslav Club, a group of Croatian and Slovene deputies in the Reichsrat, adopted the May Declaration, which sought the unification of all lands of the monarchy inhabited by Slovenes, Croats and Serbs in one independent entity.

A meeting in Zagreb on 2 and 3 March 1918 produced the Zagreb Resolution, which proclaimed the unity of the three peoples and demanded self-determination. In the summer, people's organizations were formed in Split, Sušak and Ljubljana. The People's Council was established in Zagreb on 5 to 8 October 1918 with 95 representatives, and on 19 October it declared itself the supreme representative body of all South-Slavic peoples in the monarchy.

The state was proclaimed on 29 October 1918. Its first president was the Slovene Anton Korošec, with the Serb Svetozar Pribićević and the Croat Ante Pavelić as vice presidents. It aspired to include all the Austro-Hungarian territories inhabited by Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, but Serbs in Vojvodina formed their own administration under the Serbian National Board in Novi Sad, and Vojvodina joined the Kingdom of Serbia on 25 November 1918. Syrmia had seceded and joined Serbia a day earlier.

Emperor Karl assigned the Austro-Hungarian Navy and its harbours to the National Council, but the Italian navy attacked and dismembered the fleet. The Armistice of Villa Giusti, signed on 4 November 1918, allowed Italy to occupy large parts of the state's territory, and Italian troops held Istria and much of Dalmatia until the Treaty of Rapallo took effect in 1921. The state was never recognised internationally.

In a note of 31 October the National Council told the governments of the United Kingdom, France, Italy and the United States that it intended to form a common state with Serbia and Montenegro. On 23 and 24 November it declared unification, but its instructions were largely ignored by the delegation, which negotiated with Regent Alexander instead. Stjepan Radić's Peasant Party called the move foolish and argued that the Croatian Parliament had never approved it.

On 1 December 1918 Regent Alexander proclaimed the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, thirty-three days after the state's proclamation. The National Council had ceased to operate and never formally ratified the proclamation.
state-protection-authority: The force began in 1945 as the Budapest Department of State Political Police. In 1946 it became the State Defence Department of the Hungarian State Police, the ÁVO, and in 1950 the State Protection Authority. Gábor Péter headed it from 1945 to 1952. László Rajk, the Communist minister of the interior, played a crucial part in organising it, and in 1949 became one of its victims: he was arrested, tried for nationalism and Titoism and executed. On 1 January 1950 the authority was removed from the Ministry of the Interior, made independent and given the Border Guard.

The authority served the Hungarian Working People's Party directly, with little reference to the norms of government, and its actions were not subject to judicial review until the early years after Stalin. It gathered intelligence through a vast network of informants. Secret arrests were followed by periods of torture lasting from 3 to 18 months, after which the public prosecutors and courts were called in to pass sentence.

Prisons and internment camps were placed under its supervision, the most notorious at Recsk, Kistarcsa, Tiszalök and Kazincbarcika. Before 1953 some camps aimed at the eventual death of their inmates through overwork and maltreatment. The first government of Imre Nagy, from 1953 to 1955, greatly improved conditions in the camps and ended these efforts.

In 1953 the authority prepared a show trial meant to prove that Raoul Wallenberg had not been taken to the Soviet Union in 1945 but had been killed by Zionists in Budapest. Leaders of the Jewish community, among them Miksa Domonkos and Lajos Stöckler, and two intended witnesses were seized and tortured. After the death of Stalin the preparations were stopped and the prisoners released in the autumn of 1953. Domonkos died shortly afterwards, mainly from the torture.

On 29 October 1956, during the revolution, the militia of József Dudás stormed the secret police headquarters and massacred the officers inside, and the crowd lynched others. The students' and workers' councils then set up armed patrols to detain members of the authority for their own safety and for later trial. When Soviet forces intervened, its officers carried out brutal reprisals against revolutionaries.

The government of János Kádár, who had himself been tortured by the authority, did not revive it under its old name. Its work passed to a department of the Ministry of the Interior, known as III, which operated with considerably more restraint. Its former headquarters at 60 Andrássy Avenue in Budapest is now a museum, the House of Terror.
states-of-germany: Federalism has a long tradition in German history. In 1796 the Holy Roman Empire was made up of more than 300 political entities, a number greatly reduced during the Napoleonic Wars, and the Empire was abolished in 1806. The Congress of Vienna created the 39-state German Confederation in 1815. The German Empire of 1871 included 25 states, three of them free cities, plus Alsace-Lorraine, and 65% of its territory and 62% of its population belonged to Prussia. The word Länder dates to the Weimar Constitution of 1919, since the states of the Empire had been called Staaten.

The Federal Republic of Germany consists of sixteen partly sovereign states. Thirteen are area-states, Berlin and Hamburg are city-states, and Bremen, made up of the cities of Bremen and Bremerhaven, is a mixture of the two. Bavaria, Saxony and Thuringia call themselves Freistaat, free state, a title that is merely stylistic. After the war the Allied military governments redrew the internal borders and established new states in all four zones of occupation, none above 30% of population or territory, to prevent any one from dominating as Prussia had. In 1952 Baden, Württemberg-Baden and Württemberg-Hohenzollern merged into Baden-Württemberg, and Saarland joined in 1957.

The individual states formed the Federal Republic in 1949. In East Germany the five states were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 14 administrative districts called Bezirke. They were reconstituted on 3 October 1990 as the five New States, and East and West Berlin joined as one city-state, which gives the present sixteen. In principle the power to make laws lies with the states, and the federation may legislate only where the Basic Law assigns it power, as in foreign and defence policy. The states alone make police law and culture, which includes schools and universities, and they take part in federal legislation through the Bundesrat.
stavanger: Stavanger is a city and municipality on the Stavanger Peninsula in south-west Norway and the administrative centre of Rogaland county. It lies in a coastal landscape bordering the sea to the west and Boknafjorden to the northeast, with the Byfjorden and Gandsfjorden along its east side. It is part of Low-Jæren, a flat area of marsh, sand and stone, and most of the municipality lies between 0 and 50 metres above sea level. Its climate is temperate oceanic and very mild by Nordic standards. The Old Norse form of the name was Stafangr; the most used interpretation is that it first named the inlet now called Vågen, the original site of the city.

The first traces of settlement come from about 10,000 years ago, when the ice retreated after the last ice age. Rich archaeological material suggests that chiefs in North Jæren held considerable power from the early Iron Age, and some historians argue that the area was an economic and military centre in the 9th and 10th centuries. Stavanger emerged in the 12th century, a time of population growth and urbanisation across northern Europe, and grew into a centre of church administration and a market town of the south-west coast. Written and archaeological sources on its first development are sparse. Its official founding year is counted as 1125, when the cathedral was completed.

In the early 20th century its industry was tied to fisheries and shipping. It was known for canning, and in the 1950s more than 50 canneries operated there, so that the town was called Norway's canned capital; the last of the factories closed in 2002. On 8 April 1940, before the German invasion, the captain of the Æger sank the German freighter Roda by his own decision after customs officials grew suspicious of its cargo. In 1969 oil was discovered in the North Sea, and Stavanger was chosen as the on-shore centre for the industry on the Norwegian sector. Statoil, now Equinor, was founded in 1972, and a period of hectic growth followed.

Old Stavanger has a collection of 18th- and 19th-century wooden houses that are protected. Stavanger Cathedral, dedicated to St Swithun, was built between 1100 and 1150 by the English bishop Reinald in Anglo-Norman style, with a Gothic choir added in the late 13th century; it is the only Norwegian cathedral almost unchanged since the 14th century. The city is the seat of the University of Stavanger, established as a university in 2004, and of the Norwegian Petroleum Museum. Stavanger and its region were a European Capital of Culture in 2008, together with Liverpool.
stavropol: Stavropol is the administrative centre of Stavropol Krai, in the North Caucasus region of southern Russia. The name is a Russian rendering of the Greek Stauropolis, City of the Cross. According to legend, soldiers building the fortress found a stone cross on the site. The name is not related to the Byzantine Stauroupolis in Asia Minor, nor to Stavropol-on-Volga, now called Tolyatti. The climate is humid continental, with short, cold winters, hot summers and rather low precipitation.

Stavropol was founded on 22 October 1777, after the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774, as a military encampment, and was granted city status in 1785. Prince Grigory Potemkin, who founded it as one of ten fortresses built between Azov and Mozdok at the request of Catherine the Great, played a leading role. Don Cossacks settled in and around Stavropol to defend the empire's borders, and in 1809 Alexander I invited several Armenian families to settle by the fortress in order to encourage trade.

Its strategic position aided the Russian conquest of the Caucasus, and by the early 19th century it was a busy trade centre. An Episcopal see of the Russian Orthodox Church was established there in 1843, and in 1847 the city became the seat of Stavropol Governorate. During the Russian Civil War it changed hands several times and was captured by the Red Army from General Denikin's Volunteer Army on 29 February 1920. It was renamed Voroshilovsk in 1935, and the original name was restored in 1943. Germans occupied it from August 1942 to January 1943. Natural gas began to be extracted near the city in 1946.

Stavropol is home to North-Caucasus Federal University, Stavropol State Agrarian University and Stavropol State Medical University. Its economy focuses on automobiles, furniture, and construction equipment and materials. Mikhail Gorbachev, born in Stavropol Krai, worked in the city for several years as head of the krai's administration, and the poets Alexander Pushkin and Mikhail Lermontov, then in political disfavour, stayed there.
stefan-dusan: Stefan Dušan was the eldest son of King Stefan Dečanski and Theodora Smilets, daughter of the Bulgarian emperor Smilets. In 1314 his father quarrelled with his own father, King Stefan Milutin, and was exiled; the family lived in Constantinople until his recall in 1320. There Dušan became acquainted with Byzantine culture and learned Greek. After a civil war Dečanski was crowned on 6 January 1322, and Dušan was crowned young king and later given Zeta, which marked him as the intended heir.

In his youth Dušan fought in two battles, defeating Bosnian forces in 1329 during the War of Hum and the Bulgarian emperor Michael III Shishman at Velbužd in 1330. He became king of Serbia on 8 September 1331 after the struggle with his father, and sealed an alliance with Bulgaria by marrying Helen, sister of Ivan Alexander.

On 16 April 1346 Dušan convoked an assembly at Skopje, attended by the Serbian archbishop, the Archbishop of Ochrid, the Bulgarian patriarch and clerics of Mount Athos. It raised the Serbian archbishopric to a patriarchate, and the first patriarch, Joanikije II, crowned Dušan Emperor and autocrat of the Serbs and Romans, a title soon enlarged to include the Greeks, Bulgarians and Albanians. He had his son Uroš crowned king of the Serbs and Greeks. Dušan gave Byzantine court titles to his nobles, such as despotes, sebastocrator and caesar, and was the first Serbian monarch to write most of his letters in Greek.

In 1347 he conquered Epirus, Aetolia and Acarnania, placing his half-brother Simeon Uroš over them, and in 1348 Thessaly, under the governor Preljub. He then sought Constantinople, for which he needed a fleet, and negotiated with Venice, which politely declined a military alliance. In 1349 he introduced Dušan's Code.

In 1354 the Hungarians occupied part of northern Serbia. Dušan repelled the invasion, and peace with Louis I of Hungary followed in May 1355. He had intended to capture Constantinople and lead a crusading army against the Turks, but died suddenly on 20 December 1355 and was buried in his foundation near Prizren. His remains were later moved to the Church of Saint Mark in Belgrade. His empire, spanning a large territory, slowly crumbled under his son Stefan Uroš V as regional aristocrats drew away from central rule.

Stefan Dušan is remembered as the most powerful Serbian ruler of the Middle Ages and remains a folk hero to Serbs. The aim of restoring his empire stayed an ideal for Serbs under Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian rule.
stendal: Stendal lies west of the Elbe valley, about 125 km west of Berlin, 170 km east of Hanover and 55 km north of Magdeburg. It is the capital of the Stendal District and the unofficial capital of the Altmark region. A deed attributed to Emperor Henry II in 1022 that seemed to mention the place is a 12th-century forgery, and the town was in fact founded and granted Magdeburg rights by the first Brandenburg margrave, Albert the Bear, about 1160.

St Mary's Church is first mentioned in 1283, and the town received walls about 1300, joined the Hanseatic League in 1358 and bought the right to mint coins from the Brandenburg margraves in 1369. A Latin school is documented from 1338. In 1502 the Elector Joachim I Nestor married Princess Elizabeth of Denmark at Stendal. The citizens turned Protestant in 1539, and Waldensian, Palatine and Swiss refugees settled in the town in the 1680s and 1690s. After the Napoleonic Wars the Altmark passed to the Prussian Province of Saxony, and Stendal had been a Prussian garrison town since the 17th century.

In World War II the town had a Luftwaffe airfield and was hit by ten air raids, and more than 300 civilians died when the Röxe district was devastated. On 4 May 1945 General Maximilian von Edelsheim signed the capitulation of the German 12th Army at the town hall. The town was in East Germany from 1949 to 1990, and the Soviet barracks remained until 1994. Construction of a nuclear power plant north of the town, begun in 1974, was abandoned after reunification.

Stendal is officially a Hanseatic city, and preserves several well-preserved medieval churches, the Tangemünde Gate, dating from 1220, and the Uenglinger Gate of the 15th century. St Mary's Church, with two towers 84 metres high, was inaugurated in 1447, and a statue of Roland stands by the 14th-century town hall. The art historian Johann Joachim Winckelmann was born here in 1717, and the writer Stendhal, who lived near the town in 1807–08, is generally believed to have taken his pen name in tribute to him.
stephen-bathory: Stephen Báthory was born on 27 September 1533 at Somlyó, in a noble Hungarian family. Around 1549–1550 he visited Italy and probably attended lectures at the University of Padua. He then joined the army of Ferdinand I and fought the Turks, and some time after 1553 he was captured by them. When Ferdinand refused to pay his ransom he joined John II Sigismund Zápolya in the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom as a commander and diplomat. After Zápolya's death in 1571 the Transylvanian estates elected him voivode of Transylvania. By 1573 he had defeated Gáspár Bekes, who was supported by the Habsburgs, in the civil war that followed.

The throne of Poland-Lithuania fell vacant in 1572 with the death of Sigismund II Augustus. After Henry III of France left it, an election in 1575 produced two claimants, and a faction around Chancellor Jan Zamoyski secured the election of Báthory, who married Anna Jagiellon and was crowned on 1 May 1576. He first had to win recognition. Lithuania accepted him after he agreed to its conditions, and Danzig, which had supported the Habsburg candidate, was defeated in the field on 17 April 1577 and then agreed to recognise him and pay compensation of 200,000 zlotys.

With Zamoyski he reorganised the courts through the Crown Tribunal of 1578 and the Lithuanian Tribunal of 1581, and he raised infantry from the peasantry. He founded the Academy of Vilnius from a Jesuit college and protected Polish Jews while promoting Catholicism. Against Ivan the Terrible in the Livonian War he took Polotsk in 1579 and Velikiye Luki in 1580, and in 1581 he besieged Pskov. The Truce of Jam Zapolski of 15 January 1582 gave the Commonwealth Polotsk, Veliz and most of Livonia.

In 1584 Báthory allowed Zamoyski to execute Samuel Zborowski for treason and murder, a conflict between the king and the nobility that remained controversial. He was planning another war against Russia when he died on 12 December 1586. He left no legitimate children. He remained interested in Hungarian affairs, never learned Polish, and sponsored works about his own deeds, so that he became a recurring figure in Polish literature.
stephen-king-of-england: Stephen was born in Blois in France, the fourth son of Stephen-Henry, Count of Blois and Chartres, who was killed at the battle of Ramlah while on crusade when Stephen was at most ten years old. His mother, Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror and Matilda of Flanders, was known for her piety and strong personality and shaped his upbringing. Placed in the court of his uncle Henry I of England, he rose in prominence and was granted extensive lands. By his marriage to Matilda of Boulogne in 1125 he gained estates in Kent and Boulogne.

In 1120 Stephen planned to sail on the White Ship from Barfleur but left it at the last moment. The ship sank with the heir to the throne, William Adelin, and nearly all its passengers, which left the succession open to challenge.

When Henry I died in 1135, Stephen crossed the Channel and took the throne with the help of his brother Henry, Bishop of Winchester, arguing that keeping order took priority over his earlier oaths to support the Empress Matilda. In 1138 Robert, Earl of Gloucester, renounced his fealty and declared for Matilda, while Geoffrey of Anjou invaded Normandy and David I of Scotland invaded northern England. Stephen created many new earldoms for loyal supporters, many of them for his advisor Waleran de Beaumont and his family.

Matilda and Robert landed in England on 30 September 1139 with 140 knights. At the Battle of Lincoln on 2 February 1141 Stephen fought on foot, and after his sword broke he used a borrowed battle axe, but he was overwhelmed and taken prisoner. He was freed only after his wife and William of Ypres captured Robert at the Rout of Winchester. By 1147 England had suffered extensively, and the chronicle of the time recorded nothing but disturbance and wickedness and robbery. The royal coinage fragmented, and unauthorised castles multiplied.

Late in his reign Stephen sought to have his son Eustace crowned, but Pope Eugene III refused. In 1153 Henry, the Empress's son, invaded England. The armies met at Wallingford, but neither side's barons wished to fight another pitched battle, and the sudden death of Eustace hastened peace. By the Treaty of Winchester Stephen recognised Henry as his heir, passing over his second son William. He died on 25 October 1154, and Henry II succeeded him. Modern historians have debated whether his personality, external events or weaknesses in the Norman state caused the long civil war.
steve-biko: Bantu Stephen Biko was born on 18 December 1946 at his grandmother's house in Tarkastad, Cape Province. His family settled in Ginsberg township at King William's Town, where Xhosa, Afrikaans and English were all spoken. His father, a former police officer who worked as a clerk, died in 1950, and the family depended on his mother's wages as a cook. Advised that law was too closely tied to political activism, Biko entered the University of Natal Medical School in 1966 and was soon elected to the Students' Representative Council.

Biko joined the National Union of South African Students but grew frustrated that white liberals dominated it and, in his view, failed to understand the black experience. He became a leading figure in founding the South African Students' Organisation, launched in July 1969, and was elected its first president. Influenced by Frantz Fanon, Malcolm X and the Black Power movement, the organisation adopted Black Consciousness as its ideology.

Biko rejected the government's division of the population into whites and non-whites, which he saw as defining people by an absence. He described blackness as a mental attitude rather than a matter of pigmentation and applied the word to Africans, Coloureds and Indians. He urged black people to free themselves of any sense of inferiority, popularised the slogan "black is beautiful", and hoped for a non-racial South Africa with one person, one vote.

The government came to regard Biko as a subversive threat and banned him in 1973. On 17 August 1977 he broke the order by driving to Cape Town with his friend Peter Jones. On 18 August they were stopped at a police roadblock near Grahamstown and arrested. Biko was beaten to death by state security officers and died on 12 September 1977. More than 20,000 people attended his funeral.

Biko is regarded as the father of Black Consciousness and as the first icon of the anti-apartheid movement. Nelson Mandela called him "the spark that lit a veld fire across South Africa". Peter Gabriel's song "Biko" was a hit in 1980 and was banned in South Africa, and Donald Woods's 1978 biography of him was the basis of the film Cry Freedom. His political legacy remains a matter of contention.
stilicho: Stilicho was the son of a Vandal cavalry officer and a provincial Roman woman. There is little to suggest that he saw himself as anything but a Roman, and he was probably a Nicene Christian like his patron Theodosius I. The main sources are the panegyrics of the poet Claudian, whom he patronised and who portrays him in a positive light, and, for the years after 404, Zosimus, who drew on one historian hostile to Stilicho and one supportive.

He rose through the army under Theodosius, who sent him in 383 to the court of the Persian king Shapur III at Ctesiphon to negotiate over the partition of Armenia. He then married Serena, the niece of Theodosius, and was promoted to senior commands. After the Battle of the Frigidus Theodosius appointed him guardian of his son Honorius, shortly before the emperor's death in 395.

Honorius became emperor in the West and his brother Arcadius in the East. Stilicho became the de facto commander-in-chief of the western armies and tied himself to the throne by giving Honorius his daughter Maria in marriage in 398 and, after her death, Thermantia in 408. In 395 he led the army into the Balkans against the Goths of Alaric but obeyed an order from Arcadius to send back the eastern troops. He defeated Alaric's forces in Macedonia in 397 and put down the revolt of Gildo in Africa.

In 402 he broke Alaric's siege of Mediolanum, where Honorius was living, and defeated him at the Battle of Pollentia on Easter Sunday, the last victory marked by a triumphal march in Rome. In 406 he surprised and captured the force of Radagaisus at Florentia, executed Radagaisus and enrolled 12,000 of his warriors, selling the rest into slavery.

To defend Italy Stilicho had weakened the Rhine frontier, and on 31 December 406 a coalition of Vandals, Alans and Suevi crossed it and devastated Gaul. His reputation never recovered. He failed to put down the rebellion of Constantine III in Britain. After rumours that he intended to place his son on the throne, the army at Ticinum mutinied on 13 August 408 and killed senior officers. Stilicho retired to Ravenna, did not resist arrest and was executed on 22 August 408. His son Eucherius was killed soon after.

In the disturbances the families of barbarian federates in Italy were massacred, and perhaps 30,000 of these soldiers joined Alaric, who stood before Rome by September 408 and sacked it in August 410. Many historians hold that the removal of Stilicho was the main catalyst of that event.
stirling: Stirling lies on the River Forth, 42 km north-east of Glasgow and 60 km north-west of Edinburgh. It stands where the flatter Lowlands meet the slopes of the Highlands along the Highland Boundary Fault, and for this reason it is called the Gateway to the Highlands. To the west and east stretches the Carse of Stirling, one of the flattest and most productive expanses of farmland in Scotland. Control of the lowest crossing point of the Forth brought military advantage in times of unrest and tolls in peacetime. Stirling remained the river's lowest reliable crossing until the Alloa Swing Bridge was built in 1885.

Stirling's oldest catalogued artefact is a stone cist found in 1879, whose bones were radiocarbon dated to between 2152 and 2021 BCE. Prehistoric carvings of cup and ring marks near King's Park date to about 3000 BCE, and Iron Age forts stand on Gillies Hill. David I created Stirling a royal burgh between 1124 and 1127. The name appears as Strivelin in early sources; scholars once thought it Brittonic, but a survey of 2017 derives it from Gaelic srib-linn, a pool in the river. A 9th-century legend says a wolf's howl woke a sentry when Danish invaders attacked, and the wolf became a symbol of the town.

On 29 July 1567 the infant James VI was anointed King of Scots in the Church of the Holy Rude, and he grew up in Stirling, educated by George Buchanan. James III and his queen, Margaret of Denmark, are buried at Cambuskenneth Abbey; the king died at the Battle of Sauchieburn. The Battle of Stirling was fought in the town on 12 September 1648. The earl of Mar failed to take the castle in 1715, and in January 1746 the army of Bonnie Prince Charlie took the town but not the castle, blowing up the church of St Ninians, where it had stored munitions. Only the tower survives.

Stirling is visually dominated by Stirling Castle, once a principal royal stronghold of the Kingdom of Scotland. It was granted city status in 2002 and is the administrative centre of the Stirling council area. The old town below the castle keeps its cobbled streets and buildings such as Mar's Wark and Argyll's Lodging. The University of Stirling opened in 1967. The custom of Walking the Marches, which inspects the town's boundaries each year, is thought to have begun in the 12th century.
stockholm: Stockholm lies on Sweden's east coast at the 59th parallel north, where the freshwater Lake Mälaren flows out into the Baltic Sea. The central parts of the city consist of fourteen islands that continue into the Stockholm archipelago. More than 30% of the city area is waterways and another 30% parks and green spaces. Its position, at the eastern end of the Central Swedish lowland and near the Bergslagen region, reflects the early orientation of Swedish trade toward the Baltic.

The area was settled from the Stone Age, in the 6th millennium BCE. Norse sagas name the location as Agnafit, and Birka, near Stockholm, was one of Sweden's major trade centres in the Viking Age. Numerous runestones were carved in the area because of its importance as a trading hub.

The earliest written mention of the name Stockholm dates from 1252, by which time the mines of Bergslagen had made it an important site in the iron trade. Stock means log in Swedish, though it may also connect to an old German word meaning fortification, and holm means islet, probably the islet of Helgeandsholmen. According to Erik's Chronicle the city was founded by Birger Jarl to protect Sweden from sea invasions by Karelians, after the pillage of Sigtuna on Lake Mälaren in the summer of 1187.

The Old Town, Gamla Stan, was built on the central island next to Helgeandsholmen from the mid-13th century onward. The city rose to prominence through the Baltic trade of the Hanseatic League, developing strong economic and cultural links with Lübeck, Hamburg, Gdańsk, Visby, Tallinn and Riga. Research and higher education in the sciences began in the 18th century. Karolinska Institutet was formalised in 1811 and KTH Royal Institute of Technology was founded in 1827. The city hosted the 1912 Summer Olympics, and the Stockholm Metro opened in 1950.

Stockholm is the capital and most populous city of Sweden. Its municipality had 984,748 inhabitants in 2022, with about 1.6 million in the urban area. It is the seat of the government and the Riksdag, and Stockholm Palace is the official residence of the Swedish monarch. The Vasa Museum is the most visited museum in Scandinavia. The Stockholm region has three World Heritage Sites: Drottningholm Palace, Skogskyrkogården and Birka. The Nobel Prize ceremonies and banquet are held in the city each year.
stoicism: The name derives from the Stoa Poikile, or painted porch, a colonnade decorated with mythic and historical battle scenes on the north side of the Agora in Athens, where Zeno of Citium and his followers gathered near the end of the fourth century BCE. Unlike the Epicureans, Zeno chose to teach in a public space. The philosophy was at first called Zenonism, a name soon dropped, probably because the Stoics did not consider their founders perfectly wise and wished to avoid a cult of personality.

Zeno's ideas developed from those of the Cynics, brought to him by Crates of Thebes, whose founding father, Antisthenes, had been a disciple of Socrates. Zeno also studied under the Megarians. His most influential successor was Chrysippus, who followed Cleanthes as head of the school and moulded what is now called Stoicism. It became the foremost popular philosophy among the educated elite of the Hellenistic world and the Roman Empire.

Stoic philosophy is traditionally divided into logic, physics and ethics. Logic, which included language, grammar, rhetoric and epistemology, was held necessary for understanding ethics. Its smallest unit was the assertible, a proposition that is either true or false. Chrysippus listed five basic argument forms, called indemonstrables, to which all other arguments reduce, and the Stoics studied paradoxes such as the Liar and the Sorites, or Heap. Along with Aristotle's term logic, their propositional logic was one of the two great systems of logic in the classical world.

In physics the universe is a material reasoning substance, logos, with an active part, a primordial fire or intelligent aether, and a passive part, matter. Each human possesses a portion of this divine logos. In ethics the Stoics taught that virtue is the only good and is enough for eudaimonia, a well-lived life, pursued through the four cardinal virtues of prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice. Health, wealth and pleasure are neither good nor bad in themselves. For Chrysippus the passions, such as distress, fear, pleasure and lust, are errors of judgement that the wise person avoids.

Stoic logic was discussed alongside Aristotle's for around five hundred years. In late antiquity the school declined, its logical writings did not survive, and only elements reached the Middle Ages through Boethius and later commentators. Knowledge of Stoic logic as a system was lost until the 20th century, when logicians such as Jan Łukasiewicz and Benson Mates reappraised it. Early Christian writers used concepts such as logos, virtue and conscience, and in the late 16th century Justus Lipsius sought in Neostoicism to join Stoicism and Christianity. Albert Ellis and Aaron T. Beck drew on Stoic ideas in cognitive psychotherapy.
strabo: Strabo was born around 64 BCE into an affluent family of Amaseia in Pontus whose members had been involved in politics since the reign of Mithridates V. His paternal grandfather served Mithridates VI in the Mithridatic Wars and, as the war drew to a close, turned several Pontic fortresses over to the Romans. Strabo studied rhetoric at Nysa under Aristodemus and came to admire Homer. About the age of 21 he moved to Rome in 44 BCE and stayed until at least 31 BCE, studying philosophy under the Peripatetic Xenarchus and the Stoic Athenodorus Cananites, and grammar under Tyrannion of Amisus, a respected authority on geography.

Strabo's life was marked by travel, made easier by the relative peace of the reign of Augustus. He went to Egypt and Kush, west to the coast of Tuscany and south to Ethiopia, besides Asia Minor and Rome. Around 25 BCE he sailed up the Nile as far as Philae.
